Al-Dahhak said its meaning is "Allah has spoken truthfully." Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: the key to the names of Allah is Muhammad, the truthful of the promise, the maker of the creation. It was also said its meaning is "Muhammad has spoken truthfully."

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Suddi said: **dhi al-dhikr** (ذِي الذِّكْرِ) means the one of enduring honour and eternal renown. Qatada said: the one of admonition for people and guidance for them. It was also said: the one of reminder, for the nations, the stories, the unseen matters, and the laws.

As for the answer to the oath, it is said to be mentioned. The Kufans and al-Zajjaj said it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, that is true, the mutual disputing of the people of the Fire﴾ [Sad: 64]. Al-Farra' said: we do not find this correct in Arabic, because it is too far removed from His saying ﴿By the Qur'an﴾. Al-Akhfash said it is ﴿Each of them denied the messengers﴾. Others said it is ﴿How many generations We destroyed﴾, with the lam omitted, meaning "for you," since the speech became long, as it was omitted in ﴿By the sun﴾ [al-Shams: 1], then He said ﴿He has succeeded﴾ [al-Shams: 9]. Al-Farra' and Tha'lab related this. These opinions must be discarded. It was also said that the answer is **Sad** itself, since its meaning is "Muhammad has spoken truthfully and Allah has spoken truthfully." That **Sad** is the answer to the oath was said by al-Farra' and Tha'lab. This is based on the answer to the oath being placed first, and on the belief that the letter Sad indicates what they mentioned. It was also said the answer is omitted. Al-Hawfi estimated it as "Indeed the truth has come to you" or something like it. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "Indeed, it is inimitable." Ibn 'Atiyya estimated it as "The matter is not as you claim," and similar estimates. It is reported that Qatada and al-Tabari said it is omitted before **bal** (بَلْ, "rather"), and said: this is the correct view. Its estimate is what we mentioned from him. It should be estimated that what is established here is the answer to the Qur'an when He swore by it, which is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Ya Sin. By the wise Qur'an. Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾ [Ya Sin: 1–3]. This estimate is strengthened by the mention of warning here in His saying ﴿They wondered that a warner from among themselves had come to them﴾, while there He said ﴿So that you may warn a people﴾ [Ya Sin: 6]. The mission includes warning and good tidings. **Bal** here marks a transition from this oath and what is sworn about, to the state of the disbelievers' arrogance and opposition in accepting your message and complying with what you brought, and in acknowledging the truth.

Hammad ibn al-Zibriqan, Sawra from al-Kisa'i, Maymun from Abu Ja'far, and al-Jahdari through al-Uqayli read **fi ghirrah** (في غِرَّةٍ), with a ghayn with dots and a ra', meaning in heedlessness and opposition. **Qablihim** (قَبْلِهِمْ) means before these people of great strength and opposition, and this is a warning to them. **Fa-nadaw** (فَنادَوْا) means they cried for help and called out for repentance, said al-Hasan. Or they raised their voices, as it is said: so-and-so is **andaa sawtan**, meaning higher in voice. This happened after witnessing the punishment, when it was no time for benefit. The majority read **wa-la-tu hina** (ولاتَ حِينَ), with the ta' fatha and the nun accusative. According to Sibawayh's view, it works like **laysa**, and its noun is omitted, its estimate being: "and it is not the time, the time of escape or flight." According to al-Akhfash's view, **hina** is the noun of **lat**, which works like **inna**, putting the noun in the accusative and the predicate in the nominative, and the predicate is omitted, its estimate being: "and it is not the time I see of escape." Abu al-Sammal read **wa-latu hinu** (ولاتُ حِينُ), with the ta' damma and the nun nominative. According to Sibawayh's view, **hinu manasin** is the noun of **lat**, and the predicate is omitted. According to al-Akhfash's view, it is the subject, and the predicate is omitted. Isa ibn 'Umar read **wa-la-ti hini** (ولاتِ حِينِ), with the ta' kasra and the nun genitive, as a predicate after **lat**. Its explanation is problematic. Al-Zamakhshari strained greatly in explaining the predicate in his saying:

*They sought our reconciliation, and it was not the time, the time of a moment, so we answered: it is not the time of survival.*

He said: he likened **awan** (أوانَ, "time") to **idh** (إذْ) in his saying: "And you, when you were healthy," in that it is a time from which the genitive complement was cut off and compensated for. The original was: "and it is not the time of reconciliation." If you say: what do you say about **hina manasin**, while the genitive complement is present? I say: he treated the cutting off of the genitive and what is genitive as a compensation for the omitted pronoun, its tanwin being a compensation for the omitted pronoun. Then he built **hin** because it is in apposition to a non-declinable noun. End of quote. This is strained. What appeared to me in explaining this irregular reading and this rare verse, the genitive after **lat**, is that the genitive is by implied **min** (مِن, "from"). It is as if he said: "it is not from the time of escape" and "it is not from the time of reconciliation," just as they used the genitive with it in their saying: **ʿalā kam jidhʿin baytuka** (on how many trunks is your house?), meaning "from a trunk," in the more correct of the two opinions. And just as they said: **lā rajulin jazāhu Allāhu khayran** (no man, may Allah reward him well), meaning "not from a man." The place of "from the time of escape" is nominative, as the noun of **lat** in the sense of **laysa**, just as you say: "it is not from a man standing," and the predicate is omitted. This is according to Sibawayh's view, or as a subject with the predicate omitted, according to al-Akhfash's view. Some of the Arabs said: some Arabs put **lat** in the genitive. Al-Farra' recited:

*And you will surely regret, and it is not the time of a moment of regret.*

( )

[Commentary of Abu Hayyan on Surah 38, verses 1–14, part 2]

Al-Akhfash interpreted *wa-lāta awānin* as elliptical for *wa-lāta ḥīna awānin*, meaning "and there is no time of opportunity," with *ḥīn* omitted and *awān* left in the genitive. Abu Ishaq said it means *wa-lāta awāninā* ("and not our time"), so the word *al-muḍāf ilayhi* (the noun governed by the construct) was omitted. Since it then lost its governing relation, it could not take i'rab (grammatical inflection), so it was given a kasra because two unvowelled letters came together. This is the reading al-Zamakhshari adopted, having taken it from Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj. Al-Mubarrad recited it as *wa-lāta awānun* with a raf'a (nominative ending). From Isa (ibn Umar): *wa-lāta ḥīnun* with a raf'a, and *manāṣ* with a fatḥa. The author of *al-Lawāmiḥ* said: "If that is established, then he may have made *ḥīn* indeclinable on a ḍamma, so there is inversion in the sentence, and he treated it like *qablu* and *ba'du* in being an adverb of termination. He made *manāṣ* indeclinable on a fatḥa together with *lāta*, on the estimate *lāta manāṣa ḥīna*. But *inna* only governs indefinite nouns when it is directly attached to them, without any intervening adverb or other word. It may be that this has a meaning I do not know." End of quote. Isa also recited *wa-lāti* with a kasra on the tā', and *ḥīna* with a naṣb (accusative) on the nūn; the explanation of the accusative of *ḥīna* has already been given.

As for *lāta*, various readings are reported: a fatḥa, a ḍamma and a kasra on the tā', and pausing on it with a tā'. This is the view of Sibawayh, al-Farra', Ibn Kaysan and al-Zajjaj. Al-Kisa'i and al-Mubarrad paused with a hā'. Some people treated the *lā* as the whole word, and they claimed that the tā' was added to *ḥīn*. Abu Ubayda chose this view and mentioned that he had seen it in the *Imam* (the 'Uthmanic codex) with its tā' written joined to *ḥīn*. But what will one make of his saying *wa-lāta sā'ata mandamin* ("and not a moment of regret") and *wa-lāta awānin*?

Al-Kalbi said: "When they fought and were compelled, some of them would say to others, *manāṣ*, meaning 'you must flee.' When the punishment came upon them, they said, *manāṣ*. So God said: ﴿and there is no time for escape﴾." Al-Qushayri said: "On this view the estimate would be: they cried out *manāṣ*, and it was omitted because what follows indicates it, that is, 'it is not the time for your calling out with it.' There is in this a kind of arbitrariness, since every generation that was destroyed would say *manāṣ* at the time of distress." End of quote. Al-Jurjani said: "That is, they cried out at a time when there is no escape, that is, a moment with no refuge and no escape. When he placed *lā* first and delayed *ḥīn*, this required a wāw, as a circumstantial clause requires when it is made into a subject and predicate, like *jā'a Zaydun rākiban* ("Zayd came riding"), then you say *jā'a Zaydun wa-huwa rākibun* ("Zayd came while he was riding"). So *ḥīn* is an adverb of time for the verb ﴿they cried out﴾." End of quote. But that the original of this sentence is "they cried out when there is no escape," and that *ḥīn* is an adverb of time for ﴿they cried out﴾, is a foreign assertion that contradicts the arrangement of the Qur'an. Its meaning in its own arrangement is perfectly clear: the clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase, meaning ﴿they cried out while they were in a time when there was no escape for them﴾.

[p. 385] When God related of the disbelievers that they were in arrogance and opposition, He followed this with what proceeded from them of corrupt words, namely their attributing to Him sorcery and lying. The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun in His words ﴿And the disbelievers said﴾, meaning "and they said," to draw attention to the quality which caused them to wonder, to the point that they attributed to the one who brought guidance and monotheism sorcery and lying.

﴿Has he made the gods into one god?﴾ They said: How can there be one god who provides for everyone and oversees all their affairs? *Ja'ala* here means *ṣayyara* (to make or render) in speech, claim and assertion, and He mentioned their wonder at what is not a matter for wonder. The pronoun in ﴿and they wondered﴾ refers to them, meaning they found it strange that a messenger should come from among themselves. The majority recited ﴿ʿujābun﴾, which is an intensive pattern, like *rajulun ṭiwālun* and *surāʿun* for *ṭawīlun* and *sarīʿun*. ʿAli, al-Sulami, Isa and Ibn Miqsam recited it with a shadda on the jīm, and they said *rajulun kurrāmun* and *ṭaʿǧāmun ṭayyābun*, and this is more emphatic than the light form *fuʿālun*. Muqatil said: *ʿujābun* is the dialect of the Azd Shanu'a. As for those who said ﴿Has he made the gods into one god?﴾, Ibn Abbas said they were the chiefs of Quraysh, and they were twenty-six.

﴿And the chiefs among them set off﴾. The apparent meaning is that they departed from the assembly of Abu Talib, when they had gathered with the Messenger present there and complained about him, as mentioned earlier in the occasion of revelation. There is an omitted element here, which would be: "they were conversing."

﴿saying, Go on﴾. The *an* here explains that omitted element. *Imshū* is a command to walk, that is, to move the feet away from that assembly. Al-Zamakhshari said: *an* here means *ay* ("that, namely"), because those departing from the assembly of discussion must speak and confer about what happened to them, so their departure implies the meaning of saying and commanding to walk, that is, some of them commanded others. It is also said: the chiefs commanded their followers and helpers. It is also permissible for *an* to be verbal (*maṣdariyya*), meaning "and they departed by saying *imshū*." It is also said that the departure here is a rushing into speech and talk, and *an* on this view is explanatory. The command to walk is not meant as the movement of steps, but its meaning is: go on in your way and persist in your conduct. It is also said that *imshū* is a supplication for the acquisition of livestock. It was said that this is weak, because the alif would have to be cut, since one says *amshā al-rajulu* only when he becomes the owner of livestock; moreover this meaning does not fit the verse. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that they said *imshū*, meaning "multiply and gather together," from *mashat al-mar'atu* when a woman's births multiply; and from this comes *al-māshiya* (livestock) for good omen. End of quote. They commanded patience toward the gods, that is, toward worshipping them and holding fast to them.

The indication by His words ﴿Indeed this﴾, meaning the emergence of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his elevation through prophethood, ﴿is surely a thing that is intended﴾. That is, it is intended that we submit to it, or God intends it and decrees its execution, so there is nothing for us but patience. Or: this matter is one of the calamities of the age that is intended for us, so there is no escaping it. Or: your religion is a thing that is sought, that is, it is pursued in order to be taken from you and for you to be overcome by it. These are four possibilities. Al-Qaffal said: This is a phrase used for threat and intimidation. The meaning is: his purpose in this statement is not to establish the religion, but his aim is to dominate us, so that he may rule over our property and children as he wishes.

﴿We have not heard of this in the last religion﴾. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Muqatil said: the religion of the Christians, because in it is the Trinity, and it does not affirm the oneness of God. Mujahid and Qatada said: the religion of the Arabs, namely Quraysh and its ilk. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the religion of the Jews and the Christians; the Jews associated Ezra with God and the Christians made God a trinity. It is also said: "the last religion" refers to what they used to hear would appear at the end of time, for before the mission (*mab'ath*) people used to sense that a prophet would emerge and a new religion and faith would arise. What confirms this view is what is reported of the sayings of the Jewish rabbis (*aḥbār*) who were in the monasteries, and what is reported from the soothsayers such as Shiqq and Sutayh and others, and what the Children of Israel used to believe, that it would come from among them. It is also said: "in the last religion" means: we have not heard from the People of the Book or the soothsayers that in the last religion there would arise the oneness of God.

﴿This is nothing but a fabrication﴾, that is, a contrivance and a lie.

﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?﴾ They denied that he should be singled out for honour from among their nobles, and that the Book should descend upon him from among them. This denial arises from a great envy that their hearts harboured and their tongues expressed.

﴿Nay, but they are in doubt about My Reminder﴾, that is, about the Qur'an which I sent down upon My Messenger; they are in doubt about it. The statement that they are in doubt implies that their words ﴿This is nothing but a fabrication﴾ are false. [p. 386]

﴿Nay, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾, that is, not yet. When they taste it, they will know that what he brought is true, and their doubt will leave them.

﴿Or do they have the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord?﴾ That is, they do not dispose of the treasuries of mercy, so that they give to whom they wish and withhold from whom they wish, and choose for the message whomever they want. Rather, it is the Mighty, who cannot be overcome, the Bestower, who owns and disposes of it, who gives what He wills to whom He wills. When He asked the question as a denial in His words ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord?﴾, and this was evidence of their lacking any disposal over the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord, He brought the denial and reproach by negating something more general, saying: ﴿Or do they have dominion over the heavens and the earth?﴾, meaning: they have no share of that at all.

﴿Then let them ascend﴾, that is, if they have any share of that, then let them climb ﴿by means of ropes﴾, the ways leading to the heaven and the ladders by which one may reach the management of the world, so that they may place the message in whomever they choose. Then He diminished and belittled them, and informed them of what their affair would come to: defeat and failure. It is said that *mā* is superfluous; it is also permissible that it is a descriptive, in which case it is intended for exaltation by way of mockery of them, or for belittlement, since *mā* as a qualifier is used in both of these senses. *Hunālika* is an adverb of place indicating what is distant. The apparent meaning is that it refers to the place in which they conferred with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with those previously mentioned words, namely Mecca. This would then be a report of the unseen about their defeat in Mecca on the day of the Conquest. The meaning is that they will become defeated in Mecca on the day of the Conquest. It is also said: *hunālika* refers to the climbing by ropes, meaning: these people, if they attempt that, are a defeated army. It is also said: *hunālika* refers to the whole collection of idols and their support, meaning they are a defeated army on this path. Mujahid and Qatada said: it refers to the day of Badr, and that was an unseen matter which God informed of through His Messenger. It is also said: it refers to the siege of the Battle of the Trench in Medina. Al-Zamakhshari said: *hunālika* refers to the place where they had put themselves forward to take on such a great utterance, from their saying to one who appoints someone to a task that is not his: "you are not there" (*laista hunālika*). End of quote. *Hunālika* may be in the position of a qualifier for *jundun* ("an army"), meaning "present there." It may also be connected to *mahzūmun* ("defeated"), and *jundun* would then be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they are an army," and *mahzūmun* is its predicate. Abu al-Baqa' said: *jundun* is the subject, *mā* is superfluous, *hunālika* is an adjective, and *mahzūmun* is the predicate. End of quote. This is remote, because it is separated from the speech that precedes it.

The meaning of ﴿of the factions﴾ is: among the factions who were zealous in falsehood and denied the messengers. When God mentioned that He had destroyed many generations before Quraysh because they denied their messengers, He here recounted those among them who have a connection with His punishment.

﴿Dhū al-Awtād﴾, that is, the possessor of the stakes (*awtād*). Its origin is the stability of a tent stretched with its pegs. Al-Afwah al-Awdi said:

"A house is not built except upon pillars,
and there is no support if stakes are not driven in."

So it was borrowed for the stability of might and kingship and the uprightness of affairs, as al-Aswad said:

"In the shade of a kingdom whose stakes are firmly set."

Al-Zamakhshari said this, having taken it from the words of others. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ata' said: he had stakes and wooden frames with which and upon which he played. Al-Suddi said: he used to kill people with stakes and nail them into the ground with them. Al-Dahhak said: it means the great, firmly-built structures. It is also said: it is an expression for the great number of his tents and the magnitude of his armies. It is also said: he would spread the one being tortured between four pillars, with each of his extremities bound to a pillar, and in each pillar an iron stake was driven, and he would leave him until he died. The same meaning is reported from al-Hasan and Mujahid. It is also said: he would stretch him between four stakes in the ground and release scorpions and snakes upon him. It is also said: he would fasten them with four stakes, then raise a rock and drop it upon him so that it crushed him. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas, in a report from Ata', said: the stakes are the soldiers, who strengthen his kingship as a stake strengthens a thing. It is also said: he built a minaret upon which he slaughtered people, as reported by Ibn Jubayr.

﴿Those are the factions﴾, that is, those who formed factions against their prophets, just as Quraysh formed factions against the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The apparent meaning is that the indication by *ulā'ika* ("those") is to the nearest previously mentioned, namely the people of Noah and those joined with them. In this there is exaltation of their status and elevation of them above those who formed factions against the Messenger of God, meaning: these great ones, when they denied, were punished, [p. 387] and so are you.

﴿Each of them merely denied the messengers, so My punishment was justly due.﴾ So their punishment became necessary. The people of Nuh (Noah) denied him and harmed him, so they were drowned. The people of Hud were destroyed by the wind. Pharaoh was drowned. Thamud were destroyed by the Blast. The people of Lut (Lot) were destroyed by being swallowed up in the earth. And the People of the Thicket (al-Aykah) were destroyed by the punishment of the Day of the Canopy. The meaning of ﴿Each of them﴾ is: whatever came from the people of Nuh and those after them. ﴿So My punishment was justly due﴾ means: their punishment became necessary, and likewise it is due upon you, O deniers of the Messenger. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Those are the factions﴾. By this demonstrative he intended to inform that the factions whom the defeated army was made up of are the very same ones, and that they are the ones from whom denial was found. He mentioned their denial first in the declarative sentence in a general manner, then came with the exceptive sentence and made it clear in it that each one of the factions denied the messengers, because when they denied one of them, they denied all of them. In the repetition of the denial and its clarification after its generality, and in the variety in its repetition, first with the declarative sentence and second with the exception, and in what the exceptive construction contains of emphasis and specification, there are kinds of intensification that record against them that they deserve the most severe and most complete punishment. Then he said: ﴿So My punishment was justly due﴾, meaning: therefore it became necessary that I punish them with their just punishment. End.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 38, verses 1–14 (part 1 of 3):**

Surah Sad: eighty-eight verses, and it is Meccan.

(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.)

﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder.﴾ ﴿Rather, those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition.﴾ ﴿How many generations before them did We destroy, and they called out, but it was no time for escape.﴾ ﴿They wondered that a warner from among themselves had come to them, and the disbelievers said, "This is a sorcerer, a liar."﴾ ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing.﴾ ﴿And the chiefs among them went off, saying, "Walk on, and be patient with your gods. Indeed, this is something intended.﴾ ﴿We have not heard of this in the last religion. This is nothing but a fabrication.﴾ ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him from among us?" Rather, they are in doubt about My reminder. Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment.﴾ ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord, the Mighty, the Bestower?﴾ ﴿Or do they have dominion over the heavens and the earth and what is between them? Then let them climb up by the means.﴾ ﴿A host of confederates, routed, is there.﴾ ﴿The people of Noah, and 'Ad, and Pharaoh, the lord of the stakes, denied before them.﴾ ﴿And Thamud, and the people of Lot, and the companions of the thicket. Those are the confederates.﴾ ﴿Each of them denied the messengers, so My punishment was justified.﴾.

*Commentary:* The word **lat** (لاتَ) is (لا), to which the letter **ta'** has been attached, as it was attached in **thumma** (ثُمَّ) and **rubba** (رُبَّ), so they said **thummata** (ثُمَّتْ) and **rubbata** (رُبَّتْ). According to Sibawayh's view, it works like **laysa** (لَيْسَ, "is not"). According to al-Akhfash's view, it works like **inna** (إنَّ, "indeed"). If the word after it is in the nominative, then according to him it is a subject (mubtada'). It has rulings that are mentioned in the science of grammar (nahw), and some of them will come here when the readings in which it appears are mentioned. **Al-manas** (المَناصُ) means escape and rescue. It is said: **nassahu yanusuhu**, meaning he escaped from him. Al-Farra' said: **al-nawsu** means retreat. It is said: **nasa 'an qarnihi yanusu nawsan wa manasan**, meaning he fled and swerved. He quoted Imru' al-Qays:

*Does the memory of Salma make you retreat, and seek escape, the one who seeks refuge?*

Harithah ibn Badr said:

*When I shorten his rein, the wild ass seeks escape with my hand, and desires the running of the mule.*

Al-Jawhari said: **istanasa** means he retreated. Al-Nahhas said: **nasa yanusu** means he advanced. **Al-watad** (الوَتَدُ) is well known, and the kasra on the ta' is more common than the fatha. It is said: **watad watid**, just as it is said **shughl shaghil**. Al-Asma'i said, quoting:

*They met on the water a stake firmly driven, and it did not fail to keep its appointment.*

They also said **wadd**, and they assimilated it. A poet said:

*It brings out the love when it is stirred, and hides it when it is restrained.*

They also said **datt**, assimilating by changing the first dal into a ta', and in it the second letter is changed to match the first, which is rare.

(p-382)

[The Qur'anic text of verses 1–14 is repeated here as above.]

This surah is Meccan. Its connection to what precedes it is that when He mentioned that the disbelievers used to say, ﴿If we had a reminder from the former peoples﴾ [al-Saffat: 168], they would have devoted worship purely to Allah. He informed that the reminder had come to them, and they disbelieved in it. In this surah He began with an oath by the Qur'an, because it is the reminder that came to them. He informed about them that they are disbelievers, and that they are in arrogance and opposition to the Messenger who brought it. Then He mentioned those whom He destroyed from the generations who opposed the messengers, so that they might take warning.

It is narrated that when Abu Talib fell ill, the Quraysh came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and at the head of Abu Talib there was a gathering of men. Abu Jahl stood up in order to prevent him, and they complained about him to Abu Talib. He said, "O son of my brother, what do you want from your people?" He said, "O uncle, I only want from them a word by which the Arabs will submit to them, and by which the non-Arabs will pay them the jizya." He said, "And what is the word?" He said, "One word." He said, "And what is it?" He said, "There is no god but Allah." They stood up and said, "Has he made the gods into one God?" (p-383) He said: then the Qur'an was revealed concerning them: ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾, until it reached ﴿This is nothing but a fabrication﴾.

The majority read **Sad** (ص) with the dal sukun. Ubayy, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu al-Sammal, Ibn Abi 'Abla, and Nasr ibn 'Asim read **Sadi** (صادِ), with the dal kasra. The apparent reason for the kasra is the meeting of two sukun letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn, the meeting of two consonants without a vowel between them). It is one of the letters of the alphabet, like qaf and nun. Al-Hasan said it is an imperative from **sada**, meaning to oppose, and from it comes **al-sada**, which is what opposes the voice in hard empty places free of bodies. That is, oppose with your deed the Qur'an. He also said: **sadaytu** means I conversed, that is, he conversed, and this is close to the first opinion.

Isa, Mahbub from Abu 'Amr, and a group read **Sada** (صادَ) with the dal fatha. Likewise they read **Qaf wa Nun** (قافَ ونُونَ) with the fatha on the fa' and the nun. It is said the fatha is for the meeting of two sukun letters, seeking lightness. It is also said that it is in the accusative as something sworn by, with the particle of oath dropped, as in the saying **Allahi la'af'alanna** (by Allah I will surely do it). It is the name of the surah, and it is not declined because it is a proper noun and feminine. Whoever read **Sadin** with the kasra and tanwin declined it, interpreting it as the Book or the Revelation. This is Ibn Abi Ishaq in one narration. Al-Hasan also read **Sadun** with the dal damma. If it is the name of the surah, then it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: this is Sad. This is the reading of Ibn al-Sumayfa' and Harun al-A'war. They also read **Qafu wa Nunu** (ق ونُونُ) with the damma on the fa' and the nun. It was said: it is a letter indicating a meaning from a verb or from a noun. Al-Dahhak said its meaning is "Allah has spoken truthfully." Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: the key to the names of Allah is Muhammad, the truthful of the promise, the maker of the creation. It was also said its meaning is "Muhammad has spoken truthfully."

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Suddi said: **dhi al-dhikr** (ذِي الذِّكْرِ) means the one of enduring honour and eternal renown. Qatada said: the one of admonition for people and guidance for them. It was also said: the one of reminder, for the nations, the stories, the unseen matters, and the laws.

As for the answer to the oath, it is said to be mentioned. The Kufans and al-Zajjaj said it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, that is true, the mutual disputing of the people of the Fire﴾ [Sad: 64]. Al-Farra' said: we do not find this correct in Arabic, because it is too far removed from His saying ﴿By the Qur'an﴾. Al-Akhfash said it is ﴿Each of them denied the messengers﴾. Others said it is ﴿How many generations We destroyed﴾, with the lam omitted, meaning "for you," since the speech became long, as it was omitted in ﴿By the sun﴾ [al-Shams: 1], then He said ﴿He has succeeded﴾ [al-Shams: 9]. Al-Farra' and Tha'lab related this. These opinions must be discarded. It was also said that the answer is **Sad** itself, since its meaning is "Muhammad has spoken truthfully and Allah has spoken truthfully." That **Sad** is the answer to the oath was said by al-Farra' and Tha'lab. This is based on the answer to the oath being placed first, and on the belief that the letter Sad indicates what they mentioned. It was also said the answer is omitted. Al-Hawfi estimated it as "Indeed the truth has come to you" or something like it. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "Indeed, it is inimitable." Ibn 'Atiyya estimated it as "The matter is not as you claim," and similar estimates. It is reported that Qatada and al-Tabari said it is omitted before **bal** (بَلْ, "rather"), and said: this is the correct view. Its estimate is what we mentioned from him. It should be estimated that what is established here is the answer to the Qur'an when He swore by it, which is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Ya Sin. By the wise Qur'an. Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾ [Ya Sin: 1–3]. This estimate is strengthened by the mention of warning here in His saying ﴿They wondered that a warner from among themselves had come to them﴾, while there He said ﴿So that you may warn a people﴾ [Ya Sin: 6]. The mission includes warning and good tidings. **Bal** here marks a transition from this oath and what is sworn about, to the state of the disbelievers' arrogance and opposition in accepting your message and complying with what you brought, and in acknowledging the truth.

Hammad ibn al-Zibriqan, Sawra from al-Kisa'i, Maymun from Abu Ja'far, and al-Jahdari through al-Uqayli read **fi ghirrah** (في غِرَّةٍ), with a ghayn with dots and a ra', meaning in heedlessness and opposition. **Qablihim** (قَبْلِهِمْ) means before these people of great strength and opposition, and this is a warning to them. **Fa-nadaw** (فَنادَوْا) means they cried for help and called out for repentance, said al-Hasan. Or they raised their voices, as it is said: so-and-so is **andaa sawtan**, meaning higher in voice. This happened after witnessing the punishment, when it was no time for benefit. The majority read **wa-la-tu hina** (ولاتَ حِينَ), with the ta' fatha and the nun accusative. According to Sibawayh's view, it works like **laysa**, and its noun is omitted, its estimate being: "and it is not the time, the time of escape or flight." According to al-Akhfash's view, **hina** is the noun of **lat**, which works like **inna**, putting the noun in the accusative and the predicate in the nominative, and the predicate is omitted, its estimate being: "and it is not the time I see of escape." Abu al-Sammal read **wa-latu hinu** (ولاتُ حِينُ), with the ta' damma and the nun nominative. According to Sibawayh's view, **hinu manasin** is the noun of **lat**, and the predicate is omitted. According to al-Akhfash's view, it is the subject, and the predicate is omitted. Isa ibn 'Umar read **wa-la-ti hini** (ولاتِ حِينِ), with the ta' kasra and the nun genitive, as a predicate after **lat**. Its explanation is problematic. Al-Zamakhshari strained greatly in explaining the predicate in his saying:

*They sought our reconciliation, and it was not the time, the time of a moment, so we answered: it is not the time of survival.*

He said: he likened **awan** (أوانَ, "time") to **idh** (إذْ) in his saying: "And you, when you were healthy," in that it is a time from which the genitive complement was cut off and compensated for. The original was: "and it is not the time of reconciliation." If you say: what do you say about **hina manasin**, while the genitive complement is present? I say: he treated the cutting off of the genitive and what is genitive as a compensation for the omitted pronoun, its tanwin being a compensation for the omitted pronoun. Then he built **hin** because it is in apposition to a non-declinable noun. End of quote. This is strained. What appeared to me in explaining this irregular reading and this rare verse, the genitive after **lat**, is that the genitive is by implied **min** (مِن, "from"). It is as if he said: "it is not from the time of escape" and "it is not from the time of reconciliation," just as they used the genitive with it in their saying: **ʿalā kam jidhʿin baytuka** (on how many trunks is your house?), meaning "from a trunk," in the more correct of the two opinions. And just as they said: **lā rajulin jazāhu Allāhu khayran** (no man, may Allah reward him well), meaning "not from a man." The place of "from the time of escape" is nominative, as the noun of **lat** in the sense of **laysa**, just as you say: "it is not from a man standing," and the predicate is omitted. This is according to Sibawayh's view, or as a subject with the predicate omitted, according to al-Akhfash's view. Some of the Arabs said: some Arabs put **lat** in the genitive. Al-Farra' recited:

*And you will surely regret, and it is not the time of a moment of regret.*

( )

[Commentary of Abu Hayyan on Surah 38, verses 1–14, part 2]

Al-Akhfash interpreted *wa-lāta awānin* as elliptical for *wa-lāta ḥīna awānin*, meaning "and there is no time of opportunity," with *ḥīn* omitted and *awān* left in the genitive. Abu Ishaq said it means *wa-lāta awāninā* ("and not our time"), so the word *al-muḍāf ilayhi* (the noun governed by the construct) was omitted. Since it then lost its governing relation, it could not take i'rab (grammatical inflection), so it was given a kasra because two unvowelled letters came together. This is the reading al-Zamakhshari adopted, having taken it from Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj. Al-Mubarrad recited it as *wa-lāta awānun* with a raf'a (nominative ending). From Isa (ibn Umar): *wa-lāta ḥīnun* with a raf'a, and *manāṣ* with a fatḥa. The author of *al-Lawāmiḥ* said: "If that is established, then he may have made *ḥīn* indeclinable on a ḍamma, so there is inversion in the sentence, and he treated it like *qablu* and *ba'du* in being an adverb of termination. He made *manāṣ* indeclinable on a fatḥa together with *lāta*, on the estimate *lāta manāṣa ḥīna*. But *inna* only governs indefinite nouns when it is directly attached to them, without any intervening adverb or other word. It may be that this has a meaning I do not know." End of quote. Isa also recited *wa-lāti* with a kasra on the tā', and *ḥīna* with a naṣb (accusative) on the nūn; the explanation of the accusative of *ḥīna* has already been given.

As for *lāta*, various readings are reported: a fatḥa, a ḍamma and a kasra on the tā', and pausing on it with a tā'. This is the view of Sibawayh, al-Farra', Ibn Kaysan and al-Zajjaj. Al-Kisa'i and al-Mubarrad paused with a hā'. Some people treated the *lā* as the whole word, and they claimed that the tā' was added to *ḥīn*. Abu Ubayda chose this view and mentioned that he had seen it in the *Imam* (the 'Uthmanic codex) with its tā' written joined to *ḥīn*. But what will one make of his saying *wa-lāta sā'ata mandamin* ("and not a moment of regret") and *wa-lāta awānin*?

Al-Kalbi said: "When they fought and were compelled, some of them would say to others, *manāṣ*, meaning 'you must flee.' When the punishment came upon them, they said, *manāṣ*. So God said: ﴿and there is no time for escape﴾." Al-Qushayri said: "On this view the estimate would be: they cried out *manāṣ*, and it was omitted because what follows indicates it, that is, 'it is not the time for your calling out with it.' There is in this a kind of arbitrariness, since every generation that was destroyed would say *manāṣ* at the time of distress." End of quote. Al-Jurjani said: "That is, they cried out at a time when there is no escape, that is, a moment with no refuge and no escape. When he placed *lā* first and delayed *ḥīn*, this required a wāw, as a circumstantial clause requires when it is made into a subject and predicate, like *jā'a Zaydun rākiban* ("Zayd came riding"), then you say *jā'a Zaydun wa-huwa rākibun* ("Zayd came while he was riding"). So *ḥīn* is an adverb of time for the verb ﴿they cried out﴾." End of quote. But that the original of this sentence is "they cried out when there is no escape," and that *ḥīn* is an adverb of time for ﴿they cried out﴾, is a foreign assertion that contradicts the arrangement of the Qur'an. Its meaning in its own arrangement is perfectly clear: the clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase, meaning ﴿they cried out while they were in a time when there was no escape for them﴾.

[p. 385] When God related of the disbelievers that they were in arrogance and opposition, He followed this with what proceeded from them of corrupt words, namely their attributing to Him sorcery and lying. The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun in His words ﴿And the disbelievers said﴾, meaning "and they said," to draw attention to the quality which caused them to wonder, to the point that they attributed to the one who brought guidance and monotheism sorcery and lying.

﴿Has he made the gods into one god?﴾ They said: How can there be one god who provides for everyone and oversees all their affairs? *Ja'ala* here means *ṣayyara* (to make or render) in speech, claim and assertion, and He mentioned their wonder at what is not a matter for wonder. The pronoun in ﴿and they wondered﴾ refers to them, meaning they found it strange that a messenger should come from among themselves. The majority recited ﴿ʿujābun﴾, which is an intensive pattern, like *rajulun ṭiwālun* and *surāʿun* for *ṭawīlun* and *sarīʿun*. ʿAli, al-Sulami, Isa and Ibn Miqsam recited it with a shadda on the jīm, and they said *rajulun kurrāmun* and *ṭaʿǧāmun ṭayyābun*, and this is more emphatic than the light form *fuʿālun*. Muqatil said: *ʿujābun* is the dialect of the Azd Shanu'a. As for those who said ﴿Has he made the gods into one god?﴾, Ibn Abbas said they were the chiefs of Quraysh, and they were twenty-six.

﴿And the chiefs among them set off﴾. The apparent meaning is that they departed from the assembly of Abu Talib, when they had gathered with the Messenger present there and complained about him, as mentioned earlier in the occasion of revelation. There is an omitted element here, which would be: "they were conversing."

﴿saying, Go on﴾. The *an* here explains that omitted element. *Imshū* is a command to walk, that is, to move the feet away from that assembly. Al-Zamakhshari said: *an* here means *ay* ("that, namely"), because those departing from the assembly of discussion must speak and confer about what happened to them, so their departure implies the meaning of saying and commanding to walk, that is, some of them commanded others. It is also said: the chiefs commanded their followers and helpers. It is also permissible for *an* to be verbal (*maṣdariyya*), meaning "and they departed by saying *imshū*." It is also said that the departure here is a rushing into speech and talk, and *an* on this view is explanatory. The command to walk is not meant as the movement of steps, but its meaning is: go on in your way and persist in your conduct. It is also said that *imshū* is a supplication for the acquisition of livestock. It was said that this is weak, because the alif would have to be cut, since one says *amshā al-rajulu* only when he becomes the owner of livestock; moreover this meaning does not fit the verse. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that they said *imshū*, meaning "multiply and gather together," from *mashat al-mar'atu* when a woman's births multiply; and from this comes *al-māshiya* (livestock) for good omen. End of quote. They commanded patience toward the gods, that is, toward worshipping them and holding fast to them.

The indication by His words ﴿Indeed this﴾, meaning the emergence of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his elevation through prophethood, ﴿is surely a thing that is intended﴾. That is, it is intended that we submit to it, or God intends it and decrees its execution, so there is nothing for us but patience. Or: this matter is one of the calamities of the age that is intended for us, so there is no escaping it. Or: your religion is a thing that is sought, that is, it is pursued in order to be taken from you and for you to be overcome by it. These are four possibilities. Al-Qaffal said: This is a phrase used for threat and intimidation. The meaning is: his purpose in this statement is not to establish the religion, but his aim is to dominate us, so that he may rule over our property and children as he wishes.

﴿We have not heard of this in the last religion﴾. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Muqatil said: the religion of the Christians, because in it is the Trinity, and it does not affirm the oneness of God. Mujahid and Qatada said: the religion of the Arabs, namely Quraysh and its ilk. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the religion of the Jews and the Christians; the Jews associated Ezra with God and the Christians made God a trinity. It is also said: "the last religion" refers to what they used to hear would appear at the end of time, for before the mission (*mab'ath*) people used to sense that a prophet would emerge and a new religion and faith would arise. What confirms this view is what is reported of the sayings of the Jewish rabbis (*aḥbār*) who were in the monasteries, and what is reported from the soothsayers such as Shiqq and Sutayh and others, and what the Children of Israel used to believe, that it would come from among them. It is also said: "in the last religion" means: we have not heard from the People of the Book or the soothsayers that in the last religion there would arise the oneness of God.

﴿This is nothing but a fabrication﴾, that is, a contrivance and a lie.

﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?﴾ They denied that he should be singled out for honour from among their nobles, and that the Book should descend upon him from among them. This denial arises from a great envy that their hearts harboured and their tongues expressed.

﴿Nay, but they are in doubt about My Reminder﴾, that is, about the Qur'an which I sent down upon My Messenger; they are in doubt about it. The statement that they are in doubt implies that their words ﴿This is nothing but a fabrication﴾ are false. [p. 386]

﴿Nay, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾, that is, not yet. When they taste it, they will know that what he brought is true, and their doubt will leave them.

﴿Or do they have the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord?﴾ That is, they do not dispose of the treasuries of mercy, so that they give to whom they wish and withhold from whom they wish, and choose for the message whomever they want. Rather, it is the Mighty, who cannot be overcome, the Bestower, who owns and disposes of it, who gives what He wills to whom He wills. When He asked the question as a denial in His words ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord?﴾, and this was evidence of their lacking any disposal over the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord, He brought the denial and reproach by negating something more general, saying: ﴿Or do they have dominion over the heavens and the earth?﴾, meaning: they have no share of that at all.

﴿Then let them ascend﴾, that is, if they have any share of that, then let them climb ﴿by means of ropes﴾, the ways leading to the heaven and the ladders by which one may reach the management of the world, so that they may place the message in whomever they choose. Then He diminished and belittled them, and informed them of what their affair would come to: defeat and failure. It is said that *mā* is superfluous; it is also permissible that it is a descriptive, in which case it is intended for exaltation by way of mockery of them, or for belittlement, since *mā* as a qualifier is used in both of these senses. *Hunālika* is an adverb of place indicating what is distant. The apparent meaning is that it refers to the place in which they conferred with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with those previously mentioned words, namely Mecca. This would then be a report of the unseen about their defeat in Mecca on the day of the Conquest. The meaning is that they will become defeated in Mecca on the day of the Conquest. It is also said: *hunālika* refers to the climbing by ropes, meaning: these people, if they attempt that, are a defeated army. It is also said: *hunālika* refers to the whole collection of idols and their support, meaning they are a defeated army on this path. Mujahid and Qatada said: it refers to the day of Badr, and that was an unseen matter which God informed of through His Messenger. It is also said: it refers to the siege of the Battle of the Trench in Medina. Al-Zamakhshari said: *hunālika* refers to the place where they had put themselves forward to take on such a great utterance, from their saying to one who appoints someone to a task that is not his: "you are not there" (*laista hunālika*). End of quote. *Hunālika* may be in the position of a qualifier for *jundun* ("an army"), meaning "present there." It may also be connected to *mahzūmun* ("defeated"), and *jundun* would then be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they are an army," and *mahzūmun* is its predicate. Abu al-Baqa' said: *jundun* is the subject, *mā* is superfluous, *hunālika* is an adjective, and *mahzūmun* is the predicate. End of quote. This is remote, because it is separated from the speech that precedes it.

The meaning of ﴿of the factions﴾ is: among the factions who were zealous in falsehood and denied the messengers. When God mentioned that He had destroyed many generations before Quraysh because they denied their messengers, He here recounted those among them who have a connection with His punishment.

﴿Dhū al-Awtād﴾, that is, the possessor of the stakes (*awtād*). Its origin is the stability of a tent stretched with its pegs. Al-Afwah al-Awdi said:

"A house is not built except upon pillars,
and there is no support if stakes are not driven in."

So it was borrowed for the stability of might and kingship and the uprightness of affairs, as al-Aswad said:

"In the shade of a kingdom whose stakes are firmly set."

Al-Zamakhshari said this, having taken it from the words of others. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ata' said: he had stakes and wooden frames with which and upon which he played. Al-Suddi said: he used to kill people with stakes and nail them into the ground with them. Al-Dahhak said: it means the great, firmly-built structures. It is also said: it is an expression for the great number of his tents and the magnitude of his armies. It is also said: he would spread the one being tortured between four pillars, with each of his extremities bound to a pillar, and in each pillar an iron stake was driven, and he would leave him until he died. The same meaning is reported from al-Hasan and Mujahid. It is also said: he would stretch him between four stakes in the ground and release scorpions and snakes upon him. It is also said: he would fasten them with four stakes, then raise a rock and drop it upon him so that it crushed him. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas, in a report from Ata', said: the stakes are the soldiers, who strengthen his kingship as a stake strengthens a thing. It is also said: he built a minaret upon which he slaughtered people, as reported by Ibn Jubayr.

﴿Those are the factions﴾, that is, those who formed factions against their prophets, just as Quraysh formed factions against the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The apparent meaning is that the indication by *ulā'ika* ("those") is to the nearest previously mentioned, namely the people of Noah and those joined with them. In this there is exaltation of their status and elevation of them above those who formed factions against the Messenger of God, meaning: these great ones, when they denied, were punished, [p. 387] and so are you.

﴿Each of them merely denied the messengers, so My punishment was justly due.﴾ So their punishment became necessary. The people of Nuh (Noah) denied him and harmed him, so they were drowned. The people of Hud were destroyed by the wind. Pharaoh was drowned. Thamud were destroyed by the Blast. The people of Lut (Lot) were destroyed by being swallowed up in the earth. And the People of the Thicket (al-Aykah) were destroyed by the punishment of the Day of the Canopy. The meaning of ﴿Each of them﴾ is: whatever came from the people of Nuh and those after them. ﴿So My punishment was justly due﴾ means: their punishment became necessary, and likewise it is due upon you, O deniers of the Messenger. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Those are the factions﴾. By this demonstrative he intended to inform that the factions whom the defeated army was made up of are the very same ones, and that they are the ones from whom denial was found. He mentioned their denial first in the declarative sentence in a general manner, then came with the exceptive sentence and made it clear in it that each one of the factions denied the messengers, because when they denied one of them, they denied all of them. In the repetition of the denial and its clarification after its generality, and in the variety in its repetition, first with the declarative sentence and second with the exception, and in what the exceptive construction contains of emphasis and specification, there are kinds of intensification that record against them that they deserve the most severe and most complete punishment. Then he said: ﴿So My punishment was justly due﴾, meaning: therefore it became necessary that I punish them with their just punishment. End.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 38, verses 1–14 (part 1 of 3):**

Surah Sad: eighty-eight verses, and it is Meccan.

(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.)

﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder.﴾ ﴿Rather, those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition.﴾ ﴿How many generations before them did We destroy, and they called out, but it was no time for escape.﴾ ﴿They wondered that a warner from among themselves had come to them, and the disbelievers said, "This is a sorcerer, a liar."﴾ ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing.﴾ ﴿And the chiefs among them went off, saying, "Walk on, and be patient with your gods. Indeed, this is something intended.﴾ ﴿We have not heard of this in the last religion. This is nothing but a fabrication.﴾ ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him from among us?" Rather, they are in doubt about My reminder. Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment.﴾ ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord, the Mighty, the Bestower?﴾ ﴿Or do they have dominion over the heavens and the earth and what is between them? Then let them climb up by the means.﴾ ﴿A host of confederates, routed, is there.﴾ ﴿The people of Noah, and 'Ad, and Pharaoh, the lord of the stakes, denied before them.﴾ ﴿And Thamud, and the people of Lot, and the companions of the thicket. Those are the confederates.﴾ ﴿Each of them denied the messengers, so My punishment was justified.﴾.

*Commentary:* The word **lat** (لاتَ) is (لا), to which the letter **ta'** has been attached, as it was attached in **thumma** (ثُمَّ) and **rubba** (رُبَّ), so they said **thummata** (ثُمَّتْ) and **rubbata** (رُبَّتْ). According to Sibawayh's view, it works like **laysa** (لَيْسَ, "is not"). According to al-Akhfash's view, it works like **inna** (إنَّ, "indeed"). If the word after it is in the nominative, then according to him it is a subject (mubtada'). It has rulings that are mentioned in the science of grammar (nahw), and some of them will come here when the readings in which it appears are mentioned. **Al-manas** (المَناصُ) means escape and rescue. It is said: **nassahu yanusuhu**, meaning he escaped from him. Al-Farra' said: **al-nawsu** means retreat. It is said: **nasa 'an qarnihi yanusu nawsan wa manasan**, meaning he fled and swerved. He quoted Imru' al-Qays:

*Does the memory of Salma make you retreat, and seek escape, the one who seeks refuge?*

Harithah ibn Badr said:

*When I shorten his rein, the wild ass seeks escape with my hand, and desires the running of the mule.*

Al-Jawhari said: **istanasa** means he retreated. Al-Nahhas said: **nasa yanusu** means he advanced. **Al-watad** (الوَتَدُ) is well known, and the kasra on the ta' is more common than the fatha. It is said: **watad watid**, just as it is said **shughl shaghil**. Al-Asma'i said, quoting:

*They met on the water a stake firmly driven, and it did not fail to keep its appointment.*

They also said **wadd**, and they assimilated it. A poet said:

*It brings out the love when it is stirred, and hides it when it is restrained.*

They also said **datt**, assimilating by changing the first dal into a ta', and in it the second letter is changed to match the first, which is rare.

(p-382)

[The Qur'anic text of verses 1–14 is repeated here as above.]

This surah is Meccan. Its connection to what precedes it is that when He mentioned that the disbelievers used to say, ﴿If we had a reminder from the former peoples﴾ [al-Saffat: 168], they would have devoted worship purely to Allah. He informed that the reminder had come to them, and they disbelieved in it. In this surah He began with an oath by the Qur'an, because it is the reminder that came to them. He informed about them that they are disbelievers, and that they are in arrogance and opposition to the Messenger who brought it. Then He mentioned those whom He destroyed from the generations who opposed the messengers, so that they might take warning.

It is narrated that when Abu Talib fell ill, the Quraysh came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and at the head of Abu Talib there was a gathering of men. Abu Jahl stood up in order to prevent him, and they complained about him to Abu Talib. He said, "O son of my brother, what do you want from your people?" He said, "O uncle, I only want from them a word by which the Arabs will submit to them, and by which the non-Arabs will pay them the jizya." He said, "And what is the word?" He said, "One word." He said, "And what is it?" He said, "There is no god but Allah." They stood up and said, "Has he made the gods into one God?" (p-383) He said: then the Qur'an was revealed concerning them: ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾, until it reached ﴿This is nothing but a fabrication﴾.

The majority read **Sad** (ص) with the dal sukun. Ubayy, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu al-Sammal, Ibn Abi 'Abla, and Nasr ibn 'Asim read **Sadi** (صادِ), with the dal kasra. The apparent reason for the kasra is the meeting of two sukun letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn, the meeting of two consonants without a vowel between them). It is one of the letters of the alphabet, like qaf and nun. Al-Hasan said it is an imperative from **sada**, meaning to oppose, and from it comes **al-sada**, which is what opposes the voice in hard empty places free of bodies. That is, oppose with your deed the Qur'an. He also said: **sadaytu** means I conversed, that is, he conversed, and this is close to the first opinion.

Isa, Mahbub from Abu 'Amr, and a group read **Sada** (صادَ) with the dal fatha. Likewise they read **Qaf wa Nun** (قافَ ونُونَ) with the fatha on the fa' and the nun. It is said the fatha is for the meeting of two sukun letters, seeking lightness. It is also said that it is in the accusative as something sworn by, with the particle of oath dropped, as in the saying **Allahi la'af'alanna** (by Allah I will surely do it). It is the name of the surah, and it is not declined because it is a proper noun and feminine. Whoever read **Sadin** with the kasra and tanwin declined it, interpreting it as the Book or the Revelation. This is Ibn Abi Ishaq in one narration. Al-Hasan also read **Sadun** with the dal damma. If it is the name of the surah, then it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: this is Sad. This is the reading of Ibn al-Sumayfa' and Harun al-A'war. They also read **Qafu wa Nunu** (ق ونُونُ) with the damma on the fa' and the nun. It was said: it is a letter indicating a meaning from a verb or from a noun. Al-Dahhak said its meaning is "Allah has spoken truthfully." Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: the key to the names of Allah is Muhammad, the truthful of the promise, the maker of the creation. It was also said its meaning is "Muhammad has spoken truthfully."

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Suddi said: **dhi al-dhikr** (ذِي الذِّكْرِ) means the one of enduring honour and eternal renown. Qatada said: the one of admonition for people and guidance for them. It was also said: the one of reminder, for the nations, the stories, the unseen matters, and the laws.

As for the answer to the oath, it is said to be mentioned. The Kufans and al-Zajjaj said it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, that is true, the mutual disputing of the people of the Fire﴾ [Sad: 64]. Al-Farra' said: we do not find this correct in Arabic, because it is too far removed from His saying ﴿By the Qur'an﴾. Al-Akhfash said it is ﴿Each of them denied the messengers﴾. Others said it is ﴿How many generations We destroyed﴾, with the lam omitted, meaning "for you," since the speech became long, as it was omitted in ﴿By the sun﴾ [al-Shams: 1], then He said ﴿He has succeeded﴾ [al-Shams: 9]. Al-Farra' and Tha'lab related this. These opinions must be discarded. It was also said that the answer is **Sad** itself, since its meaning is "Muhammad has spoken truthfully and Allah has spoken truthfully." That **Sad** is the answer to the oath was said by al-Farra' and Tha'lab. This is based on the answer to the oath being placed first, and on the belief that the letter Sad indicates what they mentioned. It was also said the answer is omitted. Al-Hawfi estimated it as "Indeed the truth has come to you" or something like it. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "Indeed, it is inimitable." Ibn 'Atiyya estimated it as "The matter is not as you claim," and similar estimates. It is reported that Qatada and al-Tabari said it is omitted before **bal** (بَلْ, "rather"), and said: this is the correct view. Its estimate is what we mentioned from him. It should be estimated that what is established here is the answer to the Qur'an when He swore by it, which is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Ya Sin. By the wise Qur'an. Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾ [Ya Sin: 1–3]. This estimate is strengthened by the mention of warning here in His saying ﴿They wondered that a warner from among themselves had come to them﴾, while there He said ﴿So that you may warn a people﴾ [Ya Sin: 6]. The mission includes warning and good tidings. **Bal** here marks a transition from this oath and what is sworn about, to the state of the disbelievers' arrogance and opposition in accepting your message and complying with what you brought, and in acknowledging the truth.

Hammad ibn al-Zibriqan, Sawra from al-Kisa'i, Maymun from Abu Ja'far, and al-Jahdari through al-Uqayli read **fi ghirrah** (في غِرَّةٍ), with a ghayn with dots and a ra', meaning in heedlessness and opposition. **Qablihim** (قَبْلِهِمْ) means before these people of great strength and opposition, and this is a warning to them. **Fa-nadaw** (فَنادَوْا) means they cried for help and called out for repentance, said al-Hasan. Or they raised their voices, as it is said: so-and-so is **andaa sawtan**, meaning higher in voice. This happened after witnessing the punishment, when it was no time for benefit. The majority read **wa-la-tu hina** (ولاتَ حِينَ), with the ta' fatha and the nun accusative. According to Sibawayh's view, it works like **laysa**, and its noun is omitted, its estimate being: "and it is not the time, the time of escape or flight." According to al-Akhfash's view, **hina** is the noun of **lat**, which works like **inna**, putting the noun in the accusative and the predicate in the nominative, and the predicate is omitted, its estimate being: "and it is not the time I see of escape." Abu al-Sammal read **wa-latu hinu** (ولاتُ حِينُ), with the ta' damma and the nun nominative. According to Sibawayh's view, **hinu manasin** is the noun of **lat**, and the predicate is omitted. According to al-Akhfash's view, it is the subject, and the predicate is omitted. Isa ibn 'Umar read **wa-la-ti hini** (ولاتِ حِينِ), with the ta' kasra and the nun genitive, as a predicate after **lat**. Its explanation is problematic. Al-Zamakhshari strained greatly in explaining the predicate in his saying:

*They sought our reconciliation, and it was not the time, the time of a moment, so we answered: it is not the time of survival.*

He said: he likened **awan** (أوانَ, "time") to **idh** (إذْ) in his saying: "And you, when you were healthy," in that it is a time from which the genitive complement was cut off and compensated for. The original was: "and it is not the time of reconciliation." If you say: what do you say about **hina manasin**, while the genitive complement is present? I say: he treated the cutting off of the genitive and what is genitive as a compensation for the omitted pronoun, its tanwin being a compensation for the omitted pronoun. Then he built **hin** because it is in apposition to a non-declinable noun. End of quote. This is strained. What appeared to me in explaining this irregular reading and this rare verse, the genitive after **lat**, is that the genitive is by implied **min** (مِن, "from"). It is as if he said: "it is not from the time of escape" and "it is not from the time of reconciliation," just as they used the genitive with it in their saying: **ʿalā kam jidhʿin baytuka** (on how many trunks is your house?), meaning "from a trunk," in the more correct of the two opinions. And just as they said: **lā rajulin jazāhu Allāhu khayran** (no man, may Allah reward him well), meaning "not from a man." The place of "from the time of escape" is nominative, as the noun of **lat** in the sense of **laysa**, just as you say: "it is not from a man standing," and the predicate is omitted. This is according to Sibawayh's view, or as a subject with the predicate omitted, according to al-Akhfash's view. Some of the Arabs said: some Arabs put **lat** in the genitive. Al-Farra' recited:

*And you will surely regret, and it is not the time of a moment of regret.*

( )

[Commentary of Abu Hayyan on Surah 38, verses 1–14, part 2]

Al-Akhfash interpreted *wa-lāta awānin* as elliptical for *wa-lāta ḥīna awānin*, meaning "and there is no time of opportunity," with *ḥīn* omitted and *awān* left in the genitive. Abu Ishaq said it means *wa-lāta awāninā* ("and not our time"), so the word *al-muḍāf ilayhi* (the noun governed by the construct) was omitted. Since it then lost its governing relation, it could not take i'rab (grammatical inflection), so it was given a kasra because two unvowelled letters came together. This is the reading al-Zamakhshari adopted, having taken it from Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj. Al-Mubarrad recited it as *wa-lāta awānun* with a raf'a (nominative ending). From Isa (ibn Umar): *wa-lāta ḥīnun* with a raf'a, and *manāṣ* with a fatḥa. The author of *al-Lawāmiḥ* said: "If that is established, then he may have made *ḥīn* indeclinable on a ḍamma, so there is inversion in the sentence, and he treated it like *qablu* and *ba'du* in being an adverb of termination. He made *manāṣ* indeclinable on a fatḥa together with *lāta*, on the estimate *lāta manāṣa ḥīna*. But *inna* only governs indefinite nouns when it is directly attached to them, without any intervening adverb or other word. It may be that this has a meaning I do not know." End of quote. Isa also recited *wa-lāti* with a kasra on the tā', and *ḥīna* with a naṣb (accusative) on the nūn; the explanation of the accusative of *ḥīna* has already been given.

As for *lāta*, various readings are reported: a fatḥa, a ḍamma and a kasra on the tā', and pausing on it with a tā'. This is the view of Sibawayh, al-Farra', Ibn Kaysan and al-Zajjaj. Al-Kisa'i and al-Mubarrad paused with a hā'. Some people treated the *lā* as the whole word, and they claimed that the tā' was added to *ḥīn*. Abu Ubayda chose this view and mentioned that he had seen it in the *Imam* (the 'Uthmanic codex) with its tā' written joined to *ḥīn*. But what will one make of his saying *wa-lāta sā'ata mandamin* ("and not a moment of regret") and *wa-lāta awānin*?

Al-Kalbi said: "When they fought and were compelled, some of them would say to others, *manāṣ*, meaning 'you must flee.' When the punishment came upon them, they said, *manāṣ*. So God said: ﴿and there is no time for escape﴾." Al-Qushayri said: "On this view the estimate would be: they cried out *manāṣ*, and it was omitted because what follows indicates it, that is, 'it is not the time for your calling out with it.' There is in this a kind of arbitrariness, since every generation that was destroyed would say *manāṣ* at the time of distress." End of quote. Al-Jurjani said: "That is, they cried out at a time when there is no escape, that is, a moment with no refuge and no escape. When he placed *lā* first and delayed *ḥīn*, this required a wāw, as a circumstantial clause requires when it is made into a subject and predicate, like *jā'a Zaydun rākiban* ("Zayd came riding"), then you say *jā'a Zaydun wa-huwa rākibun* ("Zayd came while he was riding"). So *ḥīn* is an adverb of time for the verb ﴿they cried out﴾." End of quote. But that the original of this sentence is "they cried out when there is no escape," and that *ḥīn* is an adverb of time for ﴿they cried out﴾, is a foreign assertion that contradicts the arrangement of the Qur'an. Its meaning in its own arrangement is perfectly clear: the clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase, meaning ﴿they cried out while they were in a time when there was no escape for them﴾.

[p. 385] When God related of the disbelievers that they were in arrogance and opposition, He followed this with what proceeded from them of corrupt words, namely their attributing to Him sorcery and lying. The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun in His words ﴿And the disbelievers said﴾, meaning "and they said," to draw attention to the quality which caused them to wonder, to the point that they attributed to the one who brought guidance and monotheism sorcery and lying.

﴿Has he made the gods into one god?﴾ They said: How can there be one god who provides for everyone and oversees all their affairs? *Ja'ala* here means *ṣayyara* (to make or render) in speech, claim and assertion, and He mentioned their wonder at what is not a matter for wonder. The pronoun in ﴿and they wondered﴾ refers to them, meaning they found it strange that a messenger should come from among themselves. The majority recited ﴿ʿujābun﴾, which is an intensive pattern, like *rajulun ṭiwālun* and *surāʿun* for *ṭawīlun* and *sarīʿun*. ʿAli, al-Sulami, Isa and Ibn Miqsam recited it with a shadda on the jīm, and they said *rajulun kurrāmun* and *ṭaʿǧāmun ṭayyābun*, and this is more emphatic than the light form *fuʿālun*. Muqatil said: *ʿujābun* is the dialect of the Azd Shanu'a. As for those who said ﴿Has he made the gods into one god?﴾, Ibn Abbas said they were the chiefs of Quraysh, and they were twenty-six.

﴿And the chiefs among them set off﴾. The apparent meaning is that they departed from the assembly of Abu Talib, when they had gathered with the Messenger present there and complained about him, as mentioned earlier in the occasion of revelation. There is an omitted element here, which would be: "they were conversing."

﴿saying, Go on﴾. The *an* here explains that omitted element. *Imshū* is a command to walk, that is, to move the feet away from that assembly. Al-Zamakhshari said: *an* here means *ay* ("that, namely"), because those departing from the assembly of discussion must speak and confer about what happened to them, so their departure implies the meaning of saying and commanding to walk, that is, some of them commanded others. It is also said: the chiefs commanded their followers and helpers. It is also permissible for *an* to be verbal (*maṣdariyya*), meaning "and they departed by saying *imshū*." It is also said that the departure here is a rushing into speech and talk, and *an* on this view is explanatory. The command to walk is not meant as the movement of steps, but its meaning is: go on in your way and persist in your conduct. It is also said that *imshū* is a supplication for the acquisition of livestock. It was said that this is weak, because the alif would have to be cut, since one says *amshā al-rajulu* only when he becomes the owner of livestock; moreover this meaning does not fit the verse. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that they said *imshū*, meaning "multiply and gather together," from *mashat al-mar'atu* when a woman's births multiply; and from this comes *al-māshiya* (livestock) for good omen. End of quote. They commanded patience toward the gods, that is, toward worshipping them and holding fast to them.

The indication by His words ﴿Indeed this﴾, meaning the emergence of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his elevation through prophethood, ﴿is surely a thing that is intended﴾. That is, it is intended that we submit to it, or God intends it and decrees its execution, so there is nothing for us but patience. Or: this matter is one of the calamities of the age that is intended for us, so there is no escaping it. Or: your religion is a thing that is sought, that is, it is pursued in order to be taken from you and for you to be overcome by it. These are four possibilities. Al-Qaffal said: This is a phrase used for threat and intimidation. The meaning is: his purpose in this statement is not to establish the religion, but his aim is to dominate us, so that he may rule over our property and children as he wishes.

﴿We have not heard of this in the last religion﴾. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Muqatil said: the religion of the Christians, because in it is the Trinity, and it does not affirm the oneness of God. Mujahid and Qatada said: the religion of the Arabs, namely Quraysh and its ilk. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the religion of the Jews and the Christians; the Jews associated Ezra with God and the Christians made God a trinity. It is also said: "the last religion" refers to what they used to hear would appear at the end of time, for before the mission (*mab'ath*) people used to sense that a prophet would emerge and a new religion and faith would arise. What confirms this view is what is reported of the sayings of the Jewish rabbis (*aḥbār*) who were in the monasteries, and what is reported from the soothsayers such as Shiqq and Sutayh and others, and what the Children of Israel used to believe, that it would come from among them. It is also said: "in the last religion" means: we have not heard from the People of the Book or the soothsayers that in the last religion there would arise the oneness of God.

﴿This is nothing but a fabrication﴾, that is, a contrivance and a lie.

﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?﴾ They denied that he should be singled out for honour from among their nobles, and that the Book should descend upon him from among them. This denial arises from a great envy that their hearts harboured and their tongues expressed.

﴿Nay, but they are in doubt about My Reminder﴾, that is, about the Qur'an which I sent down upon My Messenger; they are in doubt about it. The statement that they are in doubt implies that their words ﴿This is nothing but a fabrication﴾ are false. [p. 386]

﴿Nay, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾, that is, not yet. When they taste it, they will know that what he brought is true, and their doubt will leave them.

﴿Or do they have the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord?﴾ That is, they do not dispose of the treasuries of mercy, so that they give to whom they wish and withhold from whom they wish, and choose for the message whomever they want. Rather, it is the Mighty, who cannot be overcome, the Bestower, who owns and disposes of it, who gives what He wills to whom He wills. When He asked the question as a denial in His words ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord?﴾, and this was evidence of their lacking any disposal over the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord, He brought the denial and reproach by negating something more general, saying: ﴿Or do they have dominion over the heavens and the earth?﴾, meaning: they have no share of that at all.

﴿Then let them ascend﴾, that is, if they have any share of that, then let them climb ﴿by means of ropes﴾, the ways leading to the heaven and the ladders by which one may reach the management of the world, so that they may place the message in whomever they choose. Then He diminished and belittled them, and informed them of what their affair would come to: defeat and failure. It is said that *mā* is superfluous; it is also permissible that it is a descriptive, in which case it is intended for exaltation by way of mockery of them, or for belittlement, since *mā* as a qualifier is used in both of these senses. *Hunālika* is an adverb of place indicating what is distant. The apparent meaning is that it refers to the place in which they conferred with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with those previously mentioned words, namely Mecca. This would then be a report of the unseen about their defeat in Mecca on the day of the Conquest. The meaning is that they will become defeated in Mecca on the day of the Conquest. It is also said: *hunālika* refers to the climbing by ropes, meaning: these people, if they attempt that, are a defeated army. It is also said: *hunālika* refers to the whole collection of idols and their support, meaning they are a defeated army on this path. Mujahid and Qatada said: it refers to the day of Badr, and that was an unseen matter which God informed of through His Messenger. It is also said: it refers to the siege of the Battle of the Trench in Medina. Al-Zamakhshari said: *hunālika* refers to the place where they had put themselves forward to take on such a great utterance, from their saying to one who appoints someone to a task that is not his: "you are not there" (*laista hunālika*). End of quote. *Hunālika* may be in the position of a qualifier for *jundun* ("an army"), meaning "present there." It may also be connected to *mahzūmun* ("defeated"), and *jundun* would then be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they are an army," and *mahzūmun* is its predicate. Abu al-Baqa' said: *jundun* is the subject, *mā* is superfluous, *hunālika* is an adjective, and *mahzūmun* is the predicate. End of quote. This is remote, because it is separated from the speech that precedes it.

The meaning of ﴿of the factions﴾ is: among the factions who were zealous in falsehood and denied the messengers. When God mentioned that He had destroyed many generations before Quraysh because they denied their messengers, He here recounted those among them who have a connection with His punishment.

﴿Dhū al-Awtād﴾, that is, the possessor of the stakes (*awtād*). Its origin is the stability of a tent stretched with its pegs. Al-Afwah al-Awdi said:

"A house is not built except upon pillars,
and there is no support if stakes are not driven in."

So it was borrowed for the stability of might and kingship and the uprightness of affairs, as al-Aswad said:

"In the shade of a kingdom whose stakes are firmly set."

Al-Zamakhshari said this, having taken it from the words of others. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ata' said: he had stakes and wooden frames with which and upon which he played. Al-Suddi said: he used to kill people with stakes and nail them into the ground with them. Al-Dahhak said: it means the great, firmly-built structures. It is also said: it is an expression for the great number of his tents and the magnitude of his armies. It is also said: he would spread the one being tortured between four pillars, with each of his extremities bound to a pillar, and in each pillar an iron stake was driven, and he would leave him until he died. The same meaning is reported from al-Hasan and Mujahid. It is also said: he would stretch him between four stakes in the ground and release scorpions and snakes upon him. It is also said: he would fasten them with four stakes, then raise a rock and drop it upon him so that it crushed him. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas, in a report from Ata', said: the stakes are the soldiers, who strengthen his kingship as a stake strengthens a thing. It is also said: he built a minaret upon which he slaughtered people, as reported by Ibn Jubayr.

﴿Those are the factions﴾, that is, those who formed factions against their prophets, just as Quraysh formed factions against the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The apparent meaning is that the indication by *ulā'ika* ("those") is to the nearest previously mentioned, namely the people of Noah and those joined with them. In this there is exaltation of their status and elevation of them above those who formed factions against the Messenger of God, meaning: these great ones, when they denied, were punished, [p. 387] and so are you.

﴿Each of them merely denied the messengers, so My punishment was justly due.﴾ So their punishment became necessary. The people of Nuh (Noah) denied him and harmed him, so they were drowned. The people of Hud were destroyed by the wind. Pharaoh was drowned. Thamud were destroyed by the Blast. The people of Lut (Lot) were destroyed by being swallowed up in the earth. And the People of the Thicket (al-Aykah) were destroyed by the punishment of the Day of the Canopy. The meaning of ﴿Each of them﴾ is: whatever came from the people of Nuh and those after them. ﴿So My punishment was justly due﴾ means: their punishment became necessary, and likewise it is due upon you, O deniers of the Messenger.
