Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: he was more persuasive and more powerful than I; when I addressed him, his speech was stronger than mine, and his strength was greater than mine. Al-Zamakhshari said: there came to me a skilled debater whom I could not refute with what I would have refuted him with. By "speech" is meant addressing the arguer in debate, or it means the suitor of a woman; if he proposed to her and then addressed me, meaning he prevailed over me in the proposal, so he beat me by marrying her instead of me. It has also been said: he overpowered me through his authority, because when he asked me, I could not oppose him.

The memorialist Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi said: in our lands there was a governor called Sayri ibn Abi Bakr. I spoke to him about asking a man on my behalf concerning a need. He said to me: "Do you not know that a ruler's request for a need is a seizure of it?" I said: "As for when he is just, then no."

Abu Haywa and Talha read *wa ʿazzanī* with a lightened *zā'*. Abu al-Fath said: he deleted one of the two *zā'*s for lightness, as Abu Zubayd said: *aḥsin bihi fa-hunna ilayhi shūs* (be kind to him, for they are fierce toward him). This is also reported from ʿAsim. ʿUbayd Allah, Abu Wa'il, Masruq, al-Ḍaḥḥak, al-Hasan and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read *wa ʿāzzanī* with an *alif* and a shadda on the *zā'*, meaning: and he overcame me.

The apparent meaning is to keep the word *naʿja* ("ewe") in its literal sense as the female of sheep, and that it is not used as a metaphor for a woman. There is no necessity to take it this way, because that statement was issued by the angels as a depiction of the case and an assumed supposition, not as the actual state of anything. So they presented the example of a man who had a single ewe, while his partner had ninety-nine. The partner wished to complete the hundred, so he coveted his partner's ewe and wanted to seize it from him. He argued with him about it in the manner of one eager to attain his aim. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿and indeed many partners oppress one another﴾. This depiction and parable is more eloquent in its purpose and more indicative of the intended meaning.

﴿He said: He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe in addition to his ewes﴾. This was not an initiation by Dawud (peace be upon him) immediately after the claimant finished his words, nor a ruling based on the apparent sense of his speech before the obligation became clear. It was said on the assumption: "If what you say is true, then indeed he has wronged you." It has also been said that there is an omission: the defendant acknowledged, then said: ﴿He has certainly wronged you﴾. However, the Qur'an does not relate the defendant's acknowledgment, because it is known from all the revealed laws that a judge does not rule until the defendant has responded. As for what al-Halimi said, that he saw in the claimant signs of weakness and humiliation, and so took his case to be that of an oppressed man as he claimed, which led him to avoid questioning the defendant and so he hastened with his words ("He has certainly wronged you"), his view is weak and cannot be relied upon.

It is reported that when Dawud (peace be upon him) heard the words of the complainant, he said to the other: "What do you say?" He acknowledged, so he said to him: "If you do not return to the truth, I will surely break what is in your eyes." Then he said to the second: ﴿He has certainly wronged you.﴾ Thereupon they smiled and departed, and he did not see them at that moment, and he saw that they went toward the sky in plain view of him.

He attributed the verbal noun to its object and made the question carry the sense of attribution, meaning: by the attribution of your ewe in the manner of a request and a demand. For this reason he used *ilā* after it.

﴿And indeed many partners oppress one another﴾: this is part of Dawud's speech, and it indicates that in his time injustice and transgression were widespread. *Al-khulaṭāʾ*: the partners who mix their property; the singular is *khalīṭ*. By this statement Dawud intended a good admonition and an encouragement to adopt the custom of righteous partners, whom he had judged to be few, and to make injustice hateful to them, and to console the wronged man for what befell him from his partner, and to show that he has an example in most partners. It was read *layabghiya* with a fatha on the *yā'*, on the assumption that the light *nūn* was dropped; the original was *layabghiyanna*, as the poet said: *iḍrib ʿanka al-humūma ṭāriqahā* ("strike away from yourself the worries that come at night"), meaning *iḍribanna*. In this case the oath and its answer form a predicate of *inna*, on the assumption of an omitted oath. In the majority reading, *layabghī* is the predicate of *inna*. It was also read *layabgh*, dropping the *yā'*, as in the line: *Muḥammad, tafdi nafsaka kullu nafs* ("Muhammad, may every soul ransom itself for you"), meaning *tafdī*, according to one of the two opinions.

*Qalīl* is its predicate, placed first, and *mā* is an additional particle conveying the sense of magnification and wonder, and *hum* is the subject (*mubtadaʾ*).

﴿Wa-ẓanna Dāwūd﴾ (And David thought). Since the dominant opinion (al-ẓann al-ghālib) closely approximates knowledge (al-'ilm), the word ẓann is used for it. Its meaning here is: David knew and was certain that We had tested him with the case of the two litigants.

Ibn 'Aṭiyya denied that ẓann can mean certainty (yaqīn). He said: "We do not find it in the speech of the Arabs. It is rather a suspension (tawqīf) between two beliefs, one of which predominates over the other. The Arabs use it for knowledge that is not based on the senses or on the indication of complete certainty. But people confuse this and say: ẓanna in the sense of ayqana." Ibn 'Aṭiyya elaborated on this at length in his book, which may be consulted there.

The majority (al-Jumhūr) read ﴿fatannāhu﴾ with the tā' and nūn doubled (فَتَنّاهُ, shaddah for intensification). 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, Abū Rajā', and al-Ḥasan, in one transmission from him, read it that way for emphasis. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk read أَفْتَنّاهُ (with alif, causative form), like the line of verse:

"Even if she has tested me, yesterday she too was tested [in her own way]."

Qatādah and Abū 'Amr, in one narration, read it with the tā' and nūn lightened, and the alif is the pronoun referring to the two litigants.

﴿Fa-istaghfara rabbahu wa-kharra rāki'an wa-anāb﴾ (So he asked his Lord for forgiveness, and fell down bowing and turned in repentance). Rāki'an is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) and khurūr means falling down to the ground. As for the meaning, either he used rukū' (bowing) to mean sujūd (prostration), or he mentioned the first stage of the falling, meaning: bowing in order to prostrate. Al-Ḥasan said: "Because one does not prostrate until one has bowed." Al-Ḥasan ibn al-Faḍl said: "He fell from his bowing," meaning he prostrated after having been bowing. Some people said: kharra is said of one who bowed even if he did not reach the ground.

What I incline towards is what the apparent meaning of the verse indicates: that those who scaled the prayer niche (al-miḥrāb) were humans, who entered upon him by an unusual entrance and at a time other than his sitting for judgment. He was alarmed by them, assuming they intended to assassinate him, since he was alone in his prayer niche worshipping his Lord. When it became clear to him that they had come with a case, and two of them came forward to be judged, as Allah the Exalted related, David, peace be upon him, had thought that their entering upon him at that time and from that direction was a deliverance from Allah from their assassinating him. But what he had supposed did not occur, so he asked forgiveness for that assumption, since it was mistaken and what he had thought would happen did not happen. He either prostrated, or returned to Allah the Exalted, and He forgave him that assumption. For this reason He indicated it by His words ﴿fa-ghafarnā lahu dhālik﴾ (so We forgave him that), and nothing preceded it except His words ﴿wa-ẓanna Dāwūd annamā fatannāhu﴾ (And David thought that We had only tested him).

It is known with certainty that the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected (ma'ṣūmūn) from sins, and it is impossible for them to commit any of them. For if we permitted any such thing concerning them, the divine laws (sharā'i') would be nullified, and we could not trust anything they say that Allah revealed to them. Therefore, what Allah the Exalted related in His Book stands as He intended, and whatever the storytellers (al-quṣṣāṣ) relate that disparages the station of prophethood, we reject it. We are, as the poet said:

"We give precedence to the judgment of reason in every doubtful matter, when the sitters of storytellers prefer the reports."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 38, verses 15–25 (part 1 of 3):

﴿They are waiting for nothing but a single blast, with no delay (fawaq) in it.﴾ ﴿They say: "Our Lord, hasten to us our share (qitt) before the Day of Reckoning."﴾ ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud, possessor of strength (dhu al-ayd). He was ever turning back (in repentance).﴾ ﴿We subjected the mountains to glorify (Us) with him at evening and at sunrise.﴾ ﴿And the birds, gathered together; each one was turning back to Him.﴾ ﴿We strengthened his kingdom and gave him wisdom and decisive speech.﴾ ﴿Has the news of the litigants reached you, when they climbed over the walls of the prayer niche (mihrab)?﴾ ﴿When they entered upon Dawud and he was alarmed by them, they said: "Do not fear. We are two litigants, one of whom has wronged the other. So judge between us with truth, do not exceed (the bounds), and guide us to the even path.﴾ ﴿This brother of mine has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe. He said: 'Commit it to my care,' and he overpowered me in speech.'﴾ ﴿He said: "He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe in addition to his ewes. Indeed many partners wrong one another, except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and few are they." And Dawud thought that We had only tested him, so he asked his Lord for forgiveness, fell down bowing and turned (to Him) in repentance.﴾ ﴿So We forgave him that, and indeed he has nearness to Us and a good final return.﴾

(Wa ma yanzuru hā'ulā') means "they are not waiting for," i.e., they await nothing. (Hā'ulā') is a demonstrative indicating the Quraysh disbelievers. The use of (hā'ulā') strengthens the view that (ulā'ika) refers to the nearer peoples, such as the people of Nuh and those mentioned after them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It may be a reference to all the confederates, since they are present in mention, or because they are as if present before God." End of quote. There is a remoteness in this, and it is a report from Him, exalted, that existence has confirmed.

(Al-sayha) is what befell them of killing, captivity and defeat, as one says: "Time shouted at them." Qatada said: He threatened them with the blast of the Resurrection and the blowing of the Trumpet. It has also been said: with a blast by which they will be destroyed in this world. The first view implies that the Messenger is waiting for something specific to happen to them. On both views they are on the path of punishment and under a dangerous matter, awaiting nothing but ruin.

The majority of readers recite (min fawaq) with a fatha on the fa'. Al-Sulami, Ibn Wathtab, al-A'mash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Talha read it with a damma. It is said that both have the same meaning, like (qiṣāṣ al-sh'ar). Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi said: with a fatha, it means recovery (ifaqa) from (afaqa wa-istarah), like (jawab) from (ajaba). Ibn Abbas said: (min fawaq) means "from repetition." Mujahid said: "from return."

(Qittana): our share of Paradise, so that we may enjoy it in this world. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Jubayr. Qatada and Mujahid also said: our share of the punishment. Abu al-Aliya and al-Kalbi said: our records (suhuf) with our faith. Al-Suddi said: the meaning is: show us our dwellings in Paradise so that we may follow you. On every view, they said this only in mockery and derision. The meaning of (qabla yawm al-hisab) is: those who claim that it will occur in this world, since they are disbelievers who do not believe in the Resurrection.

Since their statement implied mockery, God, exalted, commanded His Prophet to be patient with their harm, and He mentioned stories of the prophets, Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub and others, and what befell them. They were patient until God relieved them, and their end was the best of ends. Likewise, you shall be patient, and your affair will end in the best outcome, and you will attain what you want of establishing your religion and extinguishing misguidance. It has been said: "Be patient over what they say," and magnify the matter of their opposition to God in their eyes, and remind them of the story of Dawud and what befell him, though he was given prophethood and kingship. So what do you suppose of you, with your disbelief and disobedience? End of quote. This is compiled from the words of al-Zamakhshari with some changes to his wording that do not suit the station of prophethood. It has also been said: He was commanded to be patient, so He mentioned the stories of the prophets so that they would be proof of the validity of his prophethood. It has been said: "Be patient over what they say," and hold fast to what you were charged with, namely enduring them and bearing their harm; and remember Dawud and his honour with God, and what befell him, and what he encountered of God's rebuke.

(Dhu al-ayd): possessor of strength in religion, in the law, in proclaiming God's command and in obedience to God. He was also physically strong. (Al-awwab): one who returns to obedience to God. This was said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd. Al-Suddi said: the one who glorifies. Describing him as (awwab) indicates that the meaning of (dhu al-ayd) is strength in religion. It is said: a man is (ayd), (ayyid), or (dhu ad) and (ayad): all meaning one who is strong. (Wal-ishraq): at the time of sunrise. Tha'lab said: "The sun shone (sharaqat) when it rose, and (ashraqat) when it lit up and became clear." In a hadith: "He, peace be upon him, prayed the forenoon prayer and said: 'O Umm Hani, this is the prayer of ishraq.'" It was at these two times that the prayer of the Children of Israel took place.

All the discussion of the mountains glorifying God in the story of Dawud has already been given in the surah of al-Anbiya. He used the present tense with the active participle to indicate that the glorification occurs gradually, moment by moment, and state after state, so it is as if the hearer is present and hears those mountains glorifying. Similar is the verse of al-A'sha:

By my life, many eyes have turned
toward the light of a fire in plains that is burning.

That is: burning little by little. Had he said (muhriqah), it would not have indicated this meaning.

The majority read (wal-tayra mahshurah) in the accusative, coordinated with (al-jibal) in "they glorify": coordination of object with object and of state with state, like your saying: "I struck Hind stripped bare and Da'd clothed." Ibn Abi Ablah and al-Jahdari read (wal-tayru mahshurah) in the nominative, as subject and predicate. (Mahshurah) came in the passive participle form because it was not meant that they gather anything, since their gatherer is God, exalted. Thus their gathering all together is more indicative of power. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (lahu) refers to Dawud, meaning each of the mountains and birds is for Dawud's sake, that is, for the sake of his glorification; they glorified because they used to echo his glorification. (Awwab) is placed in the position of (musabbih). It has also been said that the pronoun refers to God, meaning each of Dawud, the mountains and the birds is (awwab), that is, glorifying and returning to glorification.

The majority read (wa-shadadna) without doubling: that is, We strengthened, as in His saying: "We will strengthen your arm with your brother" (al-Qasas 35). Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ablah read it with doubling of the dal. It is an inclusive expression for whatever God gave him of strength, troops and blessing, so restricting it to some particular things is not evident. Al-Suddi said: with troops. It was said: he used to spend the night around his prayer niche with forty thousand Muslims guarding him, though this is remote by ordinary custom. It was also said: with a awe that God cast into the hearts of his people. (Al-hikmah) here means: prophethood, or the Psalms (al-Zabur), or understanding in religion, or every speech and the instilling of truth. These are the views.

**(Abu Hayyan on the Verses, continued)**

﴿And decisive speech﴾. ʿAli and al-Shaʿbi said: it is imposing the oath upon the defendant and the burden of proof upon the claimant. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi said: judging between people with the truth, reaching it correctly and understanding it. Al-Shaʿbi also said: it is the phrase *amma baʿdu* ("to proceed"), because he was the first to say it and it separated one speech from another. Al-Zamakhshari said: because when one begins to speak about a matter of importance, he opens with the remembrance and praise of God; then, when he wishes to move on to the purpose he is aiming at, he separates it from the remembrance of God by saying *amma baʿdu*. It is also possible that by *al-khitab* is meant the measured speech that contains neither damaging brevity nor tiresome prolixity. Among what has come in describing the speech of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is: "A decisive statement, neither trivial nor verbose." End of quotation. Since God Most High had perfected the soul of His prophet Dawud with wisdom, He followed it with a description of the perfection of his creation in speech and worship, and so He said: ﴿and decisive speech﴾.

﴿Has there reached you the report of the litigants?﴾ When God Most High praised Dawud (peace be upon him) with what He praised him with, He mentioned this story so that it would be known that a story like this does not detract from the praise of him or from the exaltation of his rank, even though it includes his seeking forgiveness from his Lord. Seeking forgiveness does not indicate the commission of any act for which forgiveness must be sought, and seeking forgiveness has always been the mark of the prophets, who are attested to as protected from sin. The use of such an interrogative form usually occurs when what follows in the narrative is remarkable, as in His saying: ﴿Has there reached you the story of Musa?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 9], so that the one addressed by this question is prepared for what comes after and listens attentively. The exegetes have mentioned in this story things that are not fitting for the stations of the prophets; we have passed over mentioning them and will speak about the words of the verse.

*Al-naba'*: the report. *Al-khabar* is originally a verbal noun, which is why it can be used for the singular, the masculine and their derivatives. Here it has come in the plural, which is why He said ﴿when they climbed over the wall﴾, meaning: when they entered. As the poet said:

*And an opponent who prepares to enter, as if they were / Stallions, jealous, each one a bright, bold warrior.*

Apparently they were a group, which is why the plural pronoun was used. If the two litigants were only two, then others must have come with them for support or companionship. There is no disagreement that they were angels, as some have said. It has also been said that they were two brothers from the Children of Israel with the same father and mother, but the first view is better known. It has also been said that *al-khasm* here refers to two, and that the expression is metaphorical, so that they were described with the plural form used for more than two, because the meaning of plurality is present in the dual. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿two litigants﴾ is two parties, so that ﴿they climbed over﴾ and ﴿they entered﴾ refers back to *al-khasm* which is the plural of the two parties. What indicates that ﴿two litigants﴾ means "two parties" is the reading of one who recited: *baghā baʿḍuhum ʿalā baʿḍ* ("some of them oppressed others"). God Most High also said: ﴿These two litigants have disputed concerning their Lord﴾ [al-Hajj: 19], meaning: "Indeed this is my brother." As for what is reported, that two angels were sent to him, the meaning is that the litigation was between two, and there is nothing to prevent others from accompanying them. The term *khasm* was applied to the whole group, and *khasmān* to the two parties, because whoever comes with a litigant for support is in the form of a litigant, and it is not far-fetched that this designation applies to him.

The element that governs the adverbial phrase (*ẓarf*, adverb of time), which is *idh* in *idh atāka* ("when it reached you"), was stated by al-Hawfi, and it was refuted on the ground that the arrival of a report to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) can only occur in his time, not in the time of Dawud. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abu al-Baqaʾ said: the governing element is *naba'* (the report). This was refuted on the same grounds: a report that occurred in the time of Dawud (peace be upon him) cannot logically reach the Messenger of God (ﷺ). And if by *al-naba'* you mean the story itself, then it does not govern anything. It has also been said that the governing element is omitted, its estimate being: "Has there reached you the litigation of the litigants?" This was stated by al-Zamakhshari. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative governed by *al-khasm*, because of the meaning of the verb it contains. *Idh dakhalū* ("when they entered") is a substitute (*badal*) for the first *idh*. It has also been said that it is in the accusative governed by *tasawwarū* ("they climbed over").

It is reported that God Most High sent to him two angels in the form of two men. They asked to enter upon him, but they found him on the day of his worship, so he prevented them. Thereupon they climbed over the niche (*miḥrab*) at him, and he did not notice until they were sitting before him.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: he divided his time into four parts: a day for worship, a day for judgment, a day for attending to his private affairs, and a day for all the Children of Israel, when he would admonish them and make them weep. They came to him at a time other than judgment, so he was startled by them, because they had descended upon him from above, and it was the day of seclusion, when the guards were around him and did not allow anyone to enter upon him, so he feared they would harm him. It has also been said that this happened at night. It is possible that his fear arose because the people of his kingdom had treated him with contempt, to the point that some of them had abandoned seeking permission, so his fear would be over the corruption of conduct, not from the intruders. Abu al-Ahwas said: he was startled by them because they had entered upon him while each of them was holding the head of the other. It has also been said: he was startled by them when he saw them climb over a very high place which could not be ascended after months even with helpers and a large number. It has also been said that they said: "We could not reach you except by climbing over, because of the barrier preventing access, and we feared the matter between us would become worse," and Dawud accepted their excuse.

When they perceived his fright, they said: ﴿Fear not﴾, meaning: we are not among those who came except for the sake of litigation. ﴿Two litigants﴾: it is possible that this is connected to their words "Fear not," as they hastened to tell him what they had come for. It is also possible that he asked them: "What is your matter?" and they said: "Two litigants," meaning: we are two litigants. ﴿One of us has oppressed the other﴾ (*baghā*: transgressed, acted unjustly), as the poet said:

*But the young man, Hamal ibn Badr, transgressed, / And transgression is its pasture and its lair.*

Abu Yazid al-Jarrad reported from al-Kisaʾi the reading *khiṣmān* with a kasra on the *kha'*. In their command to him and their forbidding him, there was a certain harshness toward the rulers, which was prompted by the dispute and contention they were in. They asked for his justice without doubting that he would judge with justice.

The majority read ﴿and do not exceed﴾ (*wa lā tushṭiṭ*) as a separated form from *ashatta* (quadriliteral). Abu Rajaʾ, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, Qatada, al-Hasan and Abu Haywa read *tashṭiṭ* from *shatta* (trilateral). Qatada also read *tushiṭṭ*, assimilated from *ashatta*. Zirr read *tushāṭiṭ* with a damma on the *ta'* and an *alif*, on the pattern of *tufāʿil*, unassimilated. It is also reported from Qatada: *tashṭiṭ* from *shaṭaṭa*. ﴿The even way﴾ (*sawāʾ al-ṣirāṭ*): the middle of the path of truth, with no inclination in it, neither here nor there.

﴿Indeed this is my brother﴾: this is the statement of the claimant of the two. According to Ibn ʿAṭiyya, *akhī* (my brother) is an explanatory apposition (*ʿaṭf bayān*), while according to al-Zamakhshari it is either a substitute (*badal*) or the predicate (*khabar*) of *inna*. The term "brotherhood" here is used metaphorically, since they were two angels, but when they appeared in the form of two humans they spoke of brotherhood. Its figurative sense is that they are brothers in religion and faith, or in the sense of companionship and association, or in the sense of partnership and mixing, based on His saying: ﴿and indeed many partners oppress one another﴾. Each of these kinds of relationship requires the prohibition of transgression and encourages justice.

The majority read ﴿ninety-nine﴾ (*tis'un wa tis'ūn*) with a kasra on the *ta'* in both words. Al-Hasan and Zayd ibn ʿAli read them with a fatha. The majority read *naʿjatan* ("a ewe") with a fatha on the *nūn*. Al-Hasan and Ibn Hurmuz read it with a kasra on the *nūn*, which is a dialect of some of the Banu Tamim. It has been said that by the ewe is meant a wife.

﴿He said: Entrust it to me﴾: i.e., return it to my guardianship. Ibn Kaysan said: make it my share (*kifl*), i.e., my portion. Ibn ʿAbbas said: give it to me. It is reported from him and from Ibn Masʿud: transfer it to my charge. From Abu al-ʿAliya: take it to me so that I may take charge of it.

﴿And he overpowered me in speech﴾. Al-Ḍaḥḥak said: if he spoke, he was more eloquent than I, and if he fought, he was stronger than I. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: he was more persuasive and more powerful than I; when I addressed him, his speech was stronger than mine, and his strength was greater than mine. Al-Zamakhshari said: there came to me a skilled debater whom I could not refute with what I would have refuted him with. By "speech" is meant addressing the arguer in debate, or it means the suitor of a woman; if he proposed to her and then addressed me, meaning he prevailed over me in the proposal, so he beat me by marrying her instead of me. It has also been said: he overpowered me through his authority, because when he asked me, I could not oppose him.

The memorialist Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi said: in our lands there was a governor called Sayri ibn Abi Bakr. I spoke to him about asking a man on my behalf concerning a need. He said to me: "Do you not know that a ruler's request for a need is a seizure of it?" I said: "As for when he is just, then no."

Abu Haywa and Talha read *wa ʿazzanī* with a lightened *zā'*. Abu al-Fath said: he deleted one of the two *zā'*s for lightness, as Abu Zubayd said: *aḥsin bihi fa-hunna ilayhi shūs* (be kind to him, for they are fierce toward him). This is also reported from ʿAsim. ʿUbayd Allah, Abu Wa'il, Masruq, al-Ḍaḥḥak, al-Hasan and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read *wa ʿāzzanī* with an *alif* and a shadda on the *zā'*, meaning: and he overcame me.

The apparent meaning is to keep the word *naʿja* ("ewe") in its literal sense as the female of sheep, and that it is not used as a metaphor for a woman. There is no necessity to take it this way, because that statement was issued by the angels as a depiction of the case and an assumed supposition, not as the actual state of anything. So they presented the example of a man who had a single ewe, while his partner had ninety-nine. The partner wished to complete the hundred, so he coveted his partner's ewe and wanted to seize it from him. He argued with him about it in the manner of one eager to attain his aim. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿and indeed many partners oppress one another﴾. This depiction and parable is more eloquent in its purpose and more indicative of the intended meaning.

﴿He said: He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe in addition to his ewes﴾. This was not an initiation by Dawud (peace be upon him) immediately after the claimant finished his words, nor a ruling based on the apparent sense of his speech before the obligation became clear. It was said on the assumption: "If what you say is true, then indeed he has wronged you." It has also been said that there is an omission: the defendant acknowledged, then said: ﴿He has certainly wronged you﴾. However, the Qur'an does not relate the defendant's acknowledgment, because it is known from all the revealed laws that a judge does not rule until the defendant has responded. As for what al-Halimi said, that he saw in the claimant signs of weakness and humiliation, and so took his case to be that of an oppressed man as he claimed, which led him to avoid questioning the defendant and so he hastened with his words ("He has certainly wronged you"), his view is weak and cannot be relied upon.

It is reported that when Dawud (peace be upon him) heard the words of the complainant, he said to the other: "What do you say?" He acknowledged, so he said to him: "If you do not return to the truth, I will surely break what is in your eyes." Then he said to the second: ﴿He has certainly wronged you.﴾ Thereupon they smiled and departed, and he did not see them at that moment, and he saw that they went toward the sky in plain view of him.

He attributed the verbal noun to its object and made the question carry the sense of attribution, meaning: by the attribution of your ewe in the manner of a request and a demand. For this reason he used *ilā* after it.

﴿And indeed many partners oppress one another﴾: this is part of Dawud's speech, and it indicates that in his time injustice and transgression were widespread. *Al-khulaṭāʾ*: the partners who mix their property; the singular is *khalīṭ*. By this statement Dawud intended a good admonition and an encouragement to adopt the custom of righteous partners, whom he had judged to be few, and to make injustice hateful to them, and to console the wronged man for what befell him from his partner, and to show that he has an example in most partners. It was read *layabghiya* with a fatha on the *yā'*, on the assumption that the light *nūn* was dropped; the original was *layabghiyanna*, as the poet said: *iḍrib ʿanka al-humūma ṭāriqahā* ("strike away from yourself the worries that come at night"), meaning *iḍribanna*. In this case the oath and its answer form a predicate of *inna*, on the assumption of an omitted oath. In the majority reading, *layabghī* is the predicate of *inna*. It was also read *layabgh*, dropping the *yā'*, as in the line: *Muḥammad, tafdi nafsaka kullu nafs* ("Muhammad, may every soul ransom itself for you"), meaning *tafdī*, according to one of the two opinions.

*Qalīl* is its predicate, placed first, and *mā* is an additional particle conveying the sense of magnification and wonder, and *hum* is the subject (*mubtadaʾ*).

﴿Wa-ẓanna Dāwūd﴾ (And David thought). Since the dominant opinion (al-ẓann al-ghālib) closely approximates knowledge (al-'ilm), the word ẓann is used for it. Its meaning here is: David knew and was certain that We had tested him with the case of the two litigants.

Ibn 'Aṭiyya denied that ẓann can mean certainty (yaqīn). He said: "We do not find it in the speech of the Arabs. It is rather a suspension (tawqīf) between two beliefs, one of which predominates over the other. The Arabs use it for knowledge that is not based on the senses or on the indication of complete certainty. But people confuse this and say: ẓanna in the sense of ayqana." Ibn 'Aṭiyya elaborated on this at length in his book, which may be consulted there.

The majority (al-Jumhūr) read ﴿fatannāhu﴾ with the tā' and nūn doubled (فَتَنّاهُ, shaddah for intensification). 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, Abū Rajā', and al-Ḥasan, in one transmission from him, read it that way for emphasis. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk read أَفْتَنّاهُ (with alif, causative form), like the line of verse:

"Even if she has tested me, yesterday she too was tested [in her own way]."

Qatādah and Abū 'Amr, in one narration, read it with the tā' and nūn lightened, and the alif is the pronoun referring to the two litigants.

﴿Fa-istaghfara rabbahu wa-kharra rāki'an wa-anāb﴾ (So he asked his Lord for forgiveness, and fell down bowing and turned in repentance). Rāki'an is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) and khurūr means falling down to the ground. As for the meaning, either he used rukū' (bowing) to mean sujūd (prostration), or he mentioned the first stage of the falling, meaning: bowing in order to prostrate. Al-Ḥasan said: "Because one does not prostrate until one has bowed." Al-Ḥasan ibn al-Faḍl said: "He fell from his bowing," meaning he prostrated after having been bowing. Some people said: kharra is said of one who bowed even if he did not reach the ground.

What I incline towards is what the apparent meaning of the verse indicates: that those who scaled the prayer niche (al-miḥrāb) were humans, who entered upon him by an unusual entrance and at a time other than his sitting for judgment. He was alarmed by them, assuming they intended to assassinate him, since he was alone in his prayer niche worshipping his Lord. When it became clear to him that they had come with a case, and two of them came forward to be judged, as Allah the Exalted related, David, peace be upon him, had thought that their entering upon him at that time and from that direction was a deliverance from Allah from their assassinating him. But what he had supposed did not occur, so he asked forgiveness for that assumption, since it was mistaken and what he had thought would happen did not happen. He either prostrated, or returned to Allah the Exalted, and He forgave him that assumption. For this reason He indicated it by His words ﴿fa-ghafarnā lahu dhālik﴾ (so We forgave him that), and nothing preceded it except His words ﴿wa-ẓanna Dāwūd annamā fatannāhu﴾ (And David thought that We had only tested him).

It is known with certainty that the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected (ma'ṣūmūn) from sins, and it is impossible for them to commit any of them. For if we permitted any such thing concerning them, the divine laws (sharā'i') would be nullified, and we could not trust anything they say that Allah revealed to them. Therefore, what Allah the Exalted related in His Book stands as He intended, and whatever the storytellers (al-quṣṣāṣ) relate that disparages the station of prophethood, we reject it. We are, as the poet said:

"We give precedence to the judgment of reason in every doubtful matter, when the sitters of storytellers prefer the reports."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 38, verses 15–25 (part 1 of 3):

﴿They are waiting for nothing but a single blast, with no delay (fawaq) in it.﴾ ﴿They say: "Our Lord, hasten to us our share (qitt) before the Day of Reckoning."﴾ ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud, possessor of strength (dhu al-ayd). He was ever turning back (in repentance).﴾ ﴿We subjected the mountains to glorify (Us) with him at evening and at sunrise.﴾ ﴿And the birds, gathered together; each one was turning back to Him.﴾ ﴿We strengthened his kingdom and gave him wisdom and decisive speech.﴾ ﴿Has the news of the litigants reached you, when they climbed over the walls of the prayer niche (mihrab)?﴾ ﴿When they entered upon Dawud and he was alarmed by them, they said: "Do not fear. We are two litigants, one of whom has wronged the other. So judge between us with truth, do not exceed (the bounds), and guide us to the even path.﴾ ﴿This brother of mine has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe. He said: 'Commit it to my care,' and he overpowered me in speech.'﴾ ﴿He said: "He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe in addition to his ewes. Indeed many partners wrong one another, except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and few are they." And Dawud thought that We had only tested him, so he asked his Lord for forgiveness, fell down bowing and turned (to Him) in repentance.﴾ ﴿So We forgave him that, and indeed he has nearness to Us and a good final return.﴾

(Wa ma yanzuru hā'ulā') means "they are not waiting for," i.e., they await nothing. (Hā'ulā') is a demonstrative indicating the Quraysh disbelievers. The use of (hā'ulā') strengthens the view that (ulā'ika) refers to the nearer peoples, such as the people of Nuh and those mentioned after them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It may be a reference to all the confederates, since they are present in mention, or because they are as if present before God." End of quote. There is a remoteness in this, and it is a report from Him, exalted, that existence has confirmed.

(Al-sayha) is what befell them of killing, captivity and defeat, as one says: "Time shouted at them." Qatada said: He threatened them with the blast of the Resurrection and the blowing of the Trumpet. It has also been said: with a blast by which they will be destroyed in this world. The first view implies that the Messenger is waiting for something specific to happen to them. On both views they are on the path of punishment and under a dangerous matter, awaiting nothing but ruin.

The majority of readers recite (min fawaq) with a fatha on the fa'. Al-Sulami, Ibn Wathtab, al-A'mash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Talha read it with a damma. It is said that both have the same meaning, like (qiṣāṣ al-sh'ar). Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi said: with a fatha, it means recovery (ifaqa) from (afaqa wa-istarah), like (jawab) from (ajaba). Ibn Abbas said: (min fawaq) means "from repetition." Mujahid said: "from return."

(Qittana): our share of Paradise, so that we may enjoy it in this world. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Jubayr. Qatada and Mujahid also said: our share of the punishment. Abu al-Aliya and al-Kalbi said: our records (suhuf) with our faith. Al-Suddi said: the meaning is: show us our dwellings in Paradise so that we may follow you. On every view, they said this only in mockery and derision. The meaning of (qabla yawm al-hisab) is: those who claim that it will occur in this world, since they are disbelievers who do not believe in the Resurrection.

Since their statement implied mockery, God, exalted, commanded His Prophet to be patient with their harm, and He mentioned stories of the prophets, Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub and others, and what befell them. They were patient until God relieved them, and their end was the best of ends. Likewise, you shall be patient, and your affair will end in the best outcome, and you will attain what you want of establishing your religion and extinguishing misguidance. It has been said: "Be patient over what they say," and magnify the matter of their opposition to God in their eyes, and remind them of the story of Dawud and what befell him, though he was given prophethood and kingship. So what do you suppose of you, with your disbelief and disobedience? End of quote. This is compiled from the words of al-Zamakhshari with some changes to his wording that do not suit the station of prophethood. It has also been said: He was commanded to be patient, so He mentioned the stories of the prophets so that they would be proof of the validity of his prophethood. It has been said: "Be patient over what they say," and hold fast to what you were charged with, namely enduring them and bearing their harm; and remember Dawud and his honour with God, and what befell him, and what he encountered of God's rebuke.

(Dhu al-ayd): possessor of strength in religion, in the law, in proclaiming God's command and in obedience to God. He was also physically strong. (Al-awwab): one who returns to obedience to God. This was said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd. Al-Suddi said: the one who glorifies. Describing him as (awwab) indicates that the meaning of (dhu al-ayd) is strength in religion. It is said: a man is (ayd), (ayyid), or (dhu ad) and (ayad): all meaning one who is strong. (Wal-ishraq): at the time of sunrise. Tha'lab said: "The sun shone (sharaqat) when it rose, and (ashraqat) when it lit up and became clear." In a hadith: "He, peace be upon him, prayed the forenoon prayer and said: 'O Umm Hani, this is the prayer of ishraq.'" It was at these two times that the prayer of the Children of Israel took place.

All the discussion of the mountains glorifying God in the story of Dawud has already been given in the surah of al-Anbiya. He used the present tense with the active participle to indicate that the glorification occurs gradually, moment by moment, and state after state, so it is as if the hearer is present and hears those mountains glorifying. Similar is the verse of al-A'sha:

By my life, many eyes have turned
toward the light of a fire in plains that is burning.

That is: burning little by little. Had he said (muhriqah), it would not have indicated this meaning.

The majority read (wal-tayra mahshurah) in the accusative, coordinated with (al-jibal) in "they glorify": coordination of object with object and of state with state, like your saying: "I struck Hind stripped bare and Da'd clothed." Ibn Abi Ablah and al-Jahdari read (wal-tayru mahshurah) in the nominative, as subject and predicate. (Mahshurah) came in the passive participle form because it was not meant that they gather anything, since their gatherer is God, exalted. Thus their gathering all together is more indicative of power. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (lahu) refers to Dawud, meaning each of the mountains and birds is for Dawud's sake, that is, for the sake of his glorification; they glorified because they used to echo his glorification. (Awwab) is placed in the position of (musabbih). It has also been said that the pronoun refers to God, meaning each of Dawud, the mountains and the birds is (awwab), that is, glorifying and returning to glorification.

The majority read (wa-shadadna) without doubling: that is, We strengthened, as in His saying: "We will strengthen your arm with your brother" (al-Qasas 35). Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ablah read it with doubling of the dal. It is an inclusive expression for whatever God gave him of strength, troops and blessing, so restricting it to some particular things is not evident. Al-Suddi said: with troops. It was said: he used to spend the night around his prayer niche with forty thousand Muslims guarding him, though this is remote by ordinary custom. It was also said: with a awe that God cast into the hearts of his people. (Al-hikmah) here means: prophethood, or the Psalms (al-Zabur), or understanding in religion, or every speech and the instilling of truth. These are the views.

**(Abu Hayyan on the Verses, continued)**

﴿And decisive speech﴾. ʿAli and al-Shaʿbi said: it is imposing the oath upon the defendant and the burden of proof upon the claimant. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi said: judging between people with the truth, reaching it correctly and understanding it. Al-Shaʿbi also said: it is the phrase *amma baʿdu* ("to proceed"), because he was the first to say it and it separated one speech from another. Al-Zamakhshari said: because when one begins to speak about a matter of importance, he opens with the remembrance and praise of God; then, when he wishes to move on to the purpose he is aiming at, he separates it from the remembrance of God by saying *amma baʿdu*. It is also possible that by *al-khitab* is meant the measured speech that contains neither damaging brevity nor tiresome prolixity. Among what has come in describing the speech of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is: "A decisive statement, neither trivial nor verbose." End of quotation. Since God Most High had perfected the soul of His prophet Dawud with wisdom, He followed it with a description of the perfection of his creation in speech and worship, and so He said: ﴿and decisive speech﴾.

﴿Has there reached you the report of the litigants?﴾ When God Most High praised Dawud (peace be upon him) with what He praised him with, He mentioned this story so that it would be known that a story like this does not detract from the praise of him or from the exaltation of his rank, even though it includes his seeking forgiveness from his Lord. Seeking forgiveness does not indicate the commission of any act for which forgiveness must be sought, and seeking forgiveness has always been the mark of the prophets, who are attested to as protected from sin. The use of such an interrogative form usually occurs when what follows in the narrative is remarkable, as in His saying: ﴿Has there reached you the story of Musa?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 9], so that the one addressed by this question is prepared for what comes after and listens attentively. The exegetes have mentioned in this story things that are not fitting for the stations of the prophets; we have passed over mentioning them and will speak about the words of the verse.

*Al-naba'*: the report. *Al-khabar* is originally a verbal noun, which is why it can be used for the singular, the masculine and their derivatives. Here it has come in the plural, which is why He said ﴿when they climbed over the wall﴾, meaning: when they entered. As the poet said:

*And an opponent who prepares to enter, as if they were / Stallions, jealous, each one a bright, bold warrior.*

Apparently they were a group, which is why the plural pronoun was used. If the two litigants were only two, then others must have come with them for support or companionship. There is no disagreement that they were angels, as some have said. It has also been said that they were two brothers from the Children of Israel with the same father and mother, but the first view is better known. It has also been said that *al-khasm* here refers to two, and that the expression is metaphorical, so that they were described with the plural form used for more than two, because the meaning of plurality is present in the dual. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿two litigants﴾ is two parties, so that ﴿they climbed over﴾ and ﴿they entered﴾ refers back to *al-khasm* which is the plural of the two parties. What indicates that ﴿two litigants﴾ means "two parties" is the reading of one who recited: *baghā baʿḍuhum ʿalā baʿḍ* ("some of them oppressed others"). God Most High also said: ﴿These two litigants have disputed concerning their Lord﴾ [al-Hajj: 19], meaning: "Indeed this is my brother." As for what is reported, that two angels were sent to him, the meaning is that the litigation was between two, and there is nothing to prevent others from accompanying them. The term *khasm* was applied to the whole group, and *khasmān* to the two parties, because whoever comes with a litigant for support is in the form of a litigant, and it is not far-fetched that this designation applies to him.

The element that governs the adverbial phrase (*ẓarf*, adverb of time), which is *idh* in *idh atāka* ("when it reached you"), was stated by al-Hawfi, and it was refuted on the ground that the arrival of a report to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) can only occur in his time, not in the time of Dawud. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abu al-Baqaʾ said: the governing element is *naba'* (the report). This was refuted on the same grounds: a report that occurred in the time of Dawud (peace be upon him) cannot logically reach the Messenger of God (ﷺ). And if by *al-naba'* you mean the story itself, then it does not govern anything. It has also been said that the governing element is omitted, its estimate being: "Has there reached you the litigation of the litigants?" This was stated by al-Zamakhshari. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative governed by *al-khasm*, because of the meaning of the verb it contains. *Idh dakhalū* ("when they entered") is a substitute (*badal*) for the first *idh*. It has also been said that it is in the accusative governed by *tasawwarū* ("they climbed over").

It is reported that God Most High sent to him two angels in the form of two men. They asked to enter upon him, but they found him on the day of his worship, so he prevented them. Thereupon they climbed over the niche (*miḥrab*) at him, and he did not notice until they were sitting before him.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: he divided his time into four parts: a day for worship, a day for judgment, a day for attending to his private affairs, and a day for all the Children of Israel, when he would admonish them and make them weep. They came to him at a time other than judgment, so he was startled by them, because they had descended upon him from above, and it was the day of seclusion, when the guards were around him and did not allow anyone to enter upon him, so he feared they would harm him. It has also been said that this happened at night. It is possible that his fear arose because the people of his kingdom had treated him with contempt, to the point that some of them had abandoned seeking permission, so his fear would be over the corruption of conduct, not from the intruders. Abu al-Ahwas said: he was startled by them because they had entered upon him while each of them was holding the head of the other. It has also been said: he was startled by them when he saw them climb over a very high place which could not be ascended after months even with helpers and a large number. It has also been said that they said: "We could not reach you except by climbing over, because of the barrier preventing access, and we feared the matter between us would become worse," and Dawud accepted their excuse.

When they perceived his fright, they said: ﴿Fear not﴾, meaning: we are not among those who came except for the sake of litigation. ﴿Two litigants﴾: it is possible that this is connected to their words "Fear not," as they hastened to tell him what they had come for. It is also possible that he asked them: "What is your matter?" and they said: "Two litigants," meaning: we are two litigants. ﴿One of us has oppressed the other﴾ (*baghā*: transgressed, acted unjustly), as the poet said:

*But the young man, Hamal ibn Badr, transgressed, / And transgression is its pasture and its lair.*

Abu Yazid al-Jarrad reported from al-Kisaʾi the reading *khiṣmān* with a kasra on the *kha'*. In their command to him and their forbidding him, there was a certain harshness toward the rulers, which was prompted by the dispute and contention they were in. They asked for his justice without doubting that he would judge with justice.

The majority read ﴿and do not exceed﴾ (*wa lā tushṭiṭ*) as a separated form from *ashatta* (quadriliteral). Abu Rajaʾ, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, Qatada, al-Hasan and Abu Haywa read *tashṭiṭ* from *shatta* (trilateral). Qatada also read *tushiṭṭ*, assimilated from *ashatta*. Zirr read *tushāṭiṭ* with a damma on the *ta'* and an *alif*, on the pattern of *tufāʿil*, unassimilated. It is also reported from Qatada: *tashṭiṭ* from *shaṭaṭa*. ﴿The even way﴾ (*sawāʾ al-ṣirāṭ*): the middle of the path of truth, with no inclination in it, neither here nor there.

﴿Indeed this is my brother﴾: this is the statement of the claimant of the two. According to Ibn ʿAṭiyya, *akhī* (my brother) is an explanatory apposition (*ʿaṭf bayān*), while according to al-Zamakhshari it is either a substitute (*badal*) or the predicate (*khabar*) of *inna*. The term "brotherhood" here is used metaphorically, since they were two angels, but when they appeared in the form of two humans they spoke of brotherhood. Its figurative sense is that they are brothers in religion and faith, or in the sense of companionship and association, or in the sense of partnership and mixing, based on His saying: ﴿and indeed many partners oppress one another﴾. Each of these kinds of relationship requires the prohibition of transgression and encourages justice.

The majority read ﴿ninety-nine﴾ (*tis'un wa tis'ūn*) with a kasra on the *ta'* in both words. Al-Hasan and Zayd ibn ʿAli read them with a fatha. The majority read *naʿjatan* ("a ewe") with a fatha on the *nūn*. Al-Hasan and Ibn Hurmuz read it with a kasra on the *nūn*, which is a dialect of some of the Banu Tamim. It has been said that by the ewe is meant a wife.

﴿He said: Entrust it to me﴾: i.e., return it to my guardianship. Ibn Kaysan said: make it my share (*kifl*), i.e., my portion. Ibn ʿAbbas said: give it to me. It is reported from him and from Ibn Masʿud: transfer it to my charge. From Abu al-ʿAliya: take it to me so that I may take charge of it.

﴿And he overpowered me in speech﴾. Al-Ḍaḥḥak said: if he spoke, he was more eloquent than I, and if he fought, he was stronger than I. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: he was more persuasive and more powerful than I; when I addressed him, his speech was stronger than mine, and his strength was greater than mine. Al-Zamakhshari said: there came to me a skilled debater whom I could not refute with what I would have refuted him with. By "speech" is meant addressing the arguer in debate, or it means the suitor of a woman; if he proposed to her and then addressed me, meaning he prevailed over me in the proposal, so he beat me by marrying her instead of me. It has also been said: he overpowered me through his authority, because when he asked me, I could not oppose him.

The memorialist Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi said: in our lands there was a governor called Sayri ibn Abi Bakr. I spoke to him about asking a man on my behalf concerning a need. He said to me: "Do you not know that a ruler's request for a need is a seizure of it?" I said: "As for when he is just, then no."

Abu Haywa and Talha read *wa ʿazzanī* with a lightened *zā'*. Abu al-Fath said: he deleted one of the two *zā'*s for lightness, as Abu Zubayd said: *aḥsin bihi fa-hunna ilayhi shūs* (be kind to him, for they are fierce toward him). This is also reported from ʿAsim. ʿUbayd Allah, Abu Wa'il, Masruq, al-Ḍaḥḥak, al-Hasan and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read *wa ʿāzzanī* with an *alif* and a shadda on the *zā'*, meaning: and he overcame me.

The apparent meaning is to keep the word *naʿja* ("ewe") in its literal sense as the female of sheep, and that it is not used as a metaphor for a woman. There is no necessity to take it this way, because that statement was issued by the angels as a depiction of the case and an assumed supposition, not as the actual state of anything. So they presented the example of a man who had a single ewe, while his partner had ninety-nine. The partner wished to complete the hundred, so he coveted his partner's ewe and wanted to seize it from him. He argued with him about it in the manner of one eager to attain his aim. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿and indeed many partners oppress one another﴾. This depiction and parable is more eloquent in its purpose and more indicative of the intended meaning.

﴿He said: He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe in addition to his ewes﴾. This was not an initiation by Dawud (peace be upon him) immediately after the claimant finished his words, nor a ruling based on the apparent sense of his speech before the obligation became clear. It was said on the assumption: "If what you say is true, then indeed he has wronged you." It has also been said that there is an omission: the defendant acknowledged, then said: ﴿He has certainly wronged you﴾. However, the Qur'an does not relate the defendant's acknowledgment, because it is known from all the revealed laws that a judge does not rule until the defendant has responded. As for what al-Halimi said, that he saw in the claimant signs of weakness and humiliation, and so took his case to be that of an oppressed man as he claimed, which led him to avoid questioning the defendant and so he hastened with his words ("He has certainly wronged you"), his view is weak and cannot be relied upon.

It is reported that when Dawud (peace be upon him) heard the words of the complainant, he said to the other: "What do you say?" He acknowledged, so he said to him: "If you do not return to the truth, I will surely break what is in your eyes." Then he said to the second: ﴿He has certainly wronged you.﴾ Thereupon they smiled and departed, and he did not see them at that moment, and he saw that they went toward the sky in plain view of him.

He attributed the verbal noun to its object and made the question carry the sense of attribution, meaning: by the attribution of your ewe in the manner of a request and a demand. For this reason he used *ilā* after it.

﴿And indeed many partners oppress one another﴾: this is part of Dawud's speech, and it indicates that in his time injustice and transgression were widespread. *Al-khulaṭāʾ*: the partners who mix their property; the singular is *khalīṭ*. By this statement Dawud intended a good admonition and an encouragement to adopt the custom of righteous partners, whom he had judged to be few, and to make injustice hateful to them, and to console the wronged man for what befell him from his partner, and to show that he has an example in most partners. It was read *layabghiya* with a fatha on the *yā'*, on the assumption that the light *nūn* was dropped; the original was *layabghiyanna*, as the poet said: *iḍrib ʿanka al-humūma ṭāriqahā* ("strike away from yourself the worries that come at night"), meaning *iḍribanna*. In this case the oath and its answer form a predicate of *inna*, on the assumption of an omitted oath. In the majority reading, *layabghī* is the predicate of *inna*. It was also read *layabgh*, dropping the *yā'*, as in the line: *Muḥammad, tafdi nafsaka kullu nafs* ("Muhammad, may every soul ransom itself for you"), meaning *tafdī*, according to one of the two opinions.

*Qalīl* is its predicate, placed first, and *mā* is an additional particle conveying the sense of magnification and wonder, and *hum* is the subject (*mubtadaʾ*).

﴿Wa-ẓanna Dāwūd﴾ (And David thought). Since the dominant opinion (al-ẓann al-ghālib) closely approximates knowledge (al-'ilm), the word ẓann is used for it. Its meaning here is: David knew and was certain that We had tested him with the case of the two litigants.

Ibn 'Aṭiyya denied that ẓann can mean certainty (yaqīn). He said: "We do not find it in the speech of the Arabs. It is rather a suspension (tawqīf) between two beliefs, one of which predominates over the other. The Arabs use it for knowledge that is not based on the senses or on the indication of complete certainty. But people confuse this and say: ẓanna in the sense of ayqana." Ibn 'Aṭiyya elaborated on this at length in his book, which may be consulted there.

The majority (al-Jumhūr) read ﴿fatannāhu﴾ with the tā' and nūn doubled (فَتَنّاهُ, shaddah for intensification). 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, Abū Rajā', and al-Ḥasan, in one transmission from him, read it that way for emphasis. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk read أَفْتَنّاهُ (with alif, causative form), like the line of verse:

"Even if she has tested me, yesterday she too was tested [in her own way]."

Qatādah and Abū 'Amr, in one narration, read it with the tā' and nūn lightened, and the alif is the pronoun referring to the two litigants.

﴿Fa-istaghfara rabbahu wa-kharra rāki'an wa-anāb﴾ (So he asked his Lord for forgiveness, and fell down bowing and turned in repentance). Rāki'an is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) and khurūr means falling down to the ground. As for the meaning, either he used rukū' (bowing) to mean sujūd (prostration), or he mentioned the first stage of the falling, meaning: bowing in order to prostrate. Al-Ḥasan said: "Because one does not prostrate until one has bowed." Al-Ḥasan ibn al-Faḍl said: "He fell from his bowing," meaning he prostrated after having been bowing. Some people said: kharra is said of one who bowed even if he did not reach the ground.

What I incline towards is what the apparent meaning of the verse indicates: that those who scaled the prayer niche (al-miḥrāb) were humans, who entered upon him by an unusual entrance and at a time other than his sitting for judgment. He was alarmed by them, assuming they intended to assassinate him, since he was alone in his prayer niche worshipping his Lord. When it became clear to him that they had come with a case, and two of them came forward to be judged, as Allah the Exalted related, David, peace be upon him, had thought that their entering upon him at that time and from that direction was a deliverance from Allah from their assassinating him. But what he had supposed did not occur, so he asked forgiveness for that assumption, since it was mistaken and what he had thought would happen did not happen. He either prostrated, or returned to Allah the Exalted, and He forgave him that assumption. For this reason He indicated it by His words ﴿fa-ghafarnā lahu dhālik﴾ (so We forgave him that), and nothing preceded it except His words ﴿wa-ẓanna Dāwūd annamā fatannāhu﴾ (And David thought that We had only tested him).

It is known with certainty that the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected (ma'ṣūmūn) from sins, and it is impossible for them to commit any of them. For if we permitted any such thing concerning them, the divine laws (sharā'i') would be nullified, and we could not trust anything they say that Allah revealed to them. Therefore, what Allah the Exalted related in His Book stands as He intended, and whatever the storytellers (al-quṣṣāṣ) relate that disparages the station of prophethood, we reject it. We are, as the poet said:

"We give precedence to the judgment of reason in every doubtful matter, when the sitters of storytellers prefer the reports."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 38, verses 15–25 (part 1 of 3):

﴿They are waiting for nothing but a single blast, with no delay (fawaq) in it.﴾ ﴿They say: "Our Lord, hasten to us our share (qitt) before the Day of Reckoning."﴾ ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud, possessor of strength (dhu al-ayd). He was ever turning back (in repentance).﴾ ﴿We subjected the mountains to glorify (Us) with him at evening and at sunrise.﴾ ﴿And the birds, gathered together; each one was turning back to Him.﴾ ﴿We strengthened his kingdom and gave him wisdom and decisive speech.﴾ ﴿Has the news of the litigants reached you, when they climbed over the walls of the prayer niche (mihrab)?﴾ ﴿When they entered upon Dawud and he was alarmed by them, they said: "Do not fear. We are two litigants, one of whom has wronged the other. So judge between us with truth, do not exceed (the bounds), and guide us to the even path.﴾ ﴿This brother of mine has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe. He said: 'Commit it to my care,' and he overpowered me in speech.'﴾ ﴿He said: "He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe in addition to his ewes. Indeed many partners wrong one another, except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and few are they." And Dawud thought that We had only tested him, so he asked his Lord for forgiveness, fell down bowing and turned (to Him) in repentance.﴾ ﴿So We forgave him that, and indeed he has nearness to Us and a good final return.﴾

(Wa ma yanzuru hā'ulā') means "they are not waiting for," i.e., they await nothing. (Hā'ulā') is a demonstrative indicating the Quraysh disbelievers. The use of (hā'ulā') strengthens the view that (ulā'ika) refers to the nearer peoples, such as the people of Nuh and those mentioned after them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It may be a reference to all the confederates, since they are present in mention, or because they are as if present before God." End of quote. There is a remoteness in this, and it is a report from Him, exalted, that existence has confirmed.

(Al-sayha) is what befell them of killing, captivity and defeat, as one says: "Time shouted at them." Qatada said: He threatened them with the blast of the Resurrection and the blowing of the Trumpet. It has also been said: with a blast by which they will be destroyed in this world. The first view implies that the Messenger is waiting for something specific to happen to them. On both views they are on the path of punishment and under a dangerous matter, awaiting nothing but ruin.

The majority of readers recite (min fawaq) with a fatha on the fa'. Al-Sulami, Ibn Wathtab, al-A'mash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Talha read it with a damma. It is said that both have the same meaning, like (qiṣāṣ al-sh'ar). Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi said: with a fatha, it means recovery (ifaqa) from (afaqa wa-istarah), like (jawab) from (ajaba). Ibn Abbas said: (min fawaq) means "from repetition." Mujahid said: "from return."

(Qittana): our share of Paradise, so that we may enjoy it in this world. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Jubayr. Qatada and Mujahid also said: our share of the punishment. Abu al-Aliya and al-Kalbi said: our records (suhuf) with our faith. Al-Suddi said: the meaning is: show us our dwellings in Paradise so that we may follow you. On every view, they said this only in mockery and derision. The meaning of (qabla yawm al-hisab) is: those who claim that it will occur in this world, since they are disbelievers who do not believe in the Resurrection.

Since their statement implied mockery, God, exalted, commanded His Prophet to be patient with their harm, and He mentioned stories of the prophets, Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub and others, and what befell them. They were patient until God relieved them, and their end was the best of ends. Likewise, you shall be patient, and your affair will end in the best outcome, and you will attain what you want of establishing your religion and extinguishing misguidance. It has been said: "Be patient over what they say," and magnify the matter of their opposition to God in their eyes, and remind them of the story of Dawud and what befell him, though he was given prophethood and kingship. So what do you suppose of you, with your disbelief and disobedience? End of quote. This is compiled from the words of al-Zamakhshari with some changes to his wording that do not suit the station of prophethood. It has also been said: He was commanded to be patient, so He mentioned the stories of the prophets so that they would be proof of the validity of his prophethood. It has been said: "Be patient over what they say," and hold fast to what you were charged with, namely enduring them and bearing their harm; and remember Dawud and his honour with God, and what befell him, and what he encountered of God's rebuke.

(Dhu al-ayd): possessor of strength in religion, in the law, in proclaiming God's command and in obedience to God. He was also physically strong. (Al-awwab): one who returns to obedience to God. This was said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd. Al-Suddi said: the one who glorifies. Describing him as (awwab) indicates that the meaning of (dhu al-ayd) is strength in religion. It is said: a man is (ayd), (ayyid), or (dhu ad) and (ayad): all meaning one who is strong. (Wal-ishraq): at the time of sunrise. Tha'lab said: "The sun shone (sharaqat) when it rose, and (ashraqat) when it lit up and became clear." In a hadith: "He, peace be upon him, prayed the forenoon prayer and said: 'O Umm Hani, this is the prayer of ishraq.'" It was at these two times that the prayer of the Children of Israel took place.

All the discussion of the mountains glorifying God in the story of Dawud has already been given in the surah of al-Anbiya. He used the present tense with the active participle to indicate that the glorification occurs gradually, moment by moment, and state after state, so it is as if the hearer is present and hears those mountains glorifying. Similar is the verse of al-A'sha:

By my life, many eyes have turned
toward the light of a fire in plains that is burning.

That is: burning little by little. Had he said (muhriqah), it would not have indicated this meaning.

The majority read (wal-tayra mahshurah) in the accusative, coordinated with (al-jibal) in "they glorify": coordination of object with object and of state with state, like your saying: "I struck Hind stripped bare and Da'd clothed." Ibn Abi Ablah and al-Jahdari read (wal-tayru mahshurah) in the nominative, as subject and predicate. (Mahshurah) came in the passive participle form because it was not meant that they gather anything, since their gatherer is God, exalted. Thus their gathering all together is more indicative of power. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (lahu) refers to Dawud, meaning each of the mountains and birds is for Dawud's sake, that is, for the sake of his glorification; they glorified because they used to echo his glorification. (Awwab) is placed in the position of (musabbih). It has also been said that the pronoun refers to God, meaning each of Dawud, the mountains and the birds is (awwab), that is, glorifying and returning to glorification.

The majority read (wa-shadadna) without doubling: that is, We strengthened, as in His saying: "We will strengthen your arm with your brother" (al-Qasas 35). Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ablah read it with doubling of the dal. It is an inclusive expression for whatever God gave him of strength, troops and blessing, so restricting it to some particular things is not evident. Al-Suddi said: with troops. It was said: he used to spend the night around his prayer niche with forty thousand Muslims guarding him, though this is remote by ordinary custom. It was also said: with a awe that God cast into the hearts of his people. (Al-hikmah) here means: prophethood, or the Psalms (al-Zabur), or understanding in religion, or every speech and the instilling of truth. These are the views.

**(Abu Hayyan on the Verses, continued)**

﴿And decisive speech﴾. ʿAli and al-Shaʿbi said: it is imposing the oath upon the defendant and the burden of proof upon the claimant. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi said: judging between people with the truth, reaching it correctly and understanding it. Al-Shaʿbi also said: it is the phrase *amma baʿdu* ("to proceed"), because he was the first to say it and it separated one speech from another. Al-Zamakhshari said: because when one begins to speak about a matter of importance, he opens with the remembrance and praise of God; then, when he wishes to move on to the purpose he is aiming at, he separates it from the remembrance of God by saying *amma baʿdu*. It is also possible that by *al-khitab* is meant the measured speech that contains neither damaging brevity nor tiresome prolixity. Among what has come in describing the speech of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is: "A decisive statement, neither trivial nor verbose." End of quotation. Since God Most High had perfected the soul of His prophet Dawud with wisdom, He followed it with a description of the perfection of his creation in speech and worship, and so He said: ﴿and decisive speech﴾.

﴿Has there reached you the report of the litigants?﴾ When God Most High praised Dawud (peace be upon him) with what He praised him with, He mentioned this story so that it would be known that a story like this does not detract from the praise of him or from the exaltation of his rank, even though it includes his seeking forgiveness from his Lord. Seeking forgiveness does not indicate the commission of any act for which forgiveness must be sought, and seeking forgiveness has always been the mark of the prophets, who are attested to as protected from sin. The use of such an interrogative form usually occurs when what follows in the narrative is remarkable, as in His saying: ﴿Has there reached you the story of Musa?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 9], so that the one addressed by this question is prepared for what comes after and listens attentively. The exegetes have mentioned in this story things that are not fitting for the stations of the prophets; we have passed over mentioning them and will speak about the words of the verse.

*Al-naba'*: the report. *Al-khabar* is originally a verbal noun, which is why it can be used for the singular, the masculine and their derivatives. Here it has come in the plural, which is why He said ﴿when they climbed over the wall﴾, meaning: when they entered. As the poet said:

*And an opponent who prepares to enter, as if they were / Stallions, jealous, each one a bright, bold warrior.*

Apparently they were a group, which is why the plural pronoun was used. If the two litigants were only two, then others must have come with them for support or companionship. There is no disagreement that they were angels, as some have said. It has also been said that they were two brothers from the Children of Israel with the same father and mother, but the first view is better known. It has also been said that *al-khasm* here refers to two, and that the expression is metaphorical, so that they were described with the plural form used for more than two, because the meaning of plurality is present in the dual. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿two litigants﴾ is two parties, so that ﴿they climbed over﴾ and ﴿they entered﴾ refers back to *al-khasm* which is the plural of the two parties. What indicates that ﴿two litigants﴾ means "two parties" is the reading of one who recited: *baghā baʿḍuhum ʿalā baʿḍ* ("some of them oppressed others"). God Most High also said: ﴿These two litigants have disputed concerning their Lord﴾ [al-Hajj: 19], meaning: "Indeed this is my brother." As for what is reported, that two angels were sent to him, the meaning is that the litigation was between two, and there is nothing to prevent others from accompanying them. The term *khasm* was applied to the whole group, and *khasmān* to the two parties, because whoever comes with a litigant for support is in the form of a litigant, and it is not far-fetched that this designation applies to him.

The element that governs the adverbial phrase (*ẓarf*, adverb of time), which is *idh* in *idh atāka* ("when it reached you"), was stated by al-Hawfi, and it was refuted on the ground that the arrival of a report to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) can only occur in his time, not in the time of Dawud. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abu al-Baqaʾ said: the governing element is *naba'* (the report). This was refuted on the same grounds: a report that occurred in the time of Dawud (peace be upon him) cannot logically reach the Messenger of God (ﷺ). And if by *al-naba'* you mean the story itself, then it does not govern anything. It has also been said that the governing element is omitted, its estimate being: "Has there reached you the litigation of the litigants?" This was stated by al-Zamakhshari. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative governed by *al-khasm*, because of the meaning of the verb it contains. *Idh dakhalū* ("when they entered") is a substitute (*badal*) for the first *idh*. It has also been said that it is in the accusative governed by *tasawwarū* ("they climbed over").

It is reported that God Most High sent to him two angels in the form of two men. They asked to enter upon him, but they found him on the day of his worship, so he prevented them. Thereupon they climbed over the niche (*miḥrab*) at him, and he did not notice until they were sitting before him.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: he divided his time into four parts: a day for worship, a day for judgment, a day for attending to his private affairs, and a day for all the Children of Israel, when he would admonish them and make them weep. They came to him at a time other than judgment, so he was startled by them, because they had descended upon him from above, and it was the day of seclusion, when the guards were around him and did not allow anyone to enter upon him, so he feared they would harm him. It has also been said that this happened at night. It is possible that his fear arose because the people of his kingdom had treated him with contempt, to the point that some of them had abandoned seeking permission, so his fear would be over the corruption of conduct, not from the intruders. Abu al-Ahwas said: he was startled by them because they had entered upon him while each of them was holding the head of the other. It has also been said: he was startled by them when he saw them climb over a very high place which could not be ascended after months even with helpers and a large number. It has also been said that they said: "We could not reach you except by climbing over, because of the barrier preventing access, and we feared the matter between us would become worse," and Dawud accepted their excuse.

When they perceived his fright, they said: ﴿Fear not﴾, meaning: we are not among those who came except for the sake of litigation. ﴿Two litigants﴾: it is possible that this is connected to their words "Fear not," as they hastened to tell him what they had come for. It is also possible that he asked them: "What is your matter?" and they said: "Two litigants," meaning: we are two litigants. ﴿One of us has oppressed the other﴾ (*baghā*: transgressed, acted unjustly), as the poet said:

*But the young man, Hamal ibn Badr, transgressed, / And transgression is its pasture and its lair.*

Abu Yazid al-Jarrad reported from al-Kisaʾi the reading *khiṣmān* with a kasra on the *kha'*. In their command to him and their forbidding him, there was a certain harshness toward the rulers, which was prompted by the dispute and contention they were in. They asked for his justice without doubting that he would judge with justice.

The majority read ﴿and do not exceed﴾ (*wa lā tushṭiṭ*) as a separated form from *ashatta* (quadriliteral). Abu Rajaʾ, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, Qatada, al-Hasan and Abu Haywa read *tashṭiṭ* from *shatta* (trilateral). Qatada also read *tushiṭṭ*, assimilated from *ashatta*. Zirr read *tushāṭiṭ* with a damma on the *ta'* and an *alif*, on the pattern of *tufāʿil*, unassimilated. It is also reported from Qatada: *tashṭiṭ* from *shaṭaṭa*. ﴿The even way﴾ (*sawāʾ al-ṣirāṭ*): the middle of the path of truth, with no inclination in it, neither here nor there.

﴿Indeed this is my brother﴾: this is the statement of the claimant of the two. According to Ibn ʿAṭiyya, *akhī* (my brother) is an explanatory apposition (*ʿaṭf bayān*), while according to al-Zamakhshari it is either a substitute (*badal*) or the predicate (*khabar*) of *inna*. The term "brotherhood" here is used metaphorically, since they were two angels, but when they appeared in the form of two humans they spoke of brotherhood. Its figurative sense is that they are brothers in religion and faith, or in the sense of companionship and association, or in the sense of partnership and mixing, based on His saying: ﴿and indeed many partners oppress one another﴾. Each of these kinds of relationship requires the prohibition of transgression and encourages justice.

The majority read ﴿ninety-nine﴾ (*tis'un wa tis'ūn*) with a kasra on the *ta'* in both words. Al-Hasan and Zayd ibn ʿAli read them with a fatha. The majority read *naʿjatan* ("a ewe") with a fatha on the *nūn*. Al-Hasan and Ibn Hurmuz read it with a kasra on the *nūn*, which is a dialect of some of the Banu Tamim. It has been said that by the ewe is meant a wife.

﴿He said: Entrust it to me﴾: i.e., return it to my guardianship. Ibn Kaysan said: make it my share (*kifl*), i.e., my portion. Ibn ʿAbbas said: give it to me. It is reported from him and from Ibn Masʿud: transfer it to my charge. From Abu al-ʿAliya: take it to me so that I may take charge of it.
