The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, had he said 'if Allah wills,' they would all have fought in the cause of Allah as horsemen." So the meaning of His words ﴿And We certainly tested Solomon and placed upon his throne a body﴾ is this, and the body that was placed is the child who was born as a half-man. Others said: Solomon fell ill with a sickness like fainting, until he became upon his throne a body as if without a soul.

When Allah commanded His Prophet (peace be upon him) to be patient with what the disbelievers of Quraysh and others said, He commanded him to mention those who were tested and were patient. So He mentioned the story of Dawud (David), the story of Sulayman, and the story of Ayyub (Job), so that he might take them as examples, and He mentioned the nearness and high station they had with Him. It would not be fitting for Him to mention, as a model to follow, someone to whom the exegetes attributed things that are too grave to be uttered and whose existence is rationally impossible, such as Satan taking the form of a prophet so that his affair becomes confused for the people, and they believe that the one in that form is the Prophet. Even if this were possible, no prophet could be trusted to have been sent. These are rather statements borrowed from the heretical Sophists (al-SufsatA'iyya). We ask Allah to preserve our minds and intellects from them.

﴿Then he turned in repentance﴾, meaning: after Our testing him, he continued to turn back and repent.

﴿He said: My Lord, forgive me﴾. This is the etiquette of the prophets and righteous people: seeking forgiveness from Allah, in humbling the self, showing lowliness and humility, and seeking advancement in the stations. In the hadith: "I seek forgiveness from Allah seventy times in a day and night." Seeking forgiveness is a preface before what the one seeking forgiveness asks, by asking for what is most important in his religion, so that the affair of his worldly life is arranged thereby, like the words of Nuh (Noah) in what Allah related of him: ﴿So I said: Seek forgiveness from your Lord, for He is ever Forgiving﴾ [Nuh: 10] ﴿He will send down the sky upon you in abundant rain﴾ [Nuh: 11], and so on. It is apparent that the request for a kingdom came after this trial. The exegetes mentioned that he remained in his kingdom twenty years before this trial and remained after it twenty years. So it is possible that he was in a kingdom before the trial, and then after it he asked for a kingdom restricted by the description that follows, namely that it should not be fitting for anyone after him. They differed about this restriction. Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and Qatadah said: "for the duration of my life, I will not take it away, and it will pass to another." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "He only intended by this a permissible aim, because a person may desire from the bounty of Allah what no one else attains, especially according to rank and prophethood. Consider His words ﴿it should not be fitting﴾: it is only a word that admits of possibility; it does not definitively establish that Allah does not give the like of that kingdom to anyone." End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Sulayman (peace be upon him) grew up in a house of kingship and prophethood and inherited both. He wished to ask his Lord for a miracle, so he asked, according to what he was accustomed to, for a kingdom exceeding the other kingdoms, with an extraordinary increase that reached the limit of a miracle, so that this would be a proof of his prophethood and would overpower those to whom he was sent. It would not be a miracle unless it breaks customary norms. That is the meaning of His words ﴿it should not be fitting for anyone after me﴾. It was also said: it was a great kingdom, and he feared that someone like it would be given to someone who would not observe Allah's limits in it, as the angels said ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?﴾ [al-Baqara: 30]. It was also said: a kingdom that I will not be stripped of, and in which no one will stand in my place. It is also possible to say: Allah knew that in what He singled him out with of that great kingdom were benefits in religion, and He knew that none other than him would manage the affairs of His beloved ones, and wisdom required that it be granted to him. So He commanded him to ask for it as a gift, in a manner by which Allah knew that none but he alone could control it, not any other of His servants. Or he wished to say: a great kingdom, and so he said ﴿it should not be fitting for anyone after me﴾, intending only the greatness and vastness of the kingdom, as you say of someone: "there is no one who has such favour and wealth," though perhaps people have similar things, but you intend to magnify what he possesses. End of quote.

When he had exaggerated in describing this kingdom that he asked for, he used, in describing Allah (Exalted), a word that indicates intensity, saying ﴿Indeed You are the Bestower﴾ [Al 'Imran: 8], meaning the One of abundant gifts, for no gift is too great for Him. When he asked for the gift that was specific to his request, He gave it to him and granted him what He mentions in His words ﴿So We subjected the wind to him﴾.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) recited "al-rih" (the wind) in the singular. Al-Hasan, Abu Rajaʼ, Qatadah, and Abu Ja'far recited "al-riyah" (the winds) in the plural, which is more general given the greatness of Sulayman's kingdom, though the singular in meaning is plural since it is a generic noun (ism jins). "Flowing" (tajri) may be a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya), meaning "flowing", or it may be an explanatory clause for His words ﴿We subjected the wind to him﴾. "At his command" means that it is not prevented from him when he wishes it to flow.

﴿Gently﴾ (rukhaan): Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: "obedient." Mujahid said: "pleasant."

﴿Wherever he directed﴾ (haythu asaab): meaning wherever he aimed and intended. Al-Zajjaj related from the Arabs: "asaba al-sawab fa-akhta al-jawab" (he hit the right thing but missed the answer), meaning he aimed. It is related from Ru'ba that two men of the people of language intended him to ask him about this word, so he came out to them and said: "Where are you aiming?" They said: "This is what we seek." It is also said: "asaba Allah bika khayran" (may Allah make good come to you through you). Al-Tha'labi recited:

"He hit the matter, but could not, so he missed the answer at the joint."

Wahb said: "haythu asaab" means "where he intended." It was said: it is also possible that asaba is the causative form of sāba, with the hamza of transitivity added, meaning where he directed his troops and made them pour forth like the flowing of clouds and rain. It was also said: asaba means "aradha" (he intended) in the dialect of Himyar. Qatadah said: in the dialect of Hajar.

﴿And the devils﴾ (al-shayatin) is conjoined to "the wind," and ﴿every builder and diver﴾ is a substitution (badal). He used forms of intensive nouns (abniyat al-mubalagha), as in His words: ﴿They made for him whatever he wished: sanctuaries, images...﴾ [Saba': 13], etc. Al-Nabigha said:

"Except Sulayman, when the God said to him: 'Stand in the wilderness and restrain them from the Fanad (a place)...'

And the army of jinn, I have permitted them, they build Tadmur with slabs and pillars."

The conjoined element of a general term is general, so the sense is: and every diver, that is, in the sea, extracting ornaments for him, and he was the first who extracted pearls. ﴿And others﴾ is conjoined to "every," so it falls within the substitution, since it is a substitution of a whole for a whole, a detailed substitution, meaning from the jinn, who are the rebellious ones. He subjected them to him until he bound them in chains for their disbelief. Al-Nabigha said in this:

"Whoever obeys you, benefit him by his obedience, as he obeyed you, and guide him to the right course. And whoever disobeys you, punish him with a punishment that deters the wrongdoer, and do not sit upon his carcass."

The explanation of ﴿bound in chains﴾ was given at the end of Surat Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and descriptions of Sulayman's kingdom in Surat al-Naml.

﴿This is Our gift﴾: a reference to what Allah the Exalted gave him of the vast kingdom, the subjugation of the wind, of humans, jinn and birds. He commanded him to bestow favour upon whom he wished and withhold from whom he wished, and He made him stand at the measure of the blessing. Then He permitted him to dispose of them as he wished, and He, Exalted, knew that he would not dispose of them except in obedience to Allah. Al-Hasan and others said: Qatadah said it refers to what the jinn did, meaning: bestow favour upon whomever you wish among them, release him from his bonds, dismiss him from his service, and hold back his affair as you wish. Ibn 'Abbas said: it refers to what He granted him of women and the power to have intercourse with them, but this may not be authentic from Ibn 'Abbas, because no mention of women has occurred here, nor of the power he was given over that. ﴿Without reckoning﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to "Our gift," meaning: this is Our gift, abundant and great, which you cannot nearly count. It is also possible that ﴿without reckoning﴾ completes ﴿so bestow favour﴾ or ﴿withhold﴾, meaning: there is no reckoning against you in giving to whom you wish or withholding from him, and in releasing whom you wish of the devils or binding him.

Allah concluded the account with what He mentioned in the story of his father, namely His words: ﴿And indeed he has near Us a station and a good return﴾ [Sad: 25]. Al-Jumhur recited "wa husna ma'ab" (and a good return) in the accusative, conjoined to "la-zulfa" (a station). Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi 'Abla recited it in the nominative, stopping at "zulfa" and beginning with "wa husnu ma'ab," which is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, its estimated sense being: "and a good return is for him."

[p. 394]

﴿O David, We have made you a khalīfah (vicegerent) on the earth, so judge between people with truth, and do not follow desire, for it will lead you astray from the way of Allah. Indeed, those who go astray from the way of Allah will have a severe punishment because they forgot the Day of Reckoning.﴾ ﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve, so woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire.﴾ ﴿Shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters on the earth? Or shall We treat the God-fearing like the wicked?﴾ ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses and that people of understanding may take heed.﴾ ﴿And We gave to David Solomon. What an excellent servant! Indeed, he was ever turning back (to Allah).﴾ ﴿When there were displayed before him in the evening the swift, well-bred horses.﴾ ﴿He said: "Indeed, I have preferred the love of good (al-khayr) over the remembrance of my Lord," until they were hidden behind the veil.﴾ ﴿"Bring them back to me," and he began to pass his hand over their legs and necks.﴾ ﴿And We certainly tested Solomon and placed upon his throne a body; then he turned back (to Allah).﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone after me. Indeed, You are the Bestower."﴾ ﴿So We subjected the wind to him, flowing gently by his command wherever he directed.﴾ ﴿And the devils, every builder and diver,﴾ ﴿and others bound together in chains.﴾ ﴿"This is Our gift, so grant (favours) or withhold, without account."﴾ ﴿And indeed, for him with Us is a nearness and a good final return.﴾

[p. 395]

His, may He be exalted, making David a khalīfah on the earth indicates his high station with Him, peace be upon him, and His choosing him, and it repels from the one who attributes to him anything that does not befit the office of prophethood. The word khalīfah may mean: one who succeeds those who came before you among the prophets; or that He elevates your rank by making you a ruler with executive authority. From this usage it is said: "the khulafā' of Allah on His earth." It has been inferred from this verse that the earth needs a khalīfah from Allah, but this does not necessarily follow from the verse; rather, its necessity comes from the Sharīʿah and from ijmāʿ (scholarly consensus). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "The term khalīfat Allah is not used except for a Messenger. As for the khulafāʾ, each one of them is the khalīfah of the one before him. What occurs in poetry of calling one of them khalīfat Allah is a figurative usage, as Qays al-Ruqayyāt said:

"Khalīfat Allah over His creation, the pens and the books have confirmed this."

The Companions said to Abū Bakr: "Khalīfat Rasūl Allah," and he was called by this during his term. When ʿUmar became ruler, they said: "Khalīfat khalīfat Rasūl Allah." The matter lengthened, and it was further extended to the future, so they called him Amīr al-Mu'minīn, and this title was restricted to the caliphs." End of quote.

﴿So judge between people with truth﴾: this is a command to persist, and an admonition to others who are in charge of people's affairs. Since he is ma'ṣūm (infallible, protected from error), he does not judge except with truth; he was first commanded to judge, and since desire may afflict one who is not infallible, he was commanded to avoid it, and the outcome of following it was mentioned, namely that it leads him astray from the way of Allah. The fāʾ in ﴿فَيُضِلَّكَ﴾ (fa-yuḍillaka, "so it will lead you astray") is a response to the prohibition, and its agent is either the pronoun of (al-hawā, "desire"), or the pronoun of the verbal noun implied by ﴿ولا تَتَّبِعِ﴾ (wa-lā tattabiʿ), meaning: the following of desire will lead you astray. Since He mentioned what results from following desire, which is being led astray from the way of Allah, He mentioned the punishment of the one who goes astray.

Al-Jumhūr (the majority of reciters) read ﴿يَضِلُّونَ﴾ (yaḍillūna) with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, because when the following of desire led them astray, they became those who go astray. Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan, according to a variant reported from them, and Abū Ḥaywah read it with a ḍammah on the yāʾ (yuḍillūna), and this reading is more general, because the one who is led astray is not necessarily the one who leads others astray; but the reading of the majority is clearer. The phrase ﴿بِما نَسُوا﴾ (bimā nasū, "because they forgot") is connected to what is connected to ﴿لَهم﴾ (lahum, "for them"), and nasū means: they abandoned. The word yawm (ﷺ... "day") may be in the accusative governed by nasū, or by what is connected to lahum, and forgetting would then be an expression for their going astray from the way of Allah.

[The word] ﴿باطِلًا﴾ (bāṭilan, "in vain") is in the accusative either as an adjective for an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a vain creation," or as a circumstantial accusative, meaning "as those who render it void," or "possessors of vanity," or as an object of purpose. The meaning of bāṭilan is: in vain, purposelessly.

﴿That﴾, meaning the vanity of their creation, ﴿is the assumption of those who disbelieve﴾, meaning their supposition. Although these people acknowledge that the Creator of the heavens and the earth is Allah, they, insofar as they deny the return, the reward and the punishment, suppose that the creation of these things is not for wisdom, and that the creation of these things is merely futility. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿أفَحَسِبْتُمْ أنَّما خَلَقْناكم عَبَثًا وأنَّكم إلَيْنا لا تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 115] ("Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?"). Thus He alerted to the Return and to the requital for it. Then He mentioned the contrast between the believer who does righteous deeds and the corrupter, and that the two are not equal, and He set righteousness against corruption and piety against wickedness. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "It is general, covering all Muslims and disbelievers." It was also said that it concerns a group of the idolaters of Quraysh who said: "We will have in the Hereafter more than we have in this world," so Allah revealed this verse. It was also said that it concerns specific people among believers and disbelievers who fought at the Battle of Badr: ʿAlī, Ḥamzah, and ʿUbaydah ibn al-Ḥārith, may Allah be pleased with them, against ʿUtbah, Shaybah, and al-Walīd ibn ʿUtbah, and He described each group with what suited them.

The interrogation with (am, "or shall") in both places is an interrogation of denial, and the meaning is: those who reform and those who corrupt are not equal before Allah, nor are the God-fearing and the wicked. How could there be equality between those who obey and those who disobey? Otherwise, requital would be nullified, and requital is certainly going to happen, and equality is ruled out.

Since equality was ruled out between that by which one earns eternal happiness, which is the Book of Allah, He said: ﴿كِتابٌ أنْزَلْناهُ﴾ ("A Book which We have sent down"). Its nominative status is by presumption of a subject, meaning: this is a Book. Al-Jumhūr read ﴿مُبارَكٌ﴾ (mubārakun, "blessed") as an adjective. It was also read as mubārakan in a necessary circumstantial status, meaning: this is a Book. Al-Jumhūr read ﴿لِيَدَّبَّرُوا آياتِهِ﴾ (liyaddabbarū āyātihi, "that they may reflect upon its verses") with the third-person plural yāʾ and a doubled dāl, and its original form is liyatadabbarū. ʿAlī read it according to this original form. Abū Jaʿfar read it with the second-person tāʾ and a single dāl. The same was reported from ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī, according to a variant reported from them, and the original is litatadabbarū with two tāʾs, one of which was dropped, according to the disagreement over it: is it the tāʾ of the present-tense prefix or the tāʾ that follows it?

The lām in liyaddabbarū is the lām of purpose (kay). The reflection (tadabbur), which is contemplation of the verses and deliberation that leads its possessor to consider the outcomes of things, is attributed to them all. The remembrance (tadhakkur) is attributed to the people of intellects (ulū al-albāb), because the possessor of intellect has within him what guides him to truth, which is his intellect, so he needs only something to remind him, and then he remembers. The one singled out for praise is omitted, and the implied sense is ﴿نِعْمَ العَبْدُ﴾ (niʿma al-ʿabd, "what an excellent servant") — he is, namely Solomon. It was also read as naʿim, according to the original form, as one says:

"The seekers among the people are excellent, the people of the Shuṭur."

He, exalted is He, praised him because he frequently returned to Him, or because of his frequent glorification of Him.

﴿Idh ʿurida﴾ ("When there were displayed"): the governing element of idh (when) is ﴿أوّابٌ﴾ (awwāb, "one who turns back"), and it was also said: the verb is "remember," according to the difference in interpreting this verse. Al-Jumhūr said: there were displayed to him thousands of horses which his father had left to him; it was also said: one thousand horses. They were run before him in the evening, and he became preoccupied with their beauty, their running, and his love for them, so he was distracted from remembering Him. He said: "Bring them back to me," and he began striking their necks and hamstrings with the sword, because they had been the cause of his neglect of that remembrance; then Allah replaced them for him with something swifter than them, the wind. Others, among them al-Thaʿlabī, said: there was a famine among the people, and horse meat was lawful for them, so he slaughtered them to be eaten, as a form of nearness to Allah and sacrificing offerings according to our practice. End of quote. In this story there are expressions that diminish the station of prophethood, which we will leave aside.

The khayr (good) in His saying ﴿حُبَّ الخَيْرِ﴾ (ḥubba al-khayr, "the love of good") means here the horses, and the Arabs call horses khayr; this was stated by Qatādah and al-Suddī. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Jubayr said: al-khayr here means wealth. The phrase ﴿حُبَّ الخَيْرِ﴾ is in the accusative. It was said: it is the object, because aḥbabtu includes the meaning of āthartu ("I preferred"), as stated by al-Farrāʾ. It was also said: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun of comparison, meaning: I loved horses like the love of good, that is, a love like the love of good. It was also said: it is transitive with ʿan, so it implies a verb that takes ʿan, meaning: I turned the love of good away from the remembrance of my Lord, or: I made the love of good substitute for the remembrance of my Lord. Abū al-Fatḥ al-Hamdānī mentioned in his book al-Tibyān that aḥbabtu has the meaning of "I stayed/clung," from the saying:

"Like a bad camel when it stayed put."

Another group said: aḥbabtu means "fell to the ground," derived from aḥabba al-baʿīr when it was exhausted and collapsed. Some said: ḥabba al-baʿīr means it knelt, and fulān means he lowered his head. Abū Zayd said: "A camel is muḥibb, and it has become exhausted (aḥabba ihbāban) when it is afflicted by sickness or a break, so it does not leave its place until it recovers or dies." Thaʿlab said: "The exhausted camel is called muḥibb," so the meaning is: I remained away from the remembrance of my Lord. On this view, (ḥubba al-khayr) is an object of purpose.

The apparent view is that the pronoun in ﴿تَوارَتْ﴾ (tawārat, "they were hidden") refers to ﴿الصّافِناتُ﴾ (al-ṣāfināt, "the swift horses"), meaning: they entered their stables, and these are the veil. It was also said: until they were hidden in the race by something that screened them from sight. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the sun, even though it has not been mentioned, because the evening (al-ʿashiyy) indicates it. A group said: the horses were displayed before Solomon while he was in prayer, so he gestured to them that he was in prayer, and they were removed from him until they entered the stables; then he said, when he finished his prayer: ﴿إنِّي أحْبَبْتُ حُبَّ الخَيْرِ﴾ meaning: the good that is with Allah in the Hereafter, because of the remembrance of my Lord, as if he were saying: that occupied me from seeing the horses until they were brought into their stables. "Bring them back to me," so he began to stroke their manes and their legs out of love for them. Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Zuhrī said: his stroking of their legs and necks was not with a sword, but with his hands, as honour and affection for them; al-Ṭabarī preferred this view. It was also said: it was washing with water. Al-Thaʿlabī said: this stroking on the legs and necks was a branding mark for being held in the cause of Allah. End of quote. This view is the one that suits the stations of the prophets, not the view attributed to the majority, for in that story there is what is not befitting to mention in relation to prophets.

The ḥattā (until) in ﴿حَتّى تَوارَتْ﴾ is a limit, so the verb before it must extend until the limit is valid; thus aḥbabtu means: I intended love. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask: to what is ﴿رُدُّوها عَلَيَّ﴾ ("bring them back to me") connected? I say: to an omitted element, its implied meaning being: he said, 'Bring them back to me,' so they concealed the pronoun of what is the answer to it, as if someone asked: 'What did Solomon say?' because this is a position that strongly calls for a question." Al-Zamakhsharī then mentioned a phrase that diminishes prophethood, which I have left out. What he proposed of this concealment is not necessary, since the sentence falls under the quotation of the speech, namely ﴿فَقالَ إنِّي أحْبَبْتُ﴾ ("He said: 'Indeed, I have preferred'"). So this sentence and the sentence ﴿رُدُّوها عَلَيَّ﴾ are both quoted with qāla. Ṭafiqa (began) is one of the verbs of approximation indicating the beginning of an action, and its predicate is omitted because the verbal noun indicates it, meaning: then he began to stroke, a stroking.

Al-Jumhūr read ﴿مَسْحًا﴾ (masḥan, "stroking"), and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read misāḥan, on the pattern of qitāl. The bāʾ in (bi-l-sūq, "on the legs") is extra, as it is in His saying: ﴿فامْسَحُوا بِوُجُوهِكم وأيْدِيكُمْ﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 43] ("then wipe your faces and your hands"). Sībawayh related: "I wiped his head and wiped his head," with the same meaning, and this was discussed in al-Māʾidah.

Al-Jumhūr read (bi-l-sūq) without a hamzah, on the pattern fuʿl, which is the plural of sāq, on the pattern faʿal with a fatḥah on the ʿayn, like usd and asad. Ibn Kathīr read it with a hamzah. Abū ʿAlī said: "It is weak, but its justification in analogy is that the ḍammah came after a wāw, and it was presumed to be on the wāw, so it was hamzated, as they do with a wāw that bears a ḍammah." The justification for hamzating sūq from transmitted usage is that Abū Ḥabbah al-Numayrī used to hamzate every quiescent wāw preceded by a ḍammah, and he used to recite:

"The love of those who kindle the fire toward Mūsā."

End of quote. It is not weak, because sāq in it has a hamzah, and the pattern faʿl with a quiescent ʿayn, so this reading came according to this dialect. Ibn Muḥaysin read it with a hamzah followed by a wāw, and Bakkār related both from Qunbul. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read bi-l-sāq in the singular, dispensing with the plural because there is no ambiguity.

Among strange opinions is that the pronoun in ruddūhā refers to the sun. They differed about the number of these horses in conflicting opinions, and they filled the pages with mention of them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 38, verses 26–40 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And We certainly tested Solomon and placed upon his throne a body﴾. The exegetes (mufassirun) related many accounts about this trial and the placing of the body, and the prophets must be cleared of them. These accounts are found in their books, but it is not permissible to transmit them. They are rather among the fabrications of the Jews and the heretics (zanadiqa). Allah did not specify what the trial was, nor what the body was that He placed upon Solomon's throne. The closest of what has been said about it is that the trial was that he did not add the exception (istithna', "if Allah wills") in the hadith in which he said: "I will certainly go around to seventy women tonight, each of whom will bear a horseman who will fight in the cause of Allah," and he did not say "if Allah wills." So he went around to them, and only one woman became pregnant, and she brought forth half a man (shiqq rajul). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, had he said 'if Allah wills,' they would all have fought in the cause of Allah as horsemen." So the meaning of His words ﴿And We certainly tested Solomon and placed upon his throne a body﴾ is this, and the body that was placed is the child who was born as a half-man. Others said: Solomon fell ill with a sickness like fainting, until he became upon his throne a body as if without a soul.

When Allah commanded His Prophet (peace be upon him) to be patient with what the disbelievers of Quraysh and others said, He commanded him to mention those who were tested and were patient. So He mentioned the story of Dawud (David), the story of Sulayman, and the story of Ayyub (Job), so that he might take them as examples, and He mentioned the nearness and high station they had with Him. It would not be fitting for Him to mention, as a model to follow, someone to whom the exegetes attributed things that are too grave to be uttered and whose existence is rationally impossible, such as Satan taking the form of a prophet so that his affair becomes confused for the people, and they believe that the one in that form is the Prophet. Even if this were possible, no prophet could be trusted to have been sent. These are rather statements borrowed from the heretical Sophists (al-SufsatA'iyya). We ask Allah to preserve our minds and intellects from them.

﴿Then he turned in repentance﴾, meaning: after Our testing him, he continued to turn back and repent.

﴿He said: My Lord, forgive me﴾. This is the etiquette of the prophets and righteous people: seeking forgiveness from Allah, in humbling the self, showing lowliness and humility, and seeking advancement in the stations. In the hadith: "I seek forgiveness from Allah seventy times in a day and night." Seeking forgiveness is a preface before what the one seeking forgiveness asks, by asking for what is most important in his religion, so that the affair of his worldly life is arranged thereby, like the words of Nuh (Noah) in what Allah related of him: ﴿So I said: Seek forgiveness from your Lord, for He is ever Forgiving﴾ [Nuh: 10] ﴿He will send down the sky upon you in abundant rain﴾ [Nuh: 11], and so on. It is apparent that the request for a kingdom came after this trial. The exegetes mentioned that he remained in his kingdom twenty years before this trial and remained after it twenty years. So it is possible that he was in a kingdom before the trial, and then after it he asked for a kingdom restricted by the description that follows, namely that it should not be fitting for anyone after him. They differed about this restriction. Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and Qatadah said: "for the duration of my life, I will not take it away, and it will pass to another." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "He only intended by this a permissible aim, because a person may desire from the bounty of Allah what no one else attains, especially according to rank and prophethood. Consider His words ﴿it should not be fitting﴾: it is only a word that admits of possibility; it does not definitively establish that Allah does not give the like of that kingdom to anyone." End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Sulayman (peace be upon him) grew up in a house of kingship and prophethood and inherited both. He wished to ask his Lord for a miracle, so he asked, according to what he was accustomed to, for a kingdom exceeding the other kingdoms, with an extraordinary increase that reached the limit of a miracle, so that this would be a proof of his prophethood and would overpower those to whom he was sent. It would not be a miracle unless it breaks customary norms. That is the meaning of His words ﴿it should not be fitting for anyone after me﴾. It was also said: it was a great kingdom, and he feared that someone like it would be given to someone who would not observe Allah's limits in it, as the angels said ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?﴾ [al-Baqara: 30]. It was also said: a kingdom that I will not be stripped of, and in which no one will stand in my place. It is also possible to say: Allah knew that in what He singled him out with of that great kingdom were benefits in religion, and He knew that none other than him would manage the affairs of His beloved ones, and wisdom required that it be granted to him. So He commanded him to ask for it as a gift, in a manner by which Allah knew that none but he alone could control it, not any other of His servants. Or he wished to say: a great kingdom, and so he said ﴿it should not be fitting for anyone after me﴾, intending only the greatness and vastness of the kingdom, as you say of someone: "there is no one who has such favour and wealth," though perhaps people have similar things, but you intend to magnify what he possesses. End of quote.

When he had exaggerated in describing this kingdom that he asked for, he used, in describing Allah (Exalted), a word that indicates intensity, saying ﴿Indeed You are the Bestower﴾ [Al 'Imran: 8], meaning the One of abundant gifts, for no gift is too great for Him. When he asked for the gift that was specific to his request, He gave it to him and granted him what He mentions in His words ﴿So We subjected the wind to him﴾.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) recited "al-rih" (the wind) in the singular. Al-Hasan, Abu Rajaʼ, Qatadah, and Abu Ja'far recited "al-riyah" (the winds) in the plural, which is more general given the greatness of Sulayman's kingdom, though the singular in meaning is plural since it is a generic noun (ism jins). "Flowing" (tajri) may be a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya), meaning "flowing", or it may be an explanatory clause for His words ﴿We subjected the wind to him﴾. "At his command" means that it is not prevented from him when he wishes it to flow.

﴿Gently﴾ (rukhaan): Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: "obedient." Mujahid said: "pleasant."

﴿Wherever he directed﴾ (haythu asaab): meaning wherever he aimed and intended. Al-Zajjaj related from the Arabs: "asaba al-sawab fa-akhta al-jawab" (he hit the right thing but missed the answer), meaning he aimed. It is related from Ru'ba that two men of the people of language intended him to ask him about this word, so he came out to them and said: "Where are you aiming?" They said: "This is what we seek." It is also said: "asaba Allah bika khayran" (may Allah make good come to you through you). Al-Tha'labi recited:

"He hit the matter, but could not, so he missed the answer at the joint."

Wahb said: "haythu asaab" means "where he intended." It was said: it is also possible that asaba is the causative form of sāba, with the hamza of transitivity added, meaning where he directed his troops and made them pour forth like the flowing of clouds and rain. It was also said: asaba means "aradha" (he intended) in the dialect of Himyar. Qatadah said: in the dialect of Hajar.

﴿And the devils﴾ (al-shayatin) is conjoined to "the wind," and ﴿every builder and diver﴾ is a substitution (badal). He used forms of intensive nouns (abniyat al-mubalagha), as in His words: ﴿They made for him whatever he wished: sanctuaries, images...﴾ [Saba': 13], etc. Al-Nabigha said:

"Except Sulayman, when the God said to him: 'Stand in the wilderness and restrain them from the Fanad (a place)...'

And the army of jinn, I have permitted them, they build Tadmur with slabs and pillars."

The conjoined element of a general term is general, so the sense is: and every diver, that is, in the sea, extracting ornaments for him, and he was the first who extracted pearls. ﴿And others﴾ is conjoined to "every," so it falls within the substitution, since it is a substitution of a whole for a whole, a detailed substitution, meaning from the jinn, who are the rebellious ones. He subjected them to him until he bound them in chains for their disbelief. Al-Nabigha said in this:

"Whoever obeys you, benefit him by his obedience, as he obeyed you, and guide him to the right course. And whoever disobeys you, punish him with a punishment that deters the wrongdoer, and do not sit upon his carcass."

The explanation of ﴿bound in chains﴾ was given at the end of Surat Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and descriptions of Sulayman's kingdom in Surat al-Naml.

﴿This is Our gift﴾: a reference to what Allah the Exalted gave him of the vast kingdom, the subjugation of the wind, of humans, jinn and birds. He commanded him to bestow favour upon whom he wished and withhold from whom he wished, and He made him stand at the measure of the blessing. Then He permitted him to dispose of them as he wished, and He, Exalted, knew that he would not dispose of them except in obedience to Allah. Al-Hasan and others said: Qatadah said it refers to what the jinn did, meaning: bestow favour upon whomever you wish among them, release him from his bonds, dismiss him from his service, and hold back his affair as you wish. Ibn 'Abbas said: it refers to what He granted him of women and the power to have intercourse with them, but this may not be authentic from Ibn 'Abbas, because no mention of women has occurred here, nor of the power he was given over that. ﴿Without reckoning﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to "Our gift," meaning: this is Our gift, abundant and great, which you cannot nearly count. It is also possible that ﴿without reckoning﴾ completes ﴿so bestow favour﴾ or ﴿withhold﴾, meaning: there is no reckoning against you in giving to whom you wish or withholding from him, and in releasing whom you wish of the devils or binding him.

Allah concluded the account with what He mentioned in the story of his father, namely His words: ﴿And indeed he has near Us a station and a good return﴾ [Sad: 25]. Al-Jumhur recited "wa husna ma'ab" (and a good return) in the accusative, conjoined to "la-zulfa" (a station). Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi 'Abla recited it in the nominative, stopping at "zulfa" and beginning with "wa husnu ma'ab," which is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, its estimated sense being: "and a good return is for him."

[p. 394]

﴿O David, We have made you a khalīfah (vicegerent) on the earth, so judge between people with truth, and do not follow desire, for it will lead you astray from the way of Allah. Indeed, those who go astray from the way of Allah will have a severe punishment because they forgot the Day of Reckoning.﴾ ﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve, so woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire.﴾ ﴿Shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters on the earth? Or shall We treat the God-fearing like the wicked?﴾ ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses and that people of understanding may take heed.﴾ ﴿And We gave to David Solomon. What an excellent servant! Indeed, he was ever turning back (to Allah).﴾ ﴿When there were displayed before him in the evening the swift, well-bred horses.﴾ ﴿He said: "Indeed, I have preferred the love of good (al-khayr) over the remembrance of my Lord," until they were hidden behind the veil.﴾ ﴿"Bring them back to me," and he began to pass his hand over their legs and necks.﴾ ﴿And We certainly tested Solomon and placed upon his throne a body; then he turned back (to Allah).﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone after me. Indeed, You are the Bestower."﴾ ﴿So We subjected the wind to him, flowing gently by his command wherever he directed.﴾ ﴿And the devils, every builder and diver,﴾ ﴿and others bound together in chains.﴾ ﴿"This is Our gift, so grant (favours) or withhold, without account."﴾ ﴿And indeed, for him with Us is a nearness and a good final return.﴾

[p. 395]

His, may He be exalted, making David a khalīfah on the earth indicates his high station with Him, peace be upon him, and His choosing him, and it repels from the one who attributes to him anything that does not befit the office of prophethood. The word khalīfah may mean: one who succeeds those who came before you among the prophets; or that He elevates your rank by making you a ruler with executive authority. From this usage it is said: "the khulafā' of Allah on His earth." It has been inferred from this verse that the earth needs a khalīfah from Allah, but this does not necessarily follow from the verse; rather, its necessity comes from the Sharīʿah and from ijmāʿ (scholarly consensus). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "The term khalīfat Allah is not used except for a Messenger. As for the khulafāʾ, each one of them is the khalīfah of the one before him. What occurs in poetry of calling one of them khalīfat Allah is a figurative usage, as Qays al-Ruqayyāt said:

"Khalīfat Allah over His creation, the pens and the books have confirmed this."

The Companions said to Abū Bakr: "Khalīfat Rasūl Allah," and he was called by this during his term. When ʿUmar became ruler, they said: "Khalīfat khalīfat Rasūl Allah." The matter lengthened, and it was further extended to the future, so they called him Amīr al-Mu'minīn, and this title was restricted to the caliphs." End of quote.

﴿So judge between people with truth﴾: this is a command to persist, and an admonition to others who are in charge of people's affairs. Since he is ma'ṣūm (infallible, protected from error), he does not judge except with truth; he was first commanded to judge, and since desire may afflict one who is not infallible, he was commanded to avoid it, and the outcome of following it was mentioned, namely that it leads him astray from the way of Allah. The fāʾ in ﴿فَيُضِلَّكَ﴾ (fa-yuḍillaka, "so it will lead you astray") is a response to the prohibition, and its agent is either the pronoun of (al-hawā, "desire"), or the pronoun of the verbal noun implied by ﴿ولا تَتَّبِعِ﴾ (wa-lā tattabiʿ), meaning: the following of desire will lead you astray. Since He mentioned what results from following desire, which is being led astray from the way of Allah, He mentioned the punishment of the one who goes astray.

Al-Jumhūr (the majority of reciters) read ﴿يَضِلُّونَ﴾ (yaḍillūna) with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, because when the following of desire led them astray, they became those who go astray. Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan, according to a variant reported from them, and Abū Ḥaywah read it with a ḍammah on the yāʾ (yuḍillūna), and this reading is more general, because the one who is led astray is not necessarily the one who leads others astray; but the reading of the majority is clearer. The phrase ﴿بِما نَسُوا﴾ (bimā nasū, "because they forgot") is connected to what is connected to ﴿لَهم﴾ (lahum, "for them"), and nasū means: they abandoned. The word yawm (ﷺ... "day") may be in the accusative governed by nasū, or by what is connected to lahum, and forgetting would then be an expression for their going astray from the way of Allah.

[The word] ﴿باطِلًا﴾ (bāṭilan, "in vain") is in the accusative either as an adjective for an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a vain creation," or as a circumstantial accusative, meaning "as those who render it void," or "possessors of vanity," or as an object of purpose. The meaning of bāṭilan is: in vain, purposelessly.

﴿That﴾, meaning the vanity of their creation, ﴿is the assumption of those who disbelieve﴾, meaning their supposition. Although these people acknowledge that the Creator of the heavens and the earth is Allah, they, insofar as they deny the return, the reward and the punishment, suppose that the creation of these things is not for wisdom, and that the creation of these things is merely futility. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿أفَحَسِبْتُمْ أنَّما خَلَقْناكم عَبَثًا وأنَّكم إلَيْنا لا تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 115] ("Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?"). Thus He alerted to the Return and to the requital for it. Then He mentioned the contrast between the believer who does righteous deeds and the corrupter, and that the two are not equal, and He set righteousness against corruption and piety against wickedness. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "It is general, covering all Muslims and disbelievers." It was also said that it concerns a group of the idolaters of Quraysh who said: "We will have in the Hereafter more than we have in this world," so Allah revealed this verse. It was also said that it concerns specific people among believers and disbelievers who fought at the Battle of Badr: ʿAlī, Ḥamzah, and ʿUbaydah ibn al-Ḥārith, may Allah be pleased with them, against ʿUtbah, Shaybah, and al-Walīd ibn ʿUtbah, and He described each group with what suited them.

The interrogation with (am, "or shall") in both places is an interrogation of denial, and the meaning is: those who reform and those who corrupt are not equal before Allah, nor are the God-fearing and the wicked. How could there be equality between those who obey and those who disobey? Otherwise, requital would be nullified, and requital is certainly going to happen, and equality is ruled out.

Since equality was ruled out between that by which one earns eternal happiness, which is the Book of Allah, He said: ﴿كِتابٌ أنْزَلْناهُ﴾ ("A Book which We have sent down"). Its nominative status is by presumption of a subject, meaning: this is a Book. Al-Jumhūr read ﴿مُبارَكٌ﴾ (mubārakun, "blessed") as an adjective. It was also read as mubārakan in a necessary circumstantial status, meaning: this is a Book. Al-Jumhūr read ﴿لِيَدَّبَّرُوا آياتِهِ﴾ (liyaddabbarū āyātihi, "that they may reflect upon its verses") with the third-person plural yāʾ and a doubled dāl, and its original form is liyatadabbarū. ʿAlī read it according to this original form. Abū Jaʿfar read it with the second-person tāʾ and a single dāl. The same was reported from ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī, according to a variant reported from them, and the original is litatadabbarū with two tāʾs, one of which was dropped, according to the disagreement over it: is it the tāʾ of the present-tense prefix or the tāʾ that follows it?

The lām in liyaddabbarū is the lām of purpose (kay). The reflection (tadabbur), which is contemplation of the verses and deliberation that leads its possessor to consider the outcomes of things, is attributed to them all. The remembrance (tadhakkur) is attributed to the people of intellects (ulū al-albāb), because the possessor of intellect has within him what guides him to truth, which is his intellect, so he needs only something to remind him, and then he remembers. The one singled out for praise is omitted, and the implied sense is ﴿نِعْمَ العَبْدُ﴾ (niʿma al-ʿabd, "what an excellent servant") — he is, namely Solomon. It was also read as naʿim, according to the original form, as one says:

"The seekers among the people are excellent, the people of the Shuṭur."

He, exalted is He, praised him because he frequently returned to Him, or because of his frequent glorification of Him.

﴿Idh ʿurida﴾ ("When there were displayed"): the governing element of idh (when) is ﴿أوّابٌ﴾ (awwāb, "one who turns back"), and it was also said: the verb is "remember," according to the difference in interpreting this verse. Al-Jumhūr said: there were displayed to him thousands of horses which his father had left to him; it was also said: one thousand horses. They were run before him in the evening, and he became preoccupied with their beauty, their running, and his love for them, so he was distracted from remembering Him. He said: "Bring them back to me," and he began striking their necks and hamstrings with the sword, because they had been the cause of his neglect of that remembrance; then Allah replaced them for him with something swifter than them, the wind. Others, among them al-Thaʿlabī, said: there was a famine among the people, and horse meat was lawful for them, so he slaughtered them to be eaten, as a form of nearness to Allah and sacrificing offerings according to our practice. End of quote. In this story there are expressions that diminish the station of prophethood, which we will leave aside.

The khayr (good) in His saying ﴿حُبَّ الخَيْرِ﴾ (ḥubba al-khayr, "the love of good") means here the horses, and the Arabs call horses khayr; this was stated by Qatādah and al-Suddī. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Jubayr said: al-khayr here means wealth. The phrase ﴿حُبَّ الخَيْرِ﴾ is in the accusative. It was said: it is the object, because aḥbabtu includes the meaning of āthartu ("I preferred"), as stated by al-Farrāʾ. It was also said: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun of comparison, meaning: I loved horses like the love of good, that is, a love like the love of good. It was also said: it is transitive with ʿan, so it implies a verb that takes ʿan, meaning: I turned the love of good away from the remembrance of my Lord, or: I made the love of good substitute for the remembrance of my Lord. Abū al-Fatḥ al-Hamdānī mentioned in his book al-Tibyān that aḥbabtu has the meaning of "I stayed/clung," from the saying:

"Like a bad camel when it stayed put."

Another group said: aḥbabtu means "fell to the ground," derived from aḥabba al-baʿīr when it was exhausted and collapsed. Some said: ḥabba al-baʿīr means it knelt, and fulān means he lowered his head. Abū Zayd said: "A camel is muḥibb, and it has become exhausted (aḥabba ihbāban) when it is afflicted by sickness or a break, so it does not leave its place until it recovers or dies." Thaʿlab said: "The exhausted camel is called muḥibb," so the meaning is: I remained away from the remembrance of my Lord. On this view, (ḥubba al-khayr) is an object of purpose.

The apparent view is that the pronoun in ﴿تَوارَتْ﴾ (tawārat, "they were hidden") refers to ﴿الصّافِناتُ﴾ (al-ṣāfināt, "the swift horses"), meaning: they entered their stables, and these are the veil. It was also said: until they were hidden in the race by something that screened them from sight. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the sun, even though it has not been mentioned, because the evening (al-ʿashiyy) indicates it. A group said: the horses were displayed before Solomon while he was in prayer, so he gestured to them that he was in prayer, and they were removed from him until they entered the stables; then he said, when he finished his prayer: ﴿إنِّي أحْبَبْتُ حُبَّ الخَيْرِ﴾ meaning: the good that is with Allah in the Hereafter, because of the remembrance of my Lord, as if he were saying: that occupied me from seeing the horses until they were brought into their stables. "Bring them back to me," so he began to stroke their manes and their legs out of love for them. Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Zuhrī said: his stroking of their legs and necks was not with a sword, but with his hands, as honour and affection for them; al-Ṭabarī preferred this view. It was also said: it was washing with water. Al-Thaʿlabī said: this stroking on the legs and necks was a branding mark for being held in the cause of Allah. End of quote. This view is the one that suits the stations of the prophets, not the view attributed to the majority, for in that story there is what is not befitting to mention in relation to prophets.

The ḥattā (until) in ﴿حَتّى تَوارَتْ﴾ is a limit, so the verb before it must extend until the limit is valid; thus aḥbabtu means: I intended love. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask: to what is ﴿رُدُّوها عَلَيَّ﴾ ("bring them back to me") connected? I say: to an omitted element, its implied meaning being: he said, 'Bring them back to me,' so they concealed the pronoun of what is the answer to it, as if someone asked: 'What did Solomon say?' because this is a position that strongly calls for a question." Al-Zamakhsharī then mentioned a phrase that diminishes prophethood, which I have left out. What he proposed of this concealment is not necessary, since the sentence falls under the quotation of the speech, namely ﴿فَقالَ إنِّي أحْبَبْتُ﴾ ("He said: 'Indeed, I have preferred'"). So this sentence and the sentence ﴿رُدُّوها عَلَيَّ﴾ are both quoted with qāla. Ṭafiqa (began) is one of the verbs of approximation indicating the beginning of an action, and its predicate is omitted because the verbal noun indicates it, meaning: then he began to stroke, a stroking.

Al-Jumhūr read ﴿مَسْحًا﴾ (masḥan, "stroking"), and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read misāḥan, on the pattern of qitāl. The bāʾ in (bi-l-sūq, "on the legs") is extra, as it is in His saying: ﴿فامْسَحُوا بِوُجُوهِكم وأيْدِيكُمْ﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 43] ("then wipe your faces and your hands"). Sībawayh related: "I wiped his head and wiped his head," with the same meaning, and this was discussed in al-Māʾidah.

Al-Jumhūr read (bi-l-sūq) without a hamzah, on the pattern fuʿl, which is the plural of sāq, on the pattern faʿal with a fatḥah on the ʿayn, like usd and asad. Ibn Kathīr read it with a hamzah. Abū ʿAlī said: "It is weak, but its justification in analogy is that the ḍammah came after a wāw, and it was presumed to be on the wāw, so it was hamzated, as they do with a wāw that bears a ḍammah." The justification for hamzating sūq from transmitted usage is that Abū Ḥabbah al-Numayrī used to hamzate every quiescent wāw preceded by a ḍammah, and he used to recite:

"The love of those who kindle the fire toward Mūsā."

End of quote. It is not weak, because sāq in it has a hamzah, and the pattern faʿl with a quiescent ʿayn, so this reading came according to this dialect. Ibn Muḥaysin read it with a hamzah followed by a wāw, and Bakkār related both from Qunbul. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read bi-l-sāq in the singular, dispensing with the plural because there is no ambiguity.

Among strange opinions is that the pronoun in ruddūhā refers to the sun. They differed about the number of these horses in conflicting opinions, and they filled the pages with mention of them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 38, verses 26–40 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And We certainly tested Solomon and placed upon his throne a body﴾. The exegetes (mufassirun) related many accounts about this trial and the placing of the body, and the prophets must be cleared of them. These accounts are found in their books, but it is not permissible to transmit them. They are rather among the fabrications of the Jews and the heretics (zanadiqa). Allah did not specify what the trial was, nor what the body was that He placed upon Solomon's throne. The closest of what has been said about it is that the trial was that he did not add the exception (istithna', "if Allah wills") in the hadith in which he said: "I will certainly go around to seventy women tonight, each of whom will bear a horseman who will fight in the cause of Allah," and he did not say "if Allah wills." So he went around to them, and only one woman became pregnant, and she brought forth half a man (shiqq rajul). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, had he said 'if Allah wills,' they would all have fought in the cause of Allah as horsemen." So the meaning of His words ﴿And We certainly tested Solomon and placed upon his throne a body﴾ is this, and the body that was placed is the child who was born as a half-man. Others said: Solomon fell ill with a sickness like fainting, until he became upon his throne a body as if without a soul.

When Allah commanded His Prophet (peace be upon him) to be patient with what the disbelievers of Quraysh and others said, He commanded him to mention those who were tested and were patient. So He mentioned the story of Dawud (David), the story of Sulayman, and the story of Ayyub (Job), so that he might take them as examples, and He mentioned the nearness and high station they had with Him. It would not be fitting for Him to mention, as a model to follow, someone to whom the exegetes attributed things that are too grave to be uttered and whose existence is rationally impossible, such as Satan taking the form of a prophet so that his affair becomes confused for the people, and they believe that the one in that form is the Prophet. Even if this were possible, no prophet could be trusted to have been sent. These are rather statements borrowed from the heretical Sophists (al-SufsatA'iyya). We ask Allah to preserve our minds and intellects from them.

﴿Then he turned in repentance﴾, meaning: after Our testing him, he continued to turn back and repent.

﴿He said: My Lord, forgive me﴾. This is the etiquette of the prophets and righteous people: seeking forgiveness from Allah, in humbling the self, showing lowliness and humility, and seeking advancement in the stations. In the hadith: "I seek forgiveness from Allah seventy times in a day and night." Seeking forgiveness is a preface before what the one seeking forgiveness asks, by asking for what is most important in his religion, so that the affair of his worldly life is arranged thereby, like the words of Nuh (Noah) in what Allah related of him: ﴿So I said: Seek forgiveness from your Lord, for He is ever Forgiving﴾ [Nuh: 10] ﴿He will send down the sky upon you in abundant rain﴾ [Nuh: 11], and so on. It is apparent that the request for a kingdom came after this trial. The exegetes mentioned that he remained in his kingdom twenty years before this trial and remained after it twenty years. So it is possible that he was in a kingdom before the trial, and then after it he asked for a kingdom restricted by the description that follows, namely that it should not be fitting for anyone after him. They differed about this restriction. Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and Qatadah said: "for the duration of my life, I will not take it away, and it will pass to another." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "He only intended by this a permissible aim, because a person may desire from the bounty of Allah what no one else attains, especially according to rank and prophethood. Consider His words ﴿it should not be fitting﴾: it is only a word that admits of possibility; it does not definitively establish that Allah does not give the like of that kingdom to anyone." End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Sulayman (peace be upon him) grew up in a house of kingship and prophethood and inherited both. He wished to ask his Lord for a miracle, so he asked, according to what he was accustomed to, for a kingdom exceeding the other kingdoms, with an extraordinary increase that reached the limit of a miracle, so that this would be a proof of his prophethood and would overpower those to whom he was sent. It would not be a miracle unless it breaks customary norms. That is the meaning of His words ﴿it should not be fitting for anyone after me﴾. It was also said: it was a great kingdom, and he feared that someone like it would be given to someone who would not observe Allah's limits in it, as the angels said ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?﴾ [al-Baqara: 30]. It was also said: a kingdom that I will not be stripped of, and in which no one will stand in my place. It is also possible to say: Allah knew that in what He singled him out with of that great kingdom were benefits in religion, and He knew that none other than him would manage the affairs of His beloved ones, and wisdom required that it be granted to him. So He commanded him to ask for it as a gift, in a manner by which Allah knew that none but he alone could control it, not any other of His servants. Or he wished to say: a great kingdom, and so he said ﴿it should not be fitting for anyone after me﴾, intending only the greatness and vastness of the kingdom, as you say of someone: "there is no one who has such favour and wealth," though perhaps people have similar things, but you intend to magnify what he possesses. End of quote.

When he had exaggerated in describing this kingdom that he asked for, he used, in describing Allah (Exalted), a word that indicates intensity, saying ﴿Indeed You are the Bestower﴾ [Al 'Imran: 8], meaning the One of abundant gifts, for no gift is too great for Him. When he asked for the gift that was specific to his request, He gave it to him and granted him what He mentions in His words ﴿So We subjected the wind to him﴾.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) recited "al-rih" (the wind) in the singular. Al-Hasan, Abu Rajaʼ, Qatadah, and Abu Ja'far recited "al-riyah" (the winds) in the plural, which is more general given the greatness of Sulayman's kingdom, though the singular in meaning is plural since it is a generic noun (ism jins). "Flowing" (tajri) may be a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya), meaning "flowing", or it may be an explanatory clause for His words ﴿We subjected the wind to him﴾. "At his command" means that it is not prevented from him when he wishes it to flow.

﴿Gently﴾ (rukhaan): Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: "obedient." Mujahid said: "pleasant."

﴿Wherever he directed﴾ (haythu asaab): meaning wherever he aimed and intended. Al-Zajjaj related from the Arabs: "asaba al-sawab fa-akhta al-jawab" (he hit the right thing but missed the answer), meaning he aimed. It is related from Ru'ba that two men of the people of language intended him to ask him about this word, so he came out to them and said: "Where are you aiming?" They said: "This is what we seek." It is also said: "asaba Allah bika khayran" (may Allah make good come to you through you). Al-Tha'labi recited:

"He hit the matter, but could not, so he missed the answer at the joint."

Wahb said: "haythu asaab" means "where he intended." It was said: it is also possible that asaba is the causative form of sāba, with the hamza of transitivity added, meaning where he directed his troops and made them pour forth like the flowing of clouds and rain. It was also said: asaba means "aradha" (he intended) in the dialect of Himyar. Qatadah said: in the dialect of Hajar.

﴿And the devils﴾ (al-shayatin) is conjoined to "the wind," and ﴿every builder and diver﴾ is a substitution (badal). He used forms of intensive nouns (abniyat al-mubalagha), as in His words: ﴿They made for him whatever he wished: sanctuaries, images...﴾ [Saba': 13], etc. Al-Nabigha said:

"Except Sulayman, when the God said to him: 'Stand in the wilderness and restrain them from the Fanad (a place)...'

And the army of jinn, I have permitted them, they build Tadmur with slabs and pillars."

The conjoined element of a general term is general, so the sense is: and every diver, that is, in the sea, extracting ornaments for him, and he was the first who extracted pearls. ﴿And others﴾ is conjoined to "every," so it falls within the substitution, since it is a substitution of a whole for a whole, a detailed substitution, meaning from the jinn, who are the rebellious ones. He subjected them to him until he bound them in chains for their disbelief. Al-Nabigha said in this:

"Whoever obeys you, benefit him by his obedience, as he obeyed you, and guide him to the right course. And whoever disobeys you, punish him with a punishment that deters the wrongdoer, and do not sit upon his carcass."

The explanation of ﴿bound in chains﴾ was given at the end of Surat Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and descriptions of Sulayman's kingdom in Surat al-Naml.

﴿This is Our gift﴾: a reference to what Allah the Exalted gave him of the vast kingdom, the subjugation of the wind, of humans, jinn and birds. He commanded him to bestow favour upon whom he wished and withhold from whom he wished, and He made him stand at the measure of the blessing. Then He permitted him to dispose of them as he wished, and He, Exalted, knew that he would not dispose of them except in obedience to Allah. Al-Hasan and others said: Qatadah said it refers to what the jinn did, meaning: bestow favour upon whomever you wish among them, release him from his bonds, dismiss him from his service, and hold back his affair as you wish. Ibn 'Abbas said: it refers to what He granted him of women and the power to have intercourse with them, but this may not be authentic from Ibn 'Abbas, because no mention of women has occurred here, nor of the power he was given over that. ﴿Without reckoning﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to "Our gift," meaning: this is Our gift, abundant and great, which you cannot nearly count. It is also possible that ﴿without reckoning﴾ completes ﴿so bestow favour﴾ or ﴿withhold﴾, meaning: there is no reckoning against you in giving to whom you wish or withholding from him, and in releasing whom you wish of the devils or binding him.

Allah concluded the account with what He mentioned in the story of his father, namely His words: ﴿And indeed he has near Us a station and a good return﴾ [Sad: 25]. Al-Jumhur recited "wa husna ma'ab" (and a good return) in the accusative, conjoined to "la-zulfa" (a station). Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi 'Abla recited it in the nominative, stopping at "zulfa" and beginning with "wa husnu ma'ab," which is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, its estimated sense being: "and a good return is for him."

[p. 394]

﴿O David, We have made you a khalīfah (vicegerent) on the earth, so judge between people with truth, and do not follow desire, for it will lead you astray from the way of Allah. Indeed, those who go astray from the way of Allah will have a severe punishment because they forgot the Day of Reckoning.﴾ ﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve, so woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire.﴾ ﴿Shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters on the earth? Or shall We treat the God-fearing like the wicked?﴾ ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses and that people of understanding may take heed.﴾ ﴿And We gave to David Solomon. What an excellent servant! Indeed, he was ever turning back (to Allah).﴾ ﴿When there were displayed before him in the evening the swift, well-bred horses.﴾ ﴿He said: "Indeed, I have preferred the love of good (al-khayr) over the remembrance of my Lord," until they were hidden behind the veil.﴾ ﴿"Bring them back to me," and he began to pass his hand over their legs and necks.﴾ ﴿And We certainly tested Solomon and placed upon his throne a body; then he turned back (to Allah).﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone after me. Indeed, You are the Bestower."﴾ ﴿So We subjected the wind to him, flowing gently by his command wherever he directed.﴾ ﴿And the devils, every builder and diver,﴾ ﴿and others bound together in chains.﴾ ﴿"This is Our gift, so grant (favours) or withhold, without account."﴾ ﴿And indeed, for him with Us is a nearness and a good final return.﴾

[p. 395]

His, may He be exalted, making David a khalīfah on the earth indicates his high station with Him, peace be upon him, and His choosing him, and it repels from the one who attributes to him anything that does not befit the office of prophethood. The word khalīfah may mean: one who succeeds those who came before you among the prophets; or that He elevates your rank by making you a ruler with executive authority. From this usage it is said: "the khulafā' of Allah on His earth." It has been inferred from this verse that the earth needs a khalīfah from Allah, but this does not necessarily follow from the verse; rather, its necessity comes from the Sharīʿah and from ijmāʿ (scholarly consensus). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "The term khalīfat Allah is not used except for a Messenger. As for the khulafāʾ, each one of them is the khalīfah of the one before him. What occurs in poetry of calling one of them khalīfat Allah is a figurative usage, as Qays al-Ruqayyāt said:

"Khalīfat Allah over His creation, the pens and the books have confirmed this."

The Companions said to Abū Bakr: "Khalīfat Rasūl Allah," and he was called by this during his term. When ʿUmar became ruler, they said: "Khalīfat khalīfat Rasūl Allah." The matter lengthened, and it was further extended to the future, so they called him Amīr al-Mu'minīn, and this title was restricted to the caliphs." End of quote.

﴿So judge between people with truth﴾: this is a command to persist, and an admonition to others who are in charge of people's affairs. Since he is ma'ṣūm (infallible, protected from error), he does not judge except with truth; he was first commanded to judge, and since desire may afflict one who is not infallible, he was commanded to avoid it, and the outcome of following it was mentioned, namely that it leads him astray from the way of Allah. The fāʾ in ﴿فَيُضِلَّكَ﴾ (fa-yuḍillaka, "so it will lead you astray") is a response to the prohibition, and its agent is either the pronoun of (al-hawā, "desire"), or the pronoun of the verbal noun implied by ﴿ولا تَتَّبِعِ﴾ (wa-lā tattabiʿ), meaning: the following of desire will lead you astray. Since He mentioned what results from following desire, which is being led astray from the way of Allah, He mentioned the punishment of the one who goes astray.

Al-Jumhūr (the majority of reciters) read ﴿يَضِلُّونَ﴾ (yaḍillūna) with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, because when the following of desire led them astray, they became those who go astray. Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan, according to a variant reported from them, and Abū Ḥaywah read it with a ḍammah on the yāʾ (yuḍillūna), and this reading is more general, because the one who is led astray is not necessarily the one who leads others astray; but the reading of the majority is clearer. The phrase ﴿بِما نَسُوا﴾ (bimā nasū, "because they forgot") is connected to what is connected to ﴿لَهم﴾ (lahum, "for them"), and nasū means: they abandoned. The word yawm (ﷺ... "day") may be in the accusative governed by nasū, or by what is connected to lahum, and forgetting would then be an expression for their going astray from the way of Allah.

[The word] ﴿باطِلًا﴾ (bāṭilan, "in vain") is in the accusative either as an adjective for an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a vain creation," or as a circumstantial accusative, meaning "as those who render it void," or "possessors of vanity," or as an object of purpose. The meaning of bāṭilan is: in vain, purposelessly.

﴿That﴾, meaning the vanity of their creation, ﴿is the assumption of those who disbelieve﴾, meaning their supposition. Although these people acknowledge that the Creator of the heavens and the earth is Allah, they, insofar as they deny the return, the reward and the punishment, suppose that the creation of these things is not for wisdom, and that the creation of these things is merely futility. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿أفَحَسِبْتُمْ أنَّما خَلَقْناكم عَبَثًا وأنَّكم إلَيْنا لا تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 115] ("Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?"). Thus He alerted to the Return and to the requital for it. Then He mentioned the contrast between the believer who does righteous deeds and the corrupter, and that the two are not equal, and He set righteousness against corruption and piety against wickedness. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "It is general, covering all Muslims and disbelievers." It was also said that it concerns a group of the idolaters of Quraysh who said: "We will have in the Hereafter more than we have in this world," so Allah revealed this verse. It was also said that it concerns specific people among believers and disbelievers who fought at the Battle of Badr: ʿAlī, Ḥamzah, and ʿUbaydah ibn al-Ḥārith, may Allah be pleased with them, against ʿUtbah, Shaybah, and al-Walīd ibn ʿUtbah, and He described each group with what suited them.

The interrogation with (am, "or shall") in both places is an interrogation of denial, and the meaning is: those who reform and those who corrupt are not equal before Allah, nor are the God-fearing and the wicked. How could there be equality between those who obey and those who disobey? Otherwise, requital would be nullified, and requital is certainly going to happen, and equality is ruled out.

Since equality was ruled out between that by which one earns eternal happiness, which is the Book of Allah, He said: ﴿كِتابٌ أنْزَلْناهُ﴾ ("A Book which We have sent down"). Its nominative status is by presumption of a subject, meaning: this is a Book. Al-Jumhūr read ﴿مُبارَكٌ﴾ (mubārakun, "blessed") as an adjective. It was also read as mubārakan in a necessary circumstantial status, meaning: this is a Book. Al-Jumhūr read ﴿لِيَدَّبَّرُوا آياتِهِ﴾ (liyaddabbarū āyātihi, "that they may reflect upon its verses") with the third-person plural yāʾ and a doubled dāl, and its original form is liyatadabbarū. ʿAlī read it according to this original form. Abū Jaʿfar read it with the second-person tāʾ and a single dāl. The same was reported from ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī, according to a variant reported from them, and the original is litatadabbarū with two tāʾs, one of which was dropped, according to the disagreement over it: is it the tāʾ of the present-tense prefix or the tāʾ that follows it?

The lām in liyaddabbarū is the lām of purpose (kay). The reflection (tadabbur), which is contemplation of the verses and deliberation that leads its possessor to consider the outcomes of things, is attributed to them all. The remembrance (tadhakkur) is attributed to the people of intellects (ulū al-albāb), because the possessor of intellect has within him what guides him to truth, which is his intellect, so he needs only something to remind him, and then he remembers. The one singled out for praise is omitted, and the implied sense is ﴿نِعْمَ العَبْدُ﴾ (niʿma al-ʿabd, "what an excellent servant") — he is, namely Solomon. It was also read as naʿim, according to the original form, as one says:

"The seekers among the people are excellent, the people of the Shuṭur."

He, exalted is He, praised him because he frequently returned to Him, or because of his frequent glorification of Him.

﴿Idh ʿurida﴾ ("When there were displayed"): the governing element of idh (when) is ﴿أوّابٌ﴾ (awwāb, "one who turns back"), and it was also said: the verb is "remember," according to the difference in interpreting this verse. Al-Jumhūr said: there were displayed to him thousands of horses which his father had left to him; it was also said: one thousand horses. They were run before him in the evening, and he became preoccupied with their beauty, their running, and his love for them, so he was distracted from remembering Him. He said: "Bring them back to me," and he began striking their necks and hamstrings with the sword, because they had been the cause of his neglect of that remembrance; then Allah replaced them for him with something swifter than them, the wind. Others, among them al-Thaʿlabī, said: there was a famine among the people, and horse meat was lawful for them, so he slaughtered them to be eaten, as a form of nearness to Allah and sacrificing offerings according to our practice. End of quote. In this story there are expressions that diminish the station of prophethood, which we will leave aside.

The khayr (good) in His saying ﴿حُبَّ الخَيْرِ﴾ (ḥubba al-khayr, "the love of good") means here the horses, and the Arabs call horses khayr; this was stated by Qatādah and al-Suddī. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Jubayr said: al-khayr here means wealth. The phrase ﴿حُبَّ الخَيْرِ﴾ is in the accusative. It was said: it is the object, because aḥbabtu includes the meaning of āthartu ("I preferred"), as stated by al-Farrāʾ. It was also said: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun of comparison, meaning: I loved horses like the love of good, that is, a love like the love of good. It was also said: it is transitive with ʿan, so it implies a verb that takes ʿan, meaning: I turned the love of good away from the remembrance of my Lord, or: I made the love of good substitute for the remembrance of my Lord. Abū al-Fatḥ al-Hamdānī mentioned in his book al-Tibyān that aḥbabtu has the meaning of "I stayed/clung," from the saying:

"Like a bad camel when it stayed put."

Another group said: aḥbabtu means "fell to the ground," derived from aḥabba al-baʿīr when it was exhausted and collapsed. Some said: ḥabba al-baʿīr means it knelt, and fulān means he lowered his head. Abū Zayd said: "A camel is muḥibb, and it has become exhausted (aḥabba ihbāban) when it is afflicted by sickness or a break, so it does not leave its place until it recovers or dies." Thaʿlab said: "The exhausted camel is called muḥibb," so the meaning is: I remained away from the remembrance of my Lord. On this view, (ḥubba al-khayr) is an object of purpose.

The apparent view is that the pronoun in ﴿تَوارَتْ﴾ (tawārat, "they were hidden") refers to ﴿الصّافِناتُ﴾ (al-ṣāfināt, "the swift horses"), meaning: they entered their stables, and these are the veil. It was also said: until they were hidden in the race by something that screened them from sight. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the sun, even though it has not been mentioned, because the evening (al-ʿashiyy) indicates it. A group said: the horses were displayed before Solomon while he was in prayer, so he gestured to them that he was in prayer, and they were removed from him until they entered the stables; then he said, when he finished his prayer: ﴿إنِّي أحْبَبْتُ حُبَّ الخَيْرِ﴾ meaning: the good that is with Allah in the Hereafter, because of the remembrance of my Lord, as if he were saying: that occupied me from seeing the horses until they were brought into their stables. "Bring them back to me," so he began to stroke their manes and their legs out of love for them. Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Zuhrī said: his stroking of their legs and necks was not with a sword, but with his hands, as honour and affection for them; al-Ṭabarī preferred this view. It was also said: it was washing with water. Al-Thaʿlabī said: this stroking on the legs and necks was a branding mark for being held in the cause of Allah. End of quote. This view is the one that suits the stations of the prophets, not the view attributed to the majority, for in that story there is what is not befitting to mention in relation to prophets.

The ḥattā (until) in ﴿حَتّى تَوارَتْ﴾ is a limit, so the verb before it must extend until the limit is valid; thus aḥbabtu means: I intended love. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask: to what is ﴿رُدُّوها عَلَيَّ﴾ ("bring them back to me") connected? I say: to an omitted element, its implied meaning being: he said, 'Bring them back to me,' so they concealed the pronoun of what is the answer to it, as if someone asked: 'What did Solomon say?' because this is a position that strongly calls for a question." Al-Zamakhsharī then mentioned a phrase that diminishes prophethood, which I have left out. What he proposed of this concealment is not necessary, since the sentence falls under the quotation of the speech, namely ﴿فَقالَ إنِّي أحْبَبْتُ﴾ ("He said: 'Indeed, I have preferred'"). So this sentence and the sentence ﴿رُدُّوها عَلَيَّ﴾ are both quoted with qāla. Ṭafiqa (began) is one of the verbs of approximation indicating the beginning of an action, and its predicate is omitted because the verbal noun indicates it, meaning: then he began to stroke, a stroking.

Al-Jumhūr read ﴿مَسْحًا﴾ (masḥan, "stroking"), and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read misāḥan, on the pattern of qitāl. The bāʾ in (bi-l-sūq, "on the legs") is extra, as it is in His saying: ﴿فامْسَحُوا بِوُجُوهِكم وأيْدِيكُمْ﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 43] ("then wipe your faces and your hands"). Sībawayh related: "I wiped his head and wiped his head," with the same meaning, and this was discussed in al-Māʾidah.

Al-Jumhūr read (bi-l-sūq) without a hamzah, on the pattern fuʿl, which is the plural of sāq, on the pattern faʿal with a fatḥah on the ʿayn, like usd and asad. Ibn Kathīr read it with a hamzah. Abū ʿAlī said: "It is weak, but its justification in analogy is that the ḍammah came after a wāw, and it was presumed to be on the wāw, so it was hamzated, as they do with a wāw that bears a ḍammah." The justification for hamzating sūq from transmitted usage is that Abū Ḥabbah al-Numayrī used to hamzate every quiescent wāw preceded by a ḍammah, and he used to recite:

"The love of those who kindle the fire toward Mūsā."

End of quote. It is not weak, because sāq in it has a hamzah, and the pattern faʿl with a quiescent ʿayn, so this reading came according to this dialect. Ibn Muḥaysin read it with a hamzah followed by a wāw, and Bakkār related both from Qunbul. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read bi-l-sāq in the singular, dispensing with the plural because there is no ambiguity.

Among strange opinions is that the pronoun in ruddūhā refers to the sun. They differed about the number of these horses in conflicting opinions, and they filled the pages with mention of them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 38, verses 26–40 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And We certainly tested Solomon and placed upon his throne a body﴾. The exegetes (mufassirun) related many accounts about this trial and the placing of the body, and the prophets must be cleared of them. These accounts are found in their books, but it is not permissible to transmit them. They are rather among the fabrications of the Jews and the heretics (zanadiqa). Allah did not specify what the trial was, nor what the body was that He placed upon Solomon's throne.
