Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It is possible that by "the abode" is meant the abode of this world, in the sense of remembrance of praise and honour from people, and the enduring praise which is the metaphorical immortality; so the verse comes in the sense of His words: ﴿a tongue of truthfulness﴾ (Maryam: 50), and His words: ﴿and We left for him among the later generations﴾ (al-Saffat: 78). End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari related this possibility as an opinion, saying: It was said that ﴿dhikrā al-dār﴾ means the good praise in this world and a tongue of truthfulness. End of quote.

The bāʾ in ﴿bi-khālisatin﴾ is the bāʾ of causation, meaning: by reason of this quality and because they are of its people; and the reading (bi-khāliṣihim) supports it.

﴿And indeed they are with Us among the chosen ones﴾, meaning: the selected ones from among their kind.

(al-akhyār): the plural of khayyir, and khayyir is like mayyit and mayyit, with plural amwāt. The discussion of al-Yasaʿ was already given in Surat al-Anʿam, and Dhu al-Kifl in Surat al-Anbiya. ʿIndanā is an adverbial complement governed by an omitted verb indicated by al-muṣṭafayn, meaning: "they are chosen with Us"; or it is governed by al-muṣṭafayn, even though it has the definite article, because they allow more latitude with adverbs and prepositional phrases than with other elements; or it is in the sense of specification, meaning "I mean: with Us." ʿIndanā cannot be the predicate, and by "nearness" is meant rank. Lamina al-muṣṭafayn is in the position of a second predicate, because of the presence of the lām; one cannot say "inna Zaydan qā'imun lamunṭaliqun." (wa-kullun): meaning "and all of them," are among the best.

His affliction reached the point that nothing remained of him except his heart and tongue. It is related that he said in his private prayer: "My God, You know that my tongue never contradicted my heart, my heart never followed my eye, I never withheld what my right hand possessed, I never ate except with an orphan with me, I never spent a night full and clothed while a hungry or naked person was with me." So Allah removed it from him.

(And remember Our servant Ibrahim) — Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Kathir and the people of Makka read "'abdanā" in the singular, with Ibrahim as a substitute of it or an explanatory apposition. The majority read it in the plural, and what follows it of the three is a substitute or explanatory apposition. The majority read "ulī al-aydī" (﴿أُولِي الأيْدِي﴾) with a yā'. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: strength in obedience to Allah. It was said: their goodness in religion and their precedence with Allah by a deed of truth, so it is like "the hands" (al-aydī), which is close to what came before. It was said: the blessings Allah bestowed on them of prophethood and status. It was also said: "al-aydī" refers to the limbs that act in goodness, and "al-abṣār" (the eyes) are those that see clearly in it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Since most actions are carried out by the hands, they came to predominate, so that every deed is described as "what their hands have done," even if it is an action in which manual performance is not possible, or the workers were amputees with no hands. On this basis the words of the Exalted came: ﴿the people of power (ūlī al-aydī) and vision﴾, meaning: the people of deeds and reflection; as if those who do not perform the deeds of the Hereafter, and do not strive for God, and do not reflect with the reflection of the people of religion, and do not seek insight into the judgment of the disabled who cannot use their limbs, and of those whose intellects are deprived and who have no discernment, are included in this; and it contains an implicit rebuke of everyone who is not among God's workers or among those who seek insight into God's religion, and a reproach for abandoning striving and contemplation while being able to do so. End of quote; and it is an abundant statement.

Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: The hand is the instrument for most actions, and the eye is the instrument for the strongest kinds of perception, so the expression of action by "hand" and of perception by "eye" is apt. The rational soul has two powers: an active power and a cognitive power, so "the people of hands and eyes" is an indication of these two states. ʿAbd Allah, al-Hasan, ʿIsa and al-Aʿmash read ﴿al-aydi﴾ (ص: ١٧) without a yāʾ. It was said: the intended meaning is al-aydī, the yāʾ being dropped, with the kasra standing in for it; and since the definite article (al) replaces the tanwīn, the yāʾ was dropped along with it, just as it is dropped with tanwīn.

This explanation is not acceptable, because the dropping of this yāʾ in the presence of al was mentioned by Sibawayh as a poetic license (ḍarūra). It was also said: ﴿al-aydi﴾ means the strength in obeying God, and (al-abṣār) is an expression for the insights by which they see the realities and look with the light of God, exalted is He.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Interpreting al-aydi as derived from ta'yid (support) is unsound and not firmly grounded; it appeared unsound to him only because of the conjunction of al-abṣār with it. It should not be dismissed, because he himself explained ﴿the people of power and vision﴾ with his statement: "meaning the people of deeds and reflection." It was also read as (al-ayādī), the plural of the plural, like awṭaf and awāṭif.

Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba, al-Aʿraj, Nafiʿ and Hisham read ﴿bi-khālisatin﴾ without tanwīn, as an idafa to dhikrā. The rest of the seven read it with tanwīn, with dhikrā being a substitute (badal) for ﴿bi-khālisatin﴾. Al-Aʿmash and Talha read (bi-khālisatihim). And ﴿akhlaṣnāhum﴾ means: we made them sincerely ours. As for (khālisatin), it is possible, and this is the more apparent view, that it is an active participle (ism fāʿil) describing a merit, rank or quality that is pure and unmixed; and it is possible that it is a verbal noun, like al-ʿāqiba, in which case the agent has been omitted: meaning, "We purified them by their purifying the remembrance of the abode," so that dhikrā is the object; or "by our purifying for them the remembrance of the abode"; or the agent is dhikrā, meaning "by the remembrance of the abode having become pure for them." In every case, al-dār is in the accusative position governed by dhikrā, and dhikrā is a verbal noun; and the abode is the abode of the Hereafter.

Qatada said: the meaning is that the reminder of the Hereafter was pure for them, and they called people to it and urged them toward it. Mujahid said: their remembrance of the Hereafter was pure for them, and their fear of it, and action according to that. Ibn Zayd said: We bestowed upon them the best of what is in the Hereafter, and purified them with it, and gave it to them. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It is possible that by "the abode" is meant the abode of this world, in the sense of remembrance of praise and honour from people, and the enduring praise which is the metaphorical immortality; so the verse comes in the sense of His words: ﴿a tongue of truthfulness﴾ (Maryam: 50), and His words: ﴿and We left for him among the later generations﴾ (al-Saffat: 78). End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari related this possibility as an opinion, saying: It was said that ﴿dhikrā al-dār﴾ means the good praise in this world and a tongue of truthfulness. End of quote.

The bāʾ in ﴿bi-khālisatin﴾ is the bāʾ of causation, meaning: by reason of this quality and because they are of its people; and the reading (bi-khāliṣihim) supports it.

﴿And indeed they are with Us among the chosen ones﴾, meaning: the selected ones from among their kind.

(al-akhyār): the plural of khayyir, and khayyir is like mayyit and mayyit, with plural amwāt. The discussion of al-Yasaʿ was already given in Surat al-Anʿam, and Dhu al-Kifl in Surat al-Anbiya. ʿIndanā is an adverbial complement governed by an omitted verb indicated by al-muṣṭafayn, meaning: "they are chosen with Us"; or it is governed by al-muṣṭafayn, even though it has the definite article, because they allow more latitude with adverbs and prepositional phrases than with other elements; or it is in the sense of specification, meaning "I mean: with Us." ʿIndanā cannot be the predicate, and by "nearness" is meant rank. (wa-kullun): meaning "and all of them," are among the best.

**[p. 400]** When He commanded His Prophet to be patient, and mentioned the trial of Dawud and Sulayman and praised them both, He mentioned one whose trial was harder than theirs, and who was at the utmost degree of patience, to the point that Allah praised him for it. Ayyub is either an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan) or a substitute (badal). al-Zamakhshari said: "idh" is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from it.

The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) read "annī" with a fatha on the hamza. 'Isa read it with a kasra. He used the first-person pronoun to relate his own words, by which he called out. Had he not related them directly, he would have said "innahu massahu," because the speaker is third person. He attributed the touch to Satan. al-Zamakhshari said: Since his whisperings to him and his obedience to him in what he whispered were a cause of what Allah afflicted him with of hardship and torment, he attributed it to him. He observed good manners in this, for he did not attribute it to Allah in his supplication, although Allah is its doer and no one can do it except Him.

It was also said: he meant what the Satan used to whisper to him during his illness about the greatness of the calamity that had befallen him, so he took refuge in Allah that He would relieve him of it by removing the affliction, or by granting him success in repelling and turning it back through patient endurance.

It is also mentioned as the cause of his trial that a man sought his help against an oppressor, and he did not help him. It was said: his livestock were in the territory of a disbelieving king, and he flattered him and did not ransom them. It was said: he was amazed by the abundance of his wealth. End of al-Zamakhshari's words.

What al-Zamakhshari mentioned does not suit the rank of the Prophets: that Ayyub had obeyed Satan in what he whispered, and that this was the cause of what Allah afflicted him with of hardship and torment; nor that a man sought his help against an oppressor and he did not help him; nor that he flattered a disbeliever; nor that he was amazed by the abundance of his wealth. Likewise, what they narrated, that Allah gave Satan power over him until he took away his family and his wealth, cannot be authentic, and Satan has no power over a human except by casting corrupt whisperings into one who is not infallible.

What we say is: Allah tested Ayyub, peace be upon him, in his body, his family and his wealth, as is related in the reports. Anas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "Ayyub remained in his affliction for eighteen years, his flesh falling away until people grew weary of him, and none remained patient with him except his wife." He did not explain to us the sequence of causes that brought about his illness.

As for his attribution of the touch to Satan, the reason for it was that three believers used to visit him. One of them apostatized. He asked about him, and it was said: Satan had cast into him that Allah does not test the Prophets and the righteous. At that point he said: "Satan has touched me" (﴿مَسَّنِيَ الشَّيْطانُ﴾). Out of compassion for the believers, he attributed to himself the touch of Satan that had caused that believer to apostatize, because a good believer feels pain when a good believer returns to disbelief. For this reason, after it came: "Strike with your foot" (﴿ارْكُضْ بِرِجْلِكَ﴾), so that he would wash and the affliction would depart from him, and no believer would apostatize because of the length of his affliction and Satan's insinuation that Allah does not test the Prophets.

It was also said: by his words "Satan has touched me" he pointed to Satan's temptation of his wife and his request that she associate partners with Allah. Complaining of this matter seems to have weighed on him more than his illness.

The majority of readers read "bi-nusbin" (﴿بِنُصْبٍ﴾) with a damma on the nun and a sukun on the sad. It was said it is the plural of "nasb," like "wathn" and "wathan." Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Abu 'Imara from Hafs, al-Ju'fi from Abu Bakr, and Abu Mu'adh from Nafi' read it with two dammas. Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, Ibn Abi 'Abla, Ya'qub, and al-Jahdari read it with two fathas. Abu Haywa, Ya'qub in one narration, and Hubayra from Hafs read it with a fatha on the nun and a sukun on the sad.

al-Zamakhshari said: "al-nusb" and "al-nasb" are like "al-rushd" and "al-rashd." "Al-nasb" is in its original form as a verbal noun, and "al-nusb" is a heavier form of "nasab." The meaning is one: fatigue and hardship. "Al-'adhab" is pain; he means his illness and the various kinds of distress he suffered from. End of al-Zamakhshari's words.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: He mentioned these readings, all of which have one meaning, its meaning being hardship. "Al-nusb" is often used for the hardship of exhaustion. Some people distinguished between these words, but the correct view is that they are dialectal variants with one meaning, from the saying: "anṣabanī al-amr" when it was hard upon me. End of his words.

al-Suddi said: "bi-nusbin" refers to the body, and "'adhabin" refers to property. In the passage there is an ellipsis, its implied sense being: So We responded to him and said, "Strike with your foot," and he struck, and a spring gushed forth, and We said to him, "This is a cool bath and a drink," in it is your cure, so he washed and was healed. (And We gave him...) The meaning of the passage and its context indicate these omitted parts.

The discussion of "running/striking" (al-rakd) has preceded in the commentary on Surat al-Anbiya'. From Qatada, al-Hasan and Muqatil: this took place in the land of al-Jabiya in Syria.

The meaning of "hadha mughtasal" (﴿هَذا مُغْتَسَلٌ﴾) is: that with which one washes. "And a drink" means what you drink. By your washing your outward body is healed, and by your drinking your inward body is healed. The apparent view is that the thing pointed to was one, and the spring that gushed forth for him was two springs: he drank from one of them and washed in the other. It was also said: he struck with his right foot, and a hot spring gushed forth, and he washed in it; and with his left foot, and a cold spring gushed forth, and he drank from it. This contradicts the apparent meaning of His words "a cool bath" (﴿مُغْتَسَلٌ بارِدٌ﴾), for that indicates one water.

It was also said: he was commanded to strike with his foot so that every disease would fall away from his body. al-Qutabi said: "al-mughtasal" is the water with which one washes. Muqatil said: it is the place where one washes. al-Hasan said: he struck with his foot and a spring of water gushed forth, and he washed in it; then he walked about forty cubits, then struck with his foot again, and a spring gushed forth, and he drank from it.

It is said: the majority hold that he struck twice, and two springs gushed forth for him, he drank from one and washed in the other. The majority also hold that Allah brought back to life for him those of his family who had died, cured the sick, and gathered together those of them who had been scattered. It was also said: He granted him children and descendants equal to his descendants who had perished, and did not return his family who had died as the same individuals. The apparent sense of this arrangement is that it is in this world. It was also said that this is a promise, and that arrangement will be in the Hereafter. It was also said: He granted him those of them who were alive, healed him of his diseases, made their lives comfortable, and they multiplied until their number increased and became like them.

"Mercy" (raḥmatan) and "a reminder" (dhikrā) are both objects of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: the granting was out of Our mercy towards him, and so that people of intellect would remember, and what good comes to the patient, and the reward that results for them. In the passage there is an ellipsis, its implied sense being: He had sworn that he would strike his wife a hundred blows for a reason that arose from her, though she had been good to him. So We provided him a release from his oath by Our saying: "And take in your hand a bundle, and strike with it" (﴿وخُذْ بِيَدِكَ ضِغْثًا فاضْرِبْ بِهِ﴾). Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-dighth" is a cluster of palm fronds. Mujahid said: it is a tamarisk (al-athl), a plant with thorns. al-Dahhak said: a bundle of mixed grass. al-Akhfash said: moist branches.

They differed about the cause that made him swear. The sum of their statements is that Satan appeared to her in the form of an advisor or a healer, and offered her the healing of Ayyub at his hands on a condition impossible for a believer to fulfill. She told him of that, and he knew that the one who had made the offer to her was Satan, and he was angry at her for making that offer to him, and so he swore. Other causes have been mentioned, and they conflict. So Allah dissolved his oath by the easiest thing for him and for her, because of her good service to him and his satisfaction with her. A similar concession has occurred in Islam: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was brought a man who had been adjudged to have committed fornication with a slave woman, and he said: 'Take a cluster containing a hundred palm-stalks and strike him with it, one blow.'"

Some scholars of jurisprudence held this view regarding oaths. He said: each of the hundred must strike the one struck, whether the ends are upright or their sides are laid flat, while the form of the blow is present. The majority hold that the matter of legal limits (hudud) should not be extended by speculation, and that fulfilling an oath (al-birr fi al-aymān) only occurs by completing the number of blows.

Allah described His Prophet with patience. He had said: "Harm has touched me" (﴿مَسَّنِيَ الضُّرُّ﴾) [al-Anbiya': 83], which shows that complaining to Allah does not contradict being described as patient. Abu Haywa, Ya'qub in one narration, and Hubayra from Hafs read it with a fatha on the nun and a sukun on the sad.

al-Zamakhshari said: "al-nusb" and "al-nasb" are like "al-rushd" and "al-rashd." "Al-nasb" is in its original form as a verbal noun, and "al-nusb" is a heavier form of "nasab." The meaning is one: fatigue and hardship. "Al-'adhab" is pain; he means his illness and the various kinds of distress he suffered from. End of al-Zamakhshari's words.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: He mentioned these readings, all of which have one meaning, its meaning being hardship. "Al-nusb" is often used for the hardship of exhaustion. Some people distinguished between these words, but the correct view is that they are dialectal variants with one meaning, from the saying: "anṣabanī al-amr" when it was hard upon me. End of his words.

al-Suddi said: "bi-nusbin" refers to the body, and "'adhabin" refers to property. In the passage there is an ellipsis, its implied sense being: So We responded to him and said, "Strike with your foot," and he struck, and a spring gushed forth, and We said to him, "This is a cool bath and a drink," in it is your cure, so he washed and was healed. (And We gave him...) The meaning of the passage and its context indicate these omitted parts.

The discussion of "running/striking" (al-rakd) has preceded in the commentary on Surat al-Anbiya'. From Qatada, al-Hasan and Muqatil: this took place in the land of al-Jabiya in Syria.

The meaning of "hadha mughtasal" (﴿هَذا مُغْتَسَلٌ﴾) is: that with which one washes. "And a drink" means what you drink. By your washing your outward body is healed, and by your drinking your inward body is healed. The apparent view is that the thing pointed to was one, and the spring that gushed forth for him was two springs: he drank from one of them and washed in the other. It was also said: he struck with his right foot, and a hot spring gushed forth, and he washed in it; and with his left foot, and a cold spring gushed forth, and he drank from it. This contradicts the apparent meaning of His words "a cool bath" (﴿مُغْتَسَلٌ بارِدٌ﴾), for that indicates one water.

It was also said: he was commanded to strike with his foot so that every disease would fall away from his body. al-Qutabi said: "al-mughtasal" is the water with which one washes. Muqatil said: it is the place where one washes. al-Hasan said: he struck with his foot and a spring of water gushed forth, and he washed in it; then he walked about forty cubits, then struck with his foot again, and a spring gushed forth, and he drank from it.

It is said: the majority hold that he struck twice, and two springs gushed forth for him, he drank from one and washed in the other. The majority also hold that Allah brought back to life for him those of his family who had died, cured the sick, and gathered together those of them who had been scattered. It was also said: He granted him children and descendants equal to his descendants who had perished, and did not return his family who had died as the same individuals. The apparent sense of this arrangement is that it is in this world. It was also said that this is a promise, and that arrangement will be in the Hereafter. It was also said: He granted him those of them who were alive, healed him of his diseases, made their lives comfortable, and they multiplied until their number increased and became like them.

"Mercy" (raḥmatan) and "a reminder" (dhikrā) are both objects of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: the granting was out of Our mercy towards him, and so that people of intellect would remember, and what good comes to the patient, and the reward that results for them. In the passage there is an ellipsis, its implied sense being: He had sworn that he would strike his wife a hundred blows for a reason that arose from her, though she had been good to him. So We provided him a release from his oath by Our saying: "And take in your hand a bundle, and strike with it" (﴿وخُذْ بِيَدِكَ ضِغْثًا فاضْرِبْ بِهِ﴾). Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-dighth" is a cluster of palm fronds. Mujahid said: it is a tamarisk (al-athl), a plant with thorns. al-Dahhak said: a bundle of mixed grass. al-Akhfash said: moist branches.

They differed about the cause that made him swear. The sum of their statements is that Satan appeared to her in the form of an advisor or a healer, and offered her the healing of Ayyub at his hands on a condition impossible for a believer to fulfill. She told him of that, and he knew that the one who had made the offer to her was Satan, and he was angry at her for making that offer to him, and so he swore. Other causes have been mentioned, and they conflict. So Allah dissolved his oath by the easiest thing for him and for her, because of her good service to him and his satisfaction with her. A similar concession has occurred in Islam: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was brought a man who had been adjudged to have committed fornication with a slave woman, and he said: 'Take a cluster containing a hundred palm-stalks and strike him with it, one blow.'"

Some scholars of jurisprudence held this view regarding oaths. He said: each of the hundred must strike the one struck, whether the ends are upright or their sides are laid flat, while the form of the blow is present. The majority hold that the matter of legal limits (hudud) should not be extended by speculation, and that fulfilling an oath (al-birr fi al-aymān) only occurs by completing the number of blows.

Allah described His Prophet with patience. He had said: "Harm has touched me" (﴿مَسَّنِيَ الضُّرُّ﴾) [al-Anbiya': 83], which shows that complaining to Allah does not contradict being described as patient. Ya'qub also said: "I only complain of my anguish and sorrow to Allah" (﴿إنَّما أشْكُو بَثِّي وحُزْنِي إلى اللَّهِ﴾) [Yusuf: 86]. Ayyub, peace be upon him, sought healing out of fear for his people, that Satan would whisper to them that if he were a Prophet he would not have been tested, and to win his people's obedience. His affliction reached the point that nothing remained of him except his heart and tongue. It is related that he said in his private prayer: "My God, You know that my tongue never contradicted my heart, my heart never followed my eye, I never withheld what my right hand possessed, I never ate except with an orphan with me, I never spent a night full and clothed while a hungry or naked person was with me." So Allah removed it from him.

(And remember Our servant Ibrahim) — Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Kathir and the people of Makka read "'abdanā" in the singular, with Ibrahim as a substitute of it or an explanatory apposition. The majority read it in the plural, and what follows it of the three is a substitute or explanatory apposition. The majority read "ulī al-aydī" (﴿أُولِي الأيْدِي﴾) with a yā'. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: strength in obedience to Allah. It was said: their goodness in religion and their precedence with Allah by a deed of truth, so it is like "the hands" (al-aydī), which is close to what came before. It was said: the blessings Allah bestowed on them of prophethood and status. It was also said: "al-aydī" refers to the limbs that act in goodness, and "al-abṣār" (the eyes) are those that see clearly in it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Since most actions are carried out by the hands, they came to predominate, so that every deed is described as "what their hands have done," even if it is an action in which manual performance is not possible, or the workers were amputees with no hands. On this basis the words of the Exalted came: ﴿the people of power (ūlī al-aydī) and vision﴾, meaning: the people of deeds and reflection; as if those who do not perform the deeds of the Hereafter, and do not strive for God, and do not reflect with the reflection of the people of religion, and do not seek insight into the judgment of the disabled who cannot use their limbs, and of those whose intellects are deprived and who have no discernment, are included in this; and it contains an implicit rebuke of everyone who is not among God's workers or among those who seek insight into God's religion, and a reproach for abandoning striving and contemplation while being able to do so. End of quote; and it is an abundant statement.

Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: The hand is the instrument for most actions, and the eye is the instrument for the strongest kinds of perception, so the expression of action by "hand" and of perception by "eye" is apt. The rational soul has two powers: an active power and a cognitive power, so "the people of hands and eyes" is an indication of these two states. ʿAbd Allah, al-Hasan, ʿIsa and al-Aʿmash read ﴿al-aydi﴾ (ص: ١٧) without a yāʾ. It was said: the intended meaning is al-aydī, the yāʾ being dropped, with the kasra standing in for it; and since the definite article (al) replaces the tanwīn, the yāʾ was dropped along with it, just as it is dropped with tanwīn.

This explanation is not acceptable, because the dropping of this yāʾ in the presence of al was mentioned by Sibawayh as a poetic license (ḍarūra). It was also said: ﴿al-aydi﴾ means the strength in obeying God, and (al-abṣār) is an expression for the insights by which they see the realities and look with the light of God, exalted is He.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Interpreting al-aydi as derived from ta'yid (support) is unsound and not firmly grounded; it appeared unsound to him only because of the conjunction of al-abṣār with it. It should not be dismissed, because he himself explained ﴿the people of power and vision﴾ with his statement: "meaning the people of deeds and reflection." It was also read as (al-ayādī), the plural of the plural, like awṭaf and awāṭif.

Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba, al-Aʿraj, Nafiʿ and Hisham read ﴿bi-khālisatin﴾ without tanwīn, as an idafa to dhikrā. The rest of the seven read it with tanwīn, with dhikrā being a substitute (badal) for ﴿bi-khālisatin﴾. Al-Aʿmash and Talha read (bi-khālisatihim). And ﴿akhlaṣnāhum﴾ means: we made them sincerely ours. As for (khālisatin), it is possible, and this is the more apparent view, that it is an active participle (ism fāʿil) describing a merit, rank or quality that is pure and unmixed; and it is possible that it is a verbal noun, like al-ʿāqiba, in which case the agent has been omitted: meaning, "We purified them by their purifying the remembrance of the abode," so that dhikrā is the object; or "by our purifying for them the remembrance of the abode"; or the agent is dhikrā, meaning "by the remembrance of the abode having become pure for them." In every case, al-dār is in the accusative position governed by dhikrā, and dhikrā is a verbal noun; and the abode is the abode of the Hereafter.

Qatada said: the meaning is that the reminder of the Hereafter was pure for them, and they called people to it and urged them toward it. Mujahid said: their remembrance of the Hereafter was pure for them, and their fear of it, and action according to that. Ibn Zayd said: We bestowed upon them the best of what is in the Hereafter, and purified them with it, and gave it to them. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It is possible that by "the abode" is meant the abode of this world, in the sense of remembrance of praise and honour from people, and the enduring praise which is the metaphorical immortality; so the verse comes in the sense of His words: ﴿a tongue of truthfulness﴾ (Maryam: 50), and His words: ﴿and We left for him among the later generations﴾ (al-Saffat: 78). End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari related this possibility as an opinion, saying: It was said that ﴿dhikrā al-dār﴾ means the good praise in this world and a tongue of truthfulness. End of quote.

The bāʾ in ﴿bi-khālisatin﴾ is the bāʾ of causation, meaning: by reason of this quality and because they are of its people; and the reading (bi-khāliṣihim) supports it.

﴿And indeed they are with Us among the chosen ones﴾, meaning: the selected ones from among their kind.

(al-akhyār): the plural of khayyir, and khayyir is like mayyit and mayyit, with plural amwāt. The discussion of al-Yasaʿ was already given in Surat al-Anʿam, and Dhu al-Kifl in Surat al-Anbiya. ʿIndanā is an adverbial complement governed by an omitted verb indicated by al-muṣṭafayn, meaning: "they are chosen with Us"; or it is governed by al-muṣṭafayn, even though it has the definite article, because they allow more latitude with adverbs and prepositional phrases than with other elements; or it is in the sense of specification, meaning "I mean: with Us." ʿIndanā cannot be the predicate, and by "nearness" is meant rank. Lamina al-muṣṭafayn is in the position of a second predicate, because of the presence of the lām; one cannot say "inna Zaydan qā'imun lamunṭaliqun." (wa-kullun): meaning "and all of them," are among the best.

**[p. 400]** When He commanded His Prophet to be patient, and mentioned the trial of Dawud and Sulayman and praised them both, He mentioned one whose trial was harder than theirs, and who was at the utmost degree of patience, to the point that Allah praised him for it. Ayyub is either an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan) or a substitute (badal). al-Zamakhshari said: "idh" is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from it.

The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) read "annī" with a fatha on the hamza. 'Isa read it with a kasra. He used the first-person pronoun to relate his own words, by which he called out. Had he not related them directly, he would have said "innahu massahu," because the speaker is third person. He attributed the touch to Satan. al-Zamakhshari said: Since his whisperings to him and his obedience to him in what he whispered were a cause of what Allah afflicted him with of hardship and torment, he attributed it to him. He observed good manners in this, for he did not attribute it to Allah in his supplication, although Allah is its doer and no one can do it except Him.

It was also said: he meant what the Satan used to whisper to him during his illness about the greatness of the calamity that had befallen him, so he took refuge in Allah that He would relieve him of it by removing the affliction, or by granting him success in repelling and turning it back through patient endurance.

It is also mentioned as the cause of his trial that a man sought his help against an oppressor, and he did not help him. It was said: his livestock were in the territory of a disbelieving king, and he flattered him and did not ransom them. It was said: he was amazed by the abundance of his wealth. End of al-Zamakhshari's words.

What al-Zamakhshari mentioned does not suit the rank of the Prophets: that Ayyub had obeyed Satan in what he whispered, and that this was the cause of what Allah afflicted him with of hardship and torment; nor that a man sought his help against an oppressor and he did not help him; nor that he flattered a disbeliever; nor that he was amazed by the abundance of his wealth. Likewise, what they narrated, that Allah gave Satan power over him until he took away his family and his wealth, cannot be authentic, and Satan has no power over a human except by casting corrupt whisperings into one who is not infallible.

What we say is: Allah tested Ayyub, peace be upon him, in his body, his family and his wealth, as is related in the reports. Anas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "Ayyub remained in his affliction for eighteen years, his flesh falling away until people grew weary of him, and none remained patient with him except his wife." He did not explain to us the sequence of causes that brought about his illness.

As for his attribution of the touch to Satan, the reason for it was that three believers used to visit him. One of them apostatized. He asked about him, and it was said: Satan had cast into him that Allah does not test the Prophets and the righteous. At that point he said: "Satan has touched me" (﴿مَسَّنِيَ الشَّيْطانُ﴾). Out of compassion for the believers, he attributed to himself the touch of Satan that had caused that believer to apostatize, because a good believer feels pain when a good believer returns to disbelief. For this reason, after it came: "Strike with your foot" (﴿ارْكُضْ بِرِجْلِكَ﴾), so that he would wash and the affliction would depart from him, and no believer would apostatize because of the length of his affliction and Satan's insinuation that Allah does not test the Prophets.

It was also said: by his words "Satan has touched me" he pointed to Satan's temptation of his wife and his request that she associate partners with Allah. Complaining of this matter seems to have weighed on him more than his illness.

The majority of readers read "bi-nusbin" (﴿بِنُصْبٍ﴾) with a damma on the nun and a sukun on the sad. It was said it is the plural of "nasb," like "wathn" and "wathan." Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It is possible that by "the abode" is meant the abode of this world, in the sense of remembrance of praise and honour from people, and the enduring praise which is the metaphorical immortality; so the verse comes in the sense of His words: ﴿a tongue of truthfulness﴾ (Maryam: 50), and His words: ﴿and We left for him among the later generations﴾ (al-Saffat: 78). End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari related this possibility as an opinion, saying: It was said that ﴿dhikrā al-dār﴾ means the good praise in this world and a tongue of truthfulness. End of quote.

﴿And indeed they are with Us among the chosen ones﴾, meaning: the selected ones from among their kind.

(al-akhyār): the plural of khayyir, and khayyir is like mayyit and mayyit, with plural amwāt. **[p. 400]** When He commanded His Prophet to be patient, and mentioned the trial of Dawud and Sulayman and praised them both, He mentioned one whose trial was harder than theirs, and who was at the utmost degree of patience, to the point that Allah praised him for it. Ayyub is either an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan) or a substitute (badal). al-Zamakhshari said: "idh" is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from it.

The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) read "annī" with a fatha on the hamza. 'Isa read it with a kasra. He used the first-person pronoun to relate his own words, by which he called out. It is also mentioned as the cause of his trial that a man sought his help against an oppressor, and he did not help him. It was said: his livestock were in the territory of a disbelieving king, and he flattered him and did not ransom them. It was said: he was amazed by the abundance of his wealth. End of al-Zamakhshari's words.

What we say is: Allah tested Ayyub, peace be upon him, in his body, his family and his wealth, as is related in the reports. Anas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "Ayyub remained in his affliction for eighteen years, his flesh falling away until people grew weary of him, and none remained patient with him except his wife." He did not explain to us the sequence of causes that brought about his illness.

As for his attribution of the touch to Satan, the reason for it was that three believers used to visit him. One of them apostatized. He asked about him, and it was said: Satan had cast into him that Allah does not test the Prophets and the righteous. At that point he said: "Satan has touched me" (﴿مَسَّنِيَ الشَّيْطانُ﴾). Out of compassion for the believers, he attributed to himself the touch of Satan that had caused that believer to apostatize, because a good believer feels pain when a good believer returns to disbelief. For this reason, after it came: "Strike with your foot" (﴿ارْكُضْ بِرِجْلِكَ﴾), so that he would wash and the affliction would depart from him, and no believer would apostatize because of the length of his affliction and Satan's insinuation that Allah does not test the Prophets.

It was also said: by his words "Satan has touched me" he pointed to Satan's temptation of his wife and his request that she associate partners with Allah. Complaining of this matter seems to have weighed on him more than his illness.

The majority of readers read "bi-nusbin" (﴿بِنُصْبٍ﴾) with a damma on the nun and a sukun on the sad. It was said it is the plural of "nasb," like "wathn" and "wathan." Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Abu 'Imara from Hafs, al-Ju'fi from Abu Bakr, and Abu Mu'adh from Nafi' read it with two dammas. Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, Ibn Abi 'Abla, Ya'qub, and al-Jahdari read it with two fathas. Abu Haywa, Ya'qub in one narration, and Hubayra from Hafs read it with a fatha on the nun and a sukun on the sad.

al-Zamakhshari said: "al-nusb" and "al-nasb" are like "al-rushd" and "al-rashd." "Al-nasb" is in its original form as a verbal noun, and "al-nusb" is a heavier form of "nasab." The meaning is one: fatigue and hardship. "Al-'adhab" is pain; he means his illness and the various kinds of distress he suffered from. End of al-Zamakhshari's words.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: He mentioned these readings, all of which have one meaning, its meaning being hardship. "Al-nusb" is often used for the hardship of exhaustion. Some people distinguished between these words, but the correct view is that they are dialectal variants with one meaning, from the saying: "anṣabanī al-amr" when it was hard upon me. End of his words.

In the passage there is an ellipsis, its implied sense being: So We responded to him and said, "Strike with your foot," and he struck, and a spring gushed forth, and We said to him, "This is a cool bath and a drink," in it is your cure, so he washed and was healed. (And We gave him...) The meaning of the passage and its context indicate these omitted parts.

The discussion of "running/striking" (al-rakd) has preceded in the commentary on Surat al-Anbiya'. From Qatada, al-Hasan and Muqatil: this took place in the land of al-Jabiya in Syria.

The meaning of "hadha mughtasal" (﴿هَذا مُغْتَسَلٌ﴾) is: that with which one washes. "And a drink" means what you drink. By your washing your outward body is healed, and by your drinking your inward body is healed. The apparent view is that the thing pointed to was one, and the spring that gushed forth for him was two springs: he drank from one of them and washed in the other. It was also said: he struck with his right foot, and a hot spring gushed forth, and he washed in it; and with his left foot, and a cold spring gushed forth, and he drank from it. This contradicts the apparent meaning of His words "a cool bath" (﴿مُغْتَسَلٌ بارِدٌ﴾), for that indicates one water.

It was also said: he was commanded to strike with his foot so that every disease would fall away from his body. al-Qutabi said: "al-mughtasal" is the water with which one washes. Muqatil said: it is the place where one washes. al-Hasan said: he struck with his foot and a spring of water gushed forth, and he washed in it; then he walked about forty cubits, then struck with his foot again, and a spring gushed forth, and he drank from it.

It is said: the majority hold that he struck twice, and two springs gushed forth for him, he drank from one and washed in the other. The majority also hold that Allah brought back to life for him those of his family who had died, cured the sick, and gathered together those of them who had been scattered. It was also said: He granted him children and descendants equal to his descendants who had perished, and did not return his family who had died as the same individuals. The apparent sense of this arrangement is that it is in this world. It was also said that this is a promise, and that arrangement will be in the Hereafter. It was also said: He granted him those of them who were alive, healed him of his diseases, made their lives comfortable, and they multiplied until their number increased and became like them.

"Mercy" (raḥmatan) and "a reminder" (dhikrā) are both objects of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: the granting was out of Our mercy towards him, and so that people of intellect would remember, and what good comes to the patient, and the reward that results for them. In the passage there is an ellipsis, its implied sense being: He had sworn that he would strike his wife a hundred blows for a reason that arose from her, though she had been good to him. So We provided him a release from his oath by Our saying: "And take in your hand a bundle, and strike with it" (﴿وخُذْ بِيَدِكَ ضِغْثًا فاضْرِبْ بِهِ﴾). Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-dighth" is a cluster of palm fronds. Mujahid said: it is a tamarisk (al-athl), a plant with thorns. al-Dahhak said: a bundle of mixed grass. al-Akhfash said: moist branches.

They differed about the cause that made him swear. The sum of their statements is that Satan appeared to her in the form of an advisor or a healer, and offered her the healing of Ayyub at his hands on a condition impossible for a believer to fulfill. She told him of that, and he knew that the one who had made the offer to her was Satan, and he was angry at her for making that offer to him, and so he swore. Other causes have been mentioned, and they conflict. So Allah dissolved his oath by the easiest thing for him and for her, because of her good service to him and his satisfaction with her. A similar concession has occurred in Islam: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was brought a man who had been adjudged to have committed fornication with a slave woman, and he said: 'Take a cluster containing a hundred palm-stalks and strike him with it, one blow.'"

Some scholars of jurisprudence held this view regarding oaths. He said: each of the hundred must strike the one struck, whether the ends are upright or their sides are laid flat, while the form of the blow is present. The majority hold that the matter of legal limits (hudud) should not be extended by speculation, and that fulfilling an oath (al-birr fi al-aymān) only occurs by completing the number of blows.

Allah described His Prophet with patience. He had said: "Harm has touched me" (﴿مَسَّنِيَ الضُّرُّ﴾) [al-Anbiya': 83], which shows that complaining to Allah does not contradict being described as patient. Ya'qub also said: "I only complain of my anguish and sorrow to Allah" (﴿إنَّما أشْكُو بَثِّي وحُزْنِي إلى اللَّهِ﴾) [Yusuf: 86]. Ayyub, peace be upon him, sought healing out of fear for his people, that Satan would whisper to them that if he were a Prophet he would not have been tested, and to win his people's obedience. His affliction reached the point that nothing remained of him except his heart and tongue. It is related that he said in his private prayer: "My God, You know that my tongue never contradicted my heart, my heart never followed my eye, I never withheld what my right hand possessed, I never ate except with an orphan with me, I never spent a night full and clothed while a hungry or naked person was with me." So Allah removed it from him.

(And remember Our servant Ibrahim) — Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Kathir and the people of Makka read "'abdanā" in the singular, with Ibrahim as a substitute of it or an explanatory apposition. The majority read it in the plural, and what follows it of the three is a substitute or explanatory apposition. The majority read "ulī al-aydī" (﴿أُولِي الأيْدِي﴾) with a yā'. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: strength in obedience to Allah. It was said: their goodness in religion and their precedence with Allah by a deed of truth, so it is like "the hands" (al-aydī), which is close to what came before. It was said: the blessings Allah bestowed on them of prophethood and status. It was also said: "al-aydī" refers to the limbs that act in goodness, and "al-abṣār" (the eyes) are those that see clearly in it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Since most actions are carried out by the hands, they came to predominate, so that every deed is described as "what their hands have done," even if it is an action in which manual performance is not possible, or the workers were amputees with no hands. On this basis the words of the Exalted came: ﴿the people of power (ūlī al-aydī) and vision﴾, meaning: the people of deeds and reflection; as if those who do not perform the deeds of the Hereafter, and do not strive for God, and do not reflect with the reflection of the people of religion, and do not seek insight into the judgment of the disabled who cannot use their limbs, and of those whose intellects are deprived and who have no discernment, are included in this; and it contains an implicit rebuke of everyone who is not among God's workers or among those who seek insight into God's religion, and a reproach for abandoning striving and contemplation while being able to do so. End of quote; and it is an abundant statement.

Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: The hand is the instrument for most actions, and the eye is the instrument for the strongest kinds of perception, so the expression of action by "hand" and of perception by "eye" is apt. The rational soul has two powers: an active power and a cognitive power, so "the people of hands and eyes" is an indication of these two states. ʿAbd Allah, al-Hasan, ʿIsa and al-Aʿmash read ﴿al-aydi﴾ (ص: ١٧) without a yāʾ. It was said: the intended meaning is al-aydī, the yāʾ being dropped, with the kasra standing in for it; and since the definite article (al) replaces the tanwīn, the yāʾ was dropped along with it, just as it is dropped with tanwīn.

This explanation is not acceptable, because the dropping of this yāʾ in the presence of al was mentioned by Sibawayh as a poetic license (ḍarūra). It was also said: ﴿al-aydi﴾ means the strength in obeying God, and (al-abṣār) is an expression for the insights by which they see the realities and look with the light of God, exalted is He.

It should not be dismissed, because he himself explained ﴿the people of power and vision﴾ with his statement: "meaning the people of deeds and reflection." It was also read as (al-ayādī), the plural of the plural, like awṭaf and awāṭif.

Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba, al-Aʿraj, Nafiʿ and Hisham read ﴿bi-khālisatin﴾ without tanwīn, as an idafa to dhikrā. In every case, al-dār is in the accusative position governed by dhikrā, and dhikrā is a verbal noun; and the abode is the abode of the Hereafter.

Qatada said: the meaning is that the reminder of the Hereafter was pure for them, and they called people to it and urged them toward it. Mujahid said: their remembrance of the Hereafter was pure for them, and their fear of it, and action according to that. The majority hold that the matter of legal limits (hudud) should not be extended by speculation, and that fulfilling an oath (al-birr fi al-aymān) only occurs by completing the number of blows.

Allah described His Prophet with patience. He had said: "Harm has touched me" (﴿مَسَّنِيَ الضُّرُّ﴾) [al-Anbiya': 83], which shows that complaining to Allah does not contradict being described as patient. Ya'qub also said: "I only complain of my anguish and sorrow to Allah" (﴿إنَّما أشْكُو بَثِّي وحُزْنِي إلى اللَّهِ﴾) [Yusuf: 86]. Ayyub, peace be upon him, sought healing out of fear for his people, that Satan would whisper to them that if he were a Prophet he would not have been tested, and to win his people's obedience. His affliction reached the point that nothing remained of him except his heart and tongue. It is related that he said in his private prayer: "My God, You know that my tongue never contradicted my heart, my heart never followed my eye, I never withheld what my right hand possessed, I never ate except with an orphan with me, I never spent a night full and clothed while a hungry or naked person was with me." So Allah removed it from him.

(And remember Our servant Ibrahim) — Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Kathir and the people of Makka read "'abdanā" in the singular, with Ibrahim as a substitute of it or an explanatory apposition. The majority read it in the plural, and what follows it of the three is a substitute or explanatory apposition. The majority read "ulī al-aydī" (﴿أُولِي الأيْدِي﴾) with a yā'. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: strength in obedience to Allah. It was said: their goodness in religion and their precedence with Allah by a deed of truth, so it is like "the hands" (al-aydī), which is close to what came before. It was said: the blessings Allah bestowed on them of prophethood and status. It was also said: "al-aydī" refers to the limbs that act in goodness, and "al-abṣār" (the eyes) are those that see clearly in it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Since most actions are carried out by the hands, they came to predominate, so that every deed is described as "what their hands have done," even if it is an action in which manual performance is not possible, or the workers were amputees with no hands. On this basis the words of the Exalted came: ﴿the people of power (ūlī al-aydī) and vision﴾, meaning: the people of deeds and reflection; as if those who do not perform the deeds of the Hereafter, and do not strive for God, and do not reflect with the reflection of the people of religion, and do not seek insight into the judgment of the disabled who cannot use their limbs, and of those whose intellects are deprived and who have no discernment, are included in this; and it contains an implicit rebuke of everyone who is not among God's workers or among those who seek insight into God's religion, and a reproach for abandoning striving and contemplation while being able to do so. End of quote; and it is an abundant statement.

Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: The hand is the instrument for most actions, and the eye is the instrument for the strongest kinds of perception, so the expression of action by "hand" and of perception by "eye" is apt. The rational soul has two powers: an active power and a cognitive power, so "the people of hands and eyes" is an indication of these two states. ʿAbd Allah, al-Hasan, ʿIsa and al-Aʿmash read ﴿al-aydi﴾ (ص: ١٧) without a yāʾ. It was said: the intended meaning is al-aydī, the yāʾ being dropped, with the kasra standing in for it; and since the definite article (al) replaces the tanwīn, the yāʾ was dropped along with it, just as it is dropped with tanwīn.

This explanation is not acceptable, because the dropping of this yāʾ in the presence of al was mentioned by Sibawayh as a poetic license (ḍarūra). It was also said: ﴿al-aydi﴾ means the strength in obeying God, and (al-abṣār) is an expression for the insights by which they see the realities and look with the light of God, exalted is He.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Interpreting al-aydi as derived from ta'yid (support) is unsound and not firmly grounded; it appeared unsound to him only because of the conjunction of al-abṣār with it. It should not be dismissed, because he himself explained ﴿the people of power and vision﴾ with his statement: "meaning the people of deeds and reflection." It was also read as (al-ayādī), the plural of the plural, like awṭaf and awāṭif.

Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba, al-Aʿraj, Nafiʿ and Hisham read ﴿bi-khālisatin﴾ without tanwīn, as an idafa to dhikrā. The rest of the seven read it with tanwīn, with dhikrā being a substitute (badal) for ﴿bi-khālisatin﴾. Al-Aʿmash and Talha read (bi-khālisatihim). And ﴿akhlaṣnāhum﴾ means: we made them sincerely ours. As for (khālisatin), it is possible, and this is the more apparent view, that it is an active participle (ism fāʿil) describing a merit, rank or quality that is pure and unmixed; and it is possible that it is a verbal noun, like al-ʿāqiba, in which case the agent has been omitted: meaning, "We purified them by their purifying the remembrance of the abode," so that dhikrā is the object; or "by our purifying for them the remembrance of the abode"; or the agent is dhikrā, meaning "by the remembrance of the abode having become pure for them." In every case, al-dār is in the accusative position governed by dhikrā, and dhikrā is a verbal noun; and the abode is the abode of the Hereafter.

Qatada said: the meaning is that the reminder of the Hereafter was pure for them, and they called people to it and urged them toward it. Mujahid said: their remembrance of the Hereafter was pure for them, and their fear of it, and action according to that. Ibn Zayd said: We bestowed upon them the best of what is in the Hereafter, and purified them with it, and gave it to them. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It is possible that by "the abode" is meant the abode of this world, in the sense of remembrance of praise and honour from people, and the enduring praise which is the metaphorical immortality; so the verse comes in the sense of His words: ﴿a tongue of truthfulness﴾ (Maryam: 50), and His words: ﴿and We left for him among the later generations﴾ (al-Saffat: 78). End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari related this possibility as an opinion, saying: It was said that ﴿dhikrā al-dār﴾ means the good praise in this world and a tongue of truthfulness. End of quote.

The bāʾ in ﴿bi-khālisatin﴾ is the bāʾ of causation, meaning: by reason of this quality and because they are of its people; and the reading (bi-khāliṣihim) supports it.

﴿And indeed they are with Us among the chosen ones﴾, meaning: the selected ones from among their kind.

(al-akhyār): the plural of khayyir, and khayyir is like mayyit and mayyit, with plural amwāt. The discussion of al-Yasaʿ was already given in Surat al-Anʿam, and Dhu al-Kifl in Surat al-Anbiya. ʿIndanā is an adverbial complement governed by an omitted verb indicated by al-muṣṭafayn, meaning: "they are chosen with Us"; or it is governed by al-muṣṭafayn, even though it has the definite article, because they allow more latitude with adverbs and prepositional phrases than with other elements; or it is in the sense of specification, meaning "I mean: with Us." ʿIndanā cannot be the predicate, and by "nearness" is meant rank. Lamina al-muṣṭafayn is in the position of a second predicate, because of the presence of the lām; one cannot say "inna Zaydan qā'imun lamunṭaliqun." (wa-kullun): meaning "and all of them," are among the best.

**[p. 400]** When He commanded His Prophet to be patient, and mentioned the trial of Dawud and Sulayman and praised them both, He mentioned one whose trial was harder than theirs, and who was at the utmost degree of patience, to the point that Allah praised him for it. Ayyub is either an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan) or a substitute (badal). al-Zamakhshari said: "idh" is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from it.

The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) read "annī" with a fatha on the hamza. 'Isa read it with a kasra. He used the first-person pronoun to relate his own words, by which he called out. Had he not related them directly, he would have said "innahu massahu," because the speaker is third person. He attributed the touch to Satan. al-Zamakhshari said: Since his whisperings to him and his obedience to him in what he whispered were a cause of what Allah afflicted him with of hardship and torment, he attributed it to him. He observed good manners in this, for he did not attribute it to Allah in his supplication, although Allah is its doer and no one can do it except Him.

It was also said: he meant what the Satan used to whisper to him during his illness about the greatness of the calamity that had befallen him, so he took refuge in Allah that He would relieve him of it by removing the affliction, or by granting him success in repelling and turning it back through patient endurance.

It is also mentioned as the cause of his trial that a man sought his help against an oppressor, and he did not help him. It was said: his livestock were in the territory of a disbelieving king, and he flattered him and did not ransom them. It was said: he was amazed by the abundance of his wealth. End of al-Zamakhshari's words.

What al-Zamakhshari mentioned does not suit the rank of the Prophets: that Ayyub had obeyed Satan in what he whispered, and that this was the cause of what Allah afflicted him with of hardship and torment; nor that a man sought his help against an oppressor and he did not help him; nor that he flattered a disbeliever; nor that he was amazed by the abundance of his wealth. Likewise, what they narrated, that Allah gave Satan power over him until he took away his family and his wealth, cannot be authentic, and Satan has no power over a human except by casting corrupt whisperings into one who is not infallible.

What we say is: Allah tested Ayyub, peace be upon him, in his body, his family and his wealth, as is related in the reports. Anas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "Ayyub remained in his affliction for eighteen years, his flesh falling away until people grew weary of him, and none remained patient with him except his wife." He did not explain to us the sequence of causes that brought about his illness.

As for his attribution of the touch to Satan, the reason for it was that three believers used to visit him. One of them apostatized. He asked about him, and it was said: Satan had cast into him that Allah does not test the Prophets and the righteous. At that point he said: "Satan has touched me" (﴿مَسَّنِيَ الشَّيْطانُ﴾). Out of compassion for the believers, he attributed to himself the touch of Satan that had caused that believer to apostatize, because a good believer feels pain when a good believer returns to disbelief. For this reason, after it came: "Strike with your foot" (﴿ارْكُضْ بِرِجْلِكَ﴾), so that he would wash and the affliction would depart from him, and no believer would apostatize because of the length of his affliction and Satan's insinuation that Allah does not test the Prophets.

It was also said: by his words "Satan has touched me" he pointed to Satan's temptation of his wife and his request that she associate partners with Allah. Complaining of this matter seems to have weighed on him more than his illness.

The majority of readers read "bi-nusbin" (﴿بِنُصْبٍ﴾) with a damma on the nun and a sukun on the sad. It was said it is the plural of "nasb," like "wathn" and "wathan." Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Abu 'Imara from Hafs, al-Ju'fi from Abu Bakr, and Abu Mu'adh from Nafi' read it with two dammas. Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, Ibn Abi 'Abla, Ya'qub, and al-Jahdari read it with two fathas. Abu Haywa, Ya'qub in one narration, and Hubayra from Hafs read it with a fatha on the nun and a sukun on the sad.

al-Zamakhshari said: "al-nusb" and "al-nasb" are like "al-rushd" and "al-rashd." "Al-nasb" is in its original form as a verbal noun, and "al-nusb" is a heavier form of "nasab." The meaning is one: fatigue and hardship. "Al-'adhab" is pain; he means his illness and the various kinds of distress he suffered from. End of al-Zamakhshari's words.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: He mentioned these readings, all of which have one meaning, its meaning being hardship. "Al-nusb" is often used for the hardship of exhaustion. Some people distinguished between these words, but the correct view is that they are dialectal variants with one meaning, from the saying: "anṣabanī al-amr" when it was hard upon me. End of his words.

al-Suddi said: "bi-nusbin" refers to the body, and "'adhabin" refers to property. In the passage there is an ellipsis, its implied sense being: So We responded to him and said, "Strike with your foot," and he struck, and a spring gushed forth, and We said to him, "This is a cool bath and a drink," in it is your cure, so he washed and was healed. (And We gave him...) The meaning of the passage and its context indicate these omitted parts.

The discussion of "running/striking" (al-rakd) has preceded in the commentary on Surat al-Anbiya'. From Qatada, al-Hasan and Muqatil: this took place in the land of al-Jabiya in Syria.

The meaning of "hadha mughtasal" (﴿هَذا مُغْتَسَلٌ﴾) is: that with which one washes. "And a drink" means what you drink. By your washing your outward body is healed, and by your drinking your inward body is healed. The apparent view is that the thing pointed to was one, and the spring that gushed forth for him was two springs: he drank from one of them and washed in the other. It was also said: he struck with his right foot, and a hot spring gushed forth, and he washed in it; and with his left foot, and a cold spring gushed forth, and he drank from it. This contradicts the apparent meaning of His words "a cool bath" (﴿مُغْتَسَلٌ بارِدٌ﴾), for that indicates one water.

It was also said: he was commanded to strike with his foot so that every disease would fall away from his body. al-Qutabi said: "al-mughtasal" is the water with which one washes. Muqatil said: it is the place where one washes. al-Hasan said: he struck with his foot and a spring of water gushed forth, and he washed in it; then he walked about forty cubits, then struck with his foot again, and a spring gushed forth, and he drank from it.

It is said: the majority hold that he struck twice, and two springs gushed forth for him, he drank from one and washed in the other. The majority also hold that Allah brought back to life for him those of his family who had died, cured the sick, and gathered together those of them who had been scattered. It was also said: He granted him children and descendants equal to his descendants who had perished, and did not return his family who had died as the same individuals. The apparent sense of this arrangement is that it is in this world. It was also said that this is a promise, and that arrangement will be in the Hereafter. It was also said: He granted him those of them who were alive, healed him of his diseases, made their lives comfortable, and they multiplied until their number increased and became like them.

"Mercy" (raḥmatan) and "a reminder" (dhikrā) are both objects of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: the granting was out of Our mercy towards him, and so that people of intellect would remember, and what good comes to the patient, and the reward that results for them. In the passage there is an ellipsis, its implied sense being: He had sworn that he would strike his wife a hundred blows for a reason that arose from her, though she had been good to him. So We provided him a release from his oath by Our saying: "And take in your hand a bundle, and strike with it" (﴿وخُذْ بِيَدِكَ ضِغْثًا فاضْرِبْ بِهِ﴾). Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-dighth" is a cluster of palm fronds. Mujahid said: it is a tamarisk (al-athl), a plant with thorns. al-Dahhak said: a bundle of mixed grass. al-Akhfash said: moist branches.

They differed about the cause that made him swear. The sum of their statements is that Satan appeared to her in the form of an advisor or a healer, and offered her the healing of Ayyub at his hands on a condition impossible for a believer to fulfill. She told him of that, and he knew that the one who had made the offer to her was Satan, and he was angry at her for making that offer to him, and so he swore. Other causes have been mentioned, and they conflict. So Allah dissolved his oath by the easiest thing for him and for her, because of her good service to him and his satisfaction with her. A similar concession has occurred in Islam: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was brought a man who had been adjudged to have committed fornication with a slave woman, and he said: 'Take a cluster containing a hundred palm-stalks and strike him with it, one blow.'"

Some scholars of jurisprudence held this view regarding oaths. He said: each of the hundred must strike the one struck, whether the ends are upright or their sides are laid flat, while the form of the blow is present. So Allah removed it from him.

End of quote.
