The meaning: whoever compelled us to evil deeds until our reward became the Fire, "so increase for him the punishment double," as came in the saying of the followers: "Our Lord, give them" [al-Ahzab: 68], that is, their masters, "double the punishment" [al-Ahzab: 68], "Our Lord, these misled us, so give them a double punishment of the Fire" [al-A'raf: 38].

[p. 407] Since the leaders were themselves misguided and misled their followers, it was fitting that they be called upon to be given double punishment, as in the saying: "Upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection." On this reading, the pronoun in His saying (qalu, "they said") refers to the followers.

﴿Whoever brought this upon us﴾ refers to the leaders. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: "﴿They say: Our Lord...﴾ up to the end is the speech of all the people of the Fire." al-Dahhak said: "﴿Whoever brought this upon us﴾ is Iblis and Qabil (Cain)." Ibn Mas'ud said: "The double punishment is snakes and scorpions."

(And they said), that is, the nobles of the disbelievers: ﴿What is wrong with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the wicked?﴾ That is, the lowly ones who have no good in them and who are not upon our religion, just as He said: ﴿And we see no one following you except those who are our lowest (arazil)﴾ [Hud: 27].

It is related that those among the disbelievers of the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) who spoke these words were Abu Jahl, Umayya ibn Khalaf, and the people of the well (al-qalib). Those they did not see were Ammar, Suhayb, Salman, and those who went their way. This was said by Mujahid and others. It is said that they would ask: "Where is Ammar? Where is Suhayb? Where is so-and-so?" They counted them among the weak Muslims, and it would be said to them: "Those are in Paradise (al-Firdaws)."

al-Nahwiyyan (the two grammarians, i.e., al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'? the reading is attributed to the two Kufan/Basran grammarians named in the source) and Hamza recited (ittakhadhnahum) with continuous pronunciation (wasl). Abu Hatim, al-Zamakhshari, and Ibn Atiyya said: it is an attributive (sifah) to rijal (men). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Like His saying: ﴿We used to count them among the wicked﴾." Ibn al-Anbari said: it is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: "and we had taken them."

Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, al-Hasan, Qatada, and the rest of the seven readers recited it with the interrogative hamza (a-ittakhadhnahum), to make them confront themselves with this, in a manner of rebuke and regret. That is: "Did we take them as objects of ridicule (sikhriyyan), when that was not the case?" Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) and his companions, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-A'raj, Nafi', Hamza, and al-Kisa'i recited (sukhriyyan) with a dammah on the sin, and its meaning is from al-sukhrah (servitude) and al-istikhdam (employment). al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Isa, Ibn Muhaysin, and the rest of the seven recited it with a kasrah on the sin, and its meaning is the well-known one of al-sukhr, which is mockery (al-huzu'). The poet said:

"There came to me a tongue by which I am not gladdened,
from a height, in which there is no lie and no mockery (sakhar)."

It is also said that with the kasrah it means from al-taskhir (subjugation).

As for "am" (or): if ittakhadhnahum is an interrogative, either with its hamza stated explicitly as in the reading of those who recited thus, or understood as interrogative with the hamza elided for indication, then "am" is apparently a connecting (muttasilah) particle, since the hamza precedes it. The meaning is: which of the two actions did we perform toward them, taking them in mockery, or disdaining and belittling them? And "our eyes were rising above them and passing over them."

It may be an interrogative in the sense of denial directed at themselves, for both mockery and deviation (of gaze). al-Hasan said: "All of that they did: they took them as objects of ridicule, and their eyes turned away from them, belittling them."

And if ittakhadhnahum is not an interrogative, then "am" is disjunctive (munqati'ah). It is also permissible for it to be disjunctive even with an interrogative preceding it, as in your saying: "Is Zayd with you, or is 'Amr with you?" You asked about Zayd, then turned away from that and asked about 'Amr. So the implied meaning is: "Rather, the eyes have turned away from them." It is also permissible that their saying ﴿Or have our eyes turned away from them?﴾ is connected to their saying ﴿What is wrong with us that we do not see men﴾, because the first interrogation indicated the absence of seeing them, and that is evidence that they were not with him. Then they allowed that they might have been with him, but their eyes did not see them.

﴿Indeed, that﴾, that is, the exchange which We have related from them, ﴿is truly (la-haqqun)﴾, that is: established and certain, which must occur among them.

The majority read ﴿mukhasamatu﴾ with a raf' (nominative) and in construct with Ahl (people). Ibn Atiyya said: it is a substitute (badal) for (la-haqqun). al-Zamakhshari said: he explains what it is, saying: ﴿mukhasamatu﴾ with tanwin, and (Ahlu) in the nominative, governed by the verbal noun with tanwin. al-Farra' does not permit this, but Sibawayh and the Basran grammarians permit it.

Ibn Abi Abla read ﴿mukhasamata ahli﴾ with a fathah on the mim and a kasrah on Ahl. al-Zamakhshari said: this is an attributive (sifah) to "that," because demonstrative nouns are described by common nouns.

In the Kitab al-Lawami' (a book of grammatical readings): "If ﴿mukhasamata ahli al-nar﴾ were read with a fathah, it would be permissible as a substitute for "that."

Ibn al-Sumayqa read ﴿mukhasama﴾ as a past verb, with (Ahlu) as its subject. He (Exalted is He) named that exchange which took place between the leaders of the disbelievers and their followers "a dispute (takhasum)," because their saying ﴿There is no welcome for them﴾ and the followers' saying ﴿Rather, you—there is no welcome for you﴾ belong to the category of disputation. So He called the whole exchange a dispute, because it was used in that sense.

(Say): O Muhammad, ﴿I am only a warner﴾, that is, a warner of the polytheists of the punishment, and that Allah—there is no god but Allah, He has no rival and no partner, and He is the One, the Subduer of everything, and that He is the Owner of the world, its high and its low, [p. 408] the Mighty who cannot be overcome, the Forgiving to those who believe in Him and follow His religion.

This is part 1 of 2 of the commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 38, verses 49–66.

﴿This is a reminder. And indeed, for the righteous is an excellent place of return,﴾ ﴿gardens of perpetual residence, whose gates are opened for them,﴾ ﴿reclining therein, calling therein for abundant fruit and drink.﴾ ﴿And with them will be women restraining their gazes, of equal age.﴾ ﴿This is what you were promised for the Day of Reckoning.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which will have no end.﴾ ﴿This is so. And indeed, for the transgressors is an evil place of return:﴾ ﴿Hell, which they will burn in, so wretched is the resting place.﴾ ﴿This, so let them taste it: scalding water and dark, cold liquid,﴾ ﴿and other punishments of similar kind, in pairs.﴾ ﴿This is a troop rushing in with you; no welcome for them. They will surely burn in the Fire.﴾ ﴿They will say, "Rather, it is you; no welcome for you! You brought this upon us, so wretched is the abode."﴾ ﴿They will say, "Our Lord, whoever brought this upon us, increase for him the punishment double in the Fire."﴾ ﴿And they will say, "What is wrong with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the wicked?﴾ ﴿Did we take them in mockery, or have our eyes turned away from them?"﴾ ﴿Indeed, that is true: the disputing of the people of the Fire.﴾ ﴿Say, "I am only a warner, and there is no deity except Allah, the One, the Subduer,﴾ ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, the Mighty, the Forgiving."﴾

(p-404) When Allah commanded him to be patient with the foolishness of his people, and mentioned a number of the prophets and their circumstances, He mentioned what the state of the believers and the disbelievers will lead to in terms of recompense, and the abode of each of the two groups. Since what He mentions is a kind of revelation, He said: "This is a reminder," as if He separated what came before it from what came after it. Do you not see that when He mentioned the people of Paradise and followed it with mention of the people of the Fire, He said: "This. And indeed, for the transgressors..."?

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "This is the mention of those prophets who have passed." It was also said: "This is a reminder," meaning: it is an honor by which you will be mentioned forever.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "jannāti" (gardens) in the accusative, and it is a substitute (badal). If ʿAdn (Eden) is a proper noun, then it is a definite substitute from an indefinite; and if it is indefinite, then it is an indefinite substitute from an indefinite.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Jannāti ʿadnin" is definite, due to His saying: "Gardens of perpetual residence which the Most Merciful has promised" [Maryam: 61]; and its accusative is as an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to "ḥusna maʾāb" (an excellent place of return), and "mufattaḥatan" (opened) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and its operator is what is in "al-muttaqīn" of the meaning of a verb. In "mufattaḥatan" there is a pronoun referring to the gardens, and "al-abwāb" (the gates) is a substitute from the pronoun, its estimate being: "opened, they are the gates," as in their saying: "Zayd was struck, the hand and the foot," and this is from substitution of part of the whole (badal al-ishtimal). End of quotation.

It is not necessary that "jannāti ʿadnin" be definite by the evidence he relied upon, namely His saying: "Gardens of perpetual residence which," [Maryam: 61]; for he believed that "allatī" is an adjective of "jannāti ʿadnin," and what he mentioned is not necessary, since it is permissible that "allatī" be a substitute from "jannāti ʿadnin." Do you not see that "alladhī" and "allatī" and their plurals are used as nouns, and so they follow the operators, and it does not necessarily follow that they are adjectives? As for its accusative as an explanatory apposition, that is not permissible; for the grammarians have two positions on this: one of them is that this only occurs in definites, so explanatory apposition follows only a definite; this is the position of the Basrans. The second is that it is permissible for it to occur in indefinites, so explanatory apposition may follow an indefinite, just as a definite may follow a definite in it; this is the position of the Kufans, and al-Farisi followed them.

As for their differing in indefiniteness and definiteness, no one has held this except this author. He permitted that in His saying: "The station of Ibrahim" [al-Baqarah: 125], parsing it as an explanatory apposition following an indefinite, namely "āyātun bayyinātun" [al-Baqarah: 99], while "maqām Ibrahim" [al-Baqarah: 125] is definite; and we have refuted him on this in its place in Al ʿImran.

As for his saying: "In 'mufattaḥatan' there is a pronoun referring to the gardens," the majority of grammarians parsed "al-abwāb" as a deputy subject (nāʾib fāʿil). Abu ʿAli came and said: If that is so, there is no pronoun returning to "jannāti ʿadnin" either in the circumstantial clause, if "mufattaḥatan" is parsed as a ḥāl, or in the adjectival clause, if it is parsed as an adjective of "jannāti ʿadnin." So he said: "In 'mufattaḥatan' there is a pronoun returning to the gardens, so that the circumstantial clause is linked to its referent, or the adjective to its modified noun, and 'al-abwāb' is a substitute." He said: whoever parses "al-abwāb" as a deputy subject, the returning pronoun to the gardens is omitted, its estimate being: "the gates of them." Abu ʿAli held that a substitute in such a case must have a pronoun, either pronounced or estimated. And when the sentence needs one estimate, it is preferable to one that needs two. As for the Kufans, the linking element for them is "al" (the definite article), because it takes the place of the pronoun, so it is as if he said: "opened for them are its gates."

As for his saying: "It is from substitution of part of the whole," if by "his saying" he means "the hand and the foot," then it is a mistake; rather, it is a substitution of part from whole (badal baʿḍ min kull). If he means "al-abwāb," then it may be correct, because the gates of the gardens are not part of the gardens.

As for his likening what he estimated from "mufattaḥatan hiya al-abwāb" to "Zayd was struck, the hand and the foot," its basis is that "al-abwāb" is a substitute from that hidden pronoun, just as "the hand and the foot" is a substitute from the apparent noun which is Zayd. Abu Ishaq said, and Ibn ʿAtiyya followed him: "Mufattaḥatan" is an adjective of "jannāti ʿadnin." Al-Hawfi said: "Mufattaḥatan" is a circumstantial clause, and its operator is an omitted verb indicated by the meaning, its estimate being: "they enter them." Zayd ibn ʿAli, ʿAbdullah ibn Rufayʿ, and Abu Haywa read: "Jannātu ʿadnin mufattaḥatun" with nominative case for both, as subject and predicate, or each of them is a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "it is the gardens of Eden, they are opened."

Al-Witakaʾ (reclining) is among the conditions of the people of felicity. "Yadʿūna fīhā" (calling therein) indicates that they have with them one whom they employ in what they request, as in His saying: "And there will circulate among them eternal youths" [al-Insan: 19].

Since the description of fruit varies in abundance, and its abundance is by the variety of its kinds, and the abundance of each kind; and since drink is one kind, which is wine, it was made singular.

"And with them are women restraining their gazes." Qatadah said: its meaning is "upon their husbands." "Atrāb" means: equals in one age; and its origin in the sons of Adam is that the dust touched their bodies at one time, and peers are more firmly established in mutual affection. The apparent meaning is that this description applies among themselves; it was also said: among their husbands, their ages are like theirs. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he means the human women. The author of al-Ghuniyan said: they are the ḥūr (wide-eyed maidens).

Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read: "wa-hādhā mā yūʿadūna" with the third person (yā' al-ghayba), since before it is "wa-ʿindahum"; and the rest of the seven read with the second person (tāʾ al-khiṭāb) by iltifat (shift of person), and the meaning: this is what the promise was made for, for the Day of Recompense.

"Inna hādhā": that is, what was mentioned for the righteous of what preceded, "la-rizquna," lasting forever, that is, it has no end.

"This, and indeed for the transgressors is an evil place of return." Al-Zajjaj said: that is, the matter is this. Abu ʿAli said: this is for the believers. Abu al-Baqa said: a subject with omitted predicate, or a predicate with omitted subject. The transgressors here are the disbelievers. Al-Jubba'i said: the people of major sins, whether they were disbelievers or not.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning is those who transgressed against Me and denied My messengers; for them is an evil place of return, that is, a place of return and destination.

"So wretched is the resting place": that is, "hādhā" is in the place of nominative case as subject whose predicate is "jahannam" (Hell), "wa-ghassāq," or a predicate of an omitted subject, that is, the punishment is this; and "ḥamīm" is the predicate of a subject, or in the place of accusative by the mode of occupation (ishtighāl), that is: "let them taste this, so let them taste it, scalding water," that is: it is scalding water, or an omitted-predicate subject, that is: from it is scalding water and from it is dark liquid, as the poet said:

"Until, when dawn shone in darkness, and the herbs were left, twisted and mown."

That is: from it is twisted, and from it is mown. These parsings are reported as sayings. It was also said: "hādhā" is the subject, and "fa-l-yadhūqūhu" is the predicate, and this is according to al-Akhfash's permission of it, such as: "Zayd, so strike him," citing the poet's words:

"And a sayer said: Khawlan, so marry their maidens."

"Al-ghassāq," according to Ibn ʿAbbas: the zamharir (extreme cold); and also from him, and from ʿAta', Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd: what flows of the pus of the people of the Fire.

From Kaʿb: a spring in Hell into which flows the venom of every venomous creature, a snake or scorpion or others, in which one is immersed, so the skin and flesh fall off from the bone.

From al-Suddi: what flows from their tears. From Ibn ʿUmar: pus flows from them, and they are given it to drink. Ibn Abi Ishaq, Qatadah, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, Hamzah, al-Kisai, Hafs, al-Fadl, Ibn Saʿdan, and Harun from Abu ʿAmr read with a doubled sin (ghassaqq). If it is an adjective, then it is of those whose modified noun is omitted; and if it is a noun, then fa"al is rare among nouns, of which there came: al-kallaʾ, al-jabbān, al-fannād, al-ʿaqqār, al-khaṭṭār. The rest of the seven read with a single sin.

The majority read "wa-ākharu" in the singular. It was said: a subject whose predicate is omitted, its estimate being: "and for them is another punishment." It was also said: its predicate is within the sentence, because "azwājun" is a subject, and "min shaklihi" is its predicate, and the sentence is the predicate of "wa-ākharu."

It was also said: its predicate is "azwājun," and "min shaklihi" is in the place of an adjective; and it is permissible that the plural be predicated of the singular, in terms of it being degrees and ranks of punishment, or he named each part of that other by the name of the whole.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "wa-ākharu," that is, "wa-ʿadhābun ākharu" (and another punishment), or "madhūqun ākharu" (another thing tasted); and "azwājun" is an adjective of "ākharu," because it is permissible that it be kinds (ḍurūb), or an adjective of the three: "ḥamīmun wa-ghassāq" and "wa-ākharu min shaklihi." End of quotation.

This is a parsing he took from al-Farra'.

Al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Jahdari, Ibn Jubayr, ʿIsa, and Abu ʿAmr read "wa-ukharu" in the plural. It is a subject, "min shaklihi" is in the place of an adjective, and "azwājun" is its predicate, that is: and other tastes of this taste, of the like of it in severity and horror. "Azwājun" means kinds.

Mujahid read "min shaklihi" with a kasra on the shin; the majority with a fatha; both are dialects with the meaning of "like" and "kind." As for when it means "opening," it is with a kasra on the shin only. From Ibn Masʿud: "wa-ākharu min shaklihi" is the zamharir.

The apparent meaning is that His saying: "This is a troop rushing in with you" is from the speech of their leaders to one another. "Fawj" is a large group. "Muqtaḥimun maʿakum," that is, into the Fire; they are the followers. Then they invoked curses on them by saying: "No welcome for them," because when the leader sees the lowly one joined with him in punishment, it grieves him that equality in punishment occurred, and that he was not the one spared from punishment while his followers were in punishment.

"Marḥaban" means: come to ample space and not narrowness; it is in the accusative by a verb that must be omitted; and because their height is an explanation of those cursed against.

It was also said: "This is a troop" is from the speech of the angels, the guardians of the Fire; and that the curse on the troop and the reason given by His saying "They are the ones who will burn in the Fire" are from their speech.

It was also said: "This is a troop rushing in with you" is from the speech of the angels, and the curse on the troop and the report that they will burn in the Fire are from the speech of the leading ones who were followed.

They said, that is, the troop: "No welcome for you," a reply to the leaders' curse upon them. Then they mentioned that what they fell into of punishment and burning of the Fire is only by what you cast upon us and adorned for us of disbelief; so it is as if you had brought the punishment or burning forward for us.

Since "no welcome for them" is from the speech of the guardians, the construction did not come as: "They say: rather, these, no welcome for them." Rather it came as the address of the followers to the leaders, so that the confrontation would be with those whom they could not confront in the world with something ugly that would heal their chests, since they caused their disbelief, and more painful to the leaders.

"So wretched is the abode": that is, the Fire; this is the intended meaning, and the supplication is like His saying: "Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister" [al-A'raf: 38]. The followers did not suffice with returning the curse on their leaders, nor with confronting them by saying: "You brought it upon us," until they asked Allah to increase their leaders double the Fire. The meaning: whoever compelled us to evil deeds until our reward became the Fire, "so increase for him the punishment double," as came in the saying of the followers: "Our Lord, give them" [al-Ahzab: 68], that is, their masters, "double the punishment" [al-Ahzab: 68], "Our Lord, these misled us, so give them a double punishment of the Fire" [al-A'raf: 38].

[p. 407] Since the leaders were themselves misguided and misled their followers, it was fitting that they be called upon to be given double punishment, as in the saying: "Upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection." On this reading, the pronoun in His saying (qalu, "they said") refers to the followers.

﴿Whoever brought this upon us﴾ refers to the leaders. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: "﴿They say: Our Lord...﴾ up to the end is the speech of all the people of the Fire." al-Dahhak said: "﴿Whoever brought this upon us﴾ is Iblis and Qabil (Cain)." Ibn Mas'ud said: "The double punishment is snakes and scorpions."

(And they said), that is, the nobles of the disbelievers: ﴿What is wrong with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the wicked?﴾ That is, the lowly ones who have no good in them and who are not upon our religion, just as He said: ﴿And we see no one following you except those who are our lowest (arazil)﴾ [Hud: 27].

It is related that those among the disbelievers of the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) who spoke these words were Abu Jahl, Umayya ibn Khalaf, and the people of the well (al-qalib). Those they did not see were Ammar, Suhayb, Salman, and those who went their way. This was said by Mujahid and others. It is said that they would ask: "Where is Ammar? Where is Suhayb? Where is so-and-so?" They counted them among the weak Muslims, and it would be said to them: "Those are in Paradise (al-Firdaws)."

al-Nahwiyyan (the two grammarians, i.e., al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'? the reading is attributed to the two Kufan/Basran grammarians named in the source) and Hamza recited (ittakhadhnahum) with continuous pronunciation (wasl). Abu Hatim, al-Zamakhshari, and Ibn Atiyya said: it is an attributive (sifah) to rijal (men). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Like His saying: ﴿We used to count them among the wicked﴾." Ibn al-Anbari said: it is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: "and we had taken them."

Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, al-Hasan, Qatada, and the rest of the seven readers recited it with the interrogative hamza (a-ittakhadhnahum), to make them confront themselves with this, in a manner of rebuke and regret. That is: "Did we take them as objects of ridicule (sikhriyyan), when that was not the case?" Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) and his companions, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-A'raj, Nafi', Hamza, and al-Kisa'i recited (sukhriyyan) with a dammah on the sin, and its meaning is from al-sukhrah (servitude) and al-istikhdam (employment). al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Isa, Ibn Muhaysin, and the rest of the seven recited it with a kasrah on the sin, and its meaning is the well-known one of al-sukhr, which is mockery (al-huzu'). The poet said:

"There came to me a tongue by which I am not gladdened,
from a height, in which there is no lie and no mockery (sakhar)."

It is also said that with the kasrah it means from al-taskhir (subjugation).

As for "am" (or): if ittakhadhnahum is an interrogative, either with its hamza stated explicitly as in the reading of those who recited thus, or understood as interrogative with the hamza elided for indication, then "am" is apparently a connecting (muttasilah) particle, since the hamza precedes it. The meaning is: which of the two actions did we perform toward them, taking them in mockery, or disdaining and belittling them? And "our eyes were rising above them and passing over them."

It may be an interrogative in the sense of denial directed at themselves, for both mockery and deviation (of gaze). al-Hasan said: "All of that they did: they took them as objects of ridicule, and their eyes turned away from them, belittling them."

And if ittakhadhnahum is not an interrogative, then "am" is disjunctive (munqati'ah). It is also permissible for it to be disjunctive even with an interrogative preceding it, as in your saying: "Is Zayd with you, or is 'Amr with you?" You asked about Zayd, then turned away from that and asked about 'Amr. So the implied meaning is: "Rather, the eyes have turned away from them." It is also permissible that their saying ﴿Or have our eyes turned away from them?﴾ is connected to their saying ﴿What is wrong with us that we do not see men﴾, because the first interrogation indicated the absence of seeing them, and that is evidence that they were not with him. Then they allowed that they might have been with him, but their eyes did not see them.

﴿Indeed, that﴾, that is, the exchange which We have related from them, ﴿is truly (la-haqqun)﴾, that is: established and certain, which must occur among them.

The majority read ﴿mukhasamatu﴾ with a raf' (nominative) and in construct with Ahl (people). Ibn Atiyya said: it is a substitute (badal) for (la-haqqun). al-Zamakhshari said: he explains what it is, saying: ﴿mukhasamatu﴾ with tanwin, and (Ahlu) in the nominative, governed by the verbal noun with tanwin. al-Farra' does not permit this, but Sibawayh and the Basran grammarians permit it.

Ibn Abi Abla read ﴿mukhasamata ahli﴾ with a fathah on the mim and a kasrah on Ahl. al-Zamakhshari said: this is an attributive (sifah) to "that," because demonstrative nouns are described by common nouns.

In the Kitab al-Lawami' (a book of grammatical readings): "If ﴿mukhasamata ahli al-nar﴾ were read with a fathah, it would be permissible as a substitute for "that."

Ibn al-Sumayqa read ﴿mukhasama﴾ as a past verb, with (Ahlu) as its subject. He (Exalted is He) named that exchange which took place between the leaders of the disbelievers and their followers "a dispute (takhasum)," because their saying ﴿There is no welcome for them﴾ and the followers' saying ﴿Rather, you—there is no welcome for you﴾ belong to the category of disputation. So He called the whole exchange a dispute, because it was used in that sense.

(Say): O Muhammad, ﴿I am only a warner﴾, that is, a warner of the polytheists of the punishment, and that Allah—there is no god but Allah, He has no rival and no partner, and He is the One, the Subduer of everything, and that He is the Owner of the world, its high and its low, [p. 408] the Mighty who cannot be overcome, the Forgiving to those who believe in Him and follow His religion.

This is part 1 of 2 of the commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 38, verses 49–66.

﴿This is a reminder. And indeed, for the righteous is an excellent place of return,﴾ ﴿gardens of perpetual residence, whose gates are opened for them,﴾ ﴿reclining therein, calling therein for abundant fruit and drink.﴾ ﴿And with them will be women restraining their gazes, of equal age.﴾ ﴿This is what you were promised for the Day of Reckoning.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which will have no end.﴾ ﴿This is so. And indeed, for the transgressors is an evil place of return:﴾ ﴿Hell, which they will burn in, so wretched is the resting place.﴾ ﴿This, so let them taste it: scalding water and dark, cold liquid,﴾ ﴿and other punishments of similar kind, in pairs.﴾ ﴿This is a troop rushing in with you; no welcome for them. They will surely burn in the Fire.﴾ ﴿They will say, "Rather, it is you; no welcome for you! You brought this upon us, so wretched is the abode."﴾ ﴿They will say, "Our Lord, whoever brought this upon us, increase for him the punishment double in the Fire."﴾ ﴿And they will say, "What is wrong with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the wicked?﴾ ﴿Did we take them in mockery, or have our eyes turned away from them?"﴾ ﴿Indeed, that is true: the disputing of the people of the Fire.﴾ ﴿Say, "I am only a warner, and there is no deity except Allah, the One, the Subduer,﴾ ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, the Mighty, the Forgiving."﴾

(p-404) When Allah commanded him to be patient with the foolishness of his people, and mentioned a number of the prophets and their circumstances, He mentioned what the state of the believers and the disbelievers will lead to in terms of recompense, and the abode of each of the two groups. Since what He mentions is a kind of revelation, He said: "This is a reminder," as if He separated what came before it from what came after it. Do you not see that when He mentioned the people of Paradise and followed it with mention of the people of the Fire, He said: "This. And indeed, for the transgressors..."?

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "This is the mention of those prophets who have passed." It was also said: "This is a reminder," meaning: it is an honor by which you will be mentioned forever.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "jannāti" (gardens) in the accusative, and it is a substitute (badal). If ʿAdn (Eden) is a proper noun, then it is a definite substitute from an indefinite; and if it is indefinite, then it is an indefinite substitute from an indefinite.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Jannāti ʿadnin" is definite, due to His saying: "Gardens of perpetual residence which the Most Merciful has promised" [Maryam: 61]; and its accusative is as an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to "ḥusna maʾāb" (an excellent place of return), and "mufattaḥatan" (opened) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and its operator is what is in "al-muttaqīn" of the meaning of a verb. In "mufattaḥatan" there is a pronoun referring to the gardens, and "al-abwāb" (the gates) is a substitute from the pronoun, its estimate being: "opened, they are the gates," as in their saying: "Zayd was struck, the hand and the foot," and this is from substitution of part of the whole (badal al-ishtimal). End of quotation.

It is not necessary that "jannāti ʿadnin" be definite by the evidence he relied upon, namely His saying: "Gardens of perpetual residence which," [Maryam: 61]; for he believed that "allatī" is an adjective of "jannāti ʿadnin," and what he mentioned is not necessary, since it is permissible that "allatī" be a substitute from "jannāti ʿadnin." Do you not see that "alladhī" and "allatī" and their plurals are used as nouns, and so they follow the operators, and it does not necessarily follow that they are adjectives? As for its accusative as an explanatory apposition, that is not permissible; for the grammarians have two positions on this: one of them is that this only occurs in definites, so explanatory apposition follows only a definite; this is the position of the Basrans. The second is that it is permissible for it to occur in indefinites, so explanatory apposition may follow an indefinite, just as a definite may follow a definite in it; this is the position of the Kufans, and al-Farisi followed them.

As for their differing in indefiniteness and definiteness, no one has held this except this author. He permitted that in His saying: "The station of Ibrahim" [al-Baqarah: 125], parsing it as an explanatory apposition following an indefinite, namely "āyātun bayyinātun" [al-Baqarah: 99], while "maqām Ibrahim" [al-Baqarah: 125] is definite; and we have refuted him on this in its place in Al ʿImran.

As for his saying: "In 'mufattaḥatan' there is a pronoun referring to the gardens," the majority of grammarians parsed "al-abwāb" as a deputy subject (nāʾib fāʿil). Abu ʿAli came and said: If that is so, there is no pronoun returning to "jannāti ʿadnin" either in the circumstantial clause, if "mufattaḥatan" is parsed as a ḥāl, or in the adjectival clause, if it is parsed as an adjective of "jannāti ʿadnin." So he said: "In 'mufattaḥatan' there is a pronoun returning to the gardens, so that the circumstantial clause is linked to its referent, or the adjective to its modified noun, and 'al-abwāb' is a substitute." He said: whoever parses "al-abwāb" as a deputy subject, the returning pronoun to the gardens is omitted, its estimate being: "the gates of them." Abu ʿAli held that a substitute in such a case must have a pronoun, either pronounced or estimated. And when the sentence needs one estimate, it is preferable to one that needs two. As for the Kufans, the linking element for them is "al" (the definite article), because it takes the place of the pronoun, so it is as if he said: "opened for them are its gates."

As for his saying: "It is from substitution of part of the whole," if by "his saying" he means "the hand and the foot," then it is a mistake; rather, it is a substitution of part from whole (badal baʿḍ min kull). If he means "al-abwāb," then it may be correct, because the gates of the gardens are not part of the gardens.

As for his likening what he estimated from "mufattaḥatan hiya al-abwāb" to "Zayd was struck, the hand and the foot," its basis is that "al-abwāb" is a substitute from that hidden pronoun, just as "the hand and the foot" is a substitute from the apparent noun which is Zayd. Abu Ishaq said, and Ibn ʿAtiyya followed him: "Mufattaḥatan" is an adjective of "jannāti ʿadnin." Al-Hawfi said: "Mufattaḥatan" is a circumstantial clause, and its operator is an omitted verb indicated by the meaning, its estimate being: "they enter them." Zayd ibn ʿAli, ʿAbdullah ibn Rufayʿ, and Abu Haywa read: "Jannātu ʿadnin mufattaḥatun" with nominative case for both, as subject and predicate, or each of them is a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "it is the gardens of Eden, they are opened."

Al-Witakaʾ (reclining) is among the conditions of the people of felicity. "Yadʿūna fīhā" (calling therein) indicates that they have with them one whom they employ in what they request, as in His saying: "And there will circulate among them eternal youths" [al-Insan: 19].

Since the description of fruit varies in abundance, and its abundance is by the variety of its kinds, and the abundance of each kind; and since drink is one kind, which is wine, it was made singular.

"And with them are women restraining their gazes." Qatadah said: its meaning is "upon their husbands." "Atrāb" means: equals in one age; and its origin in the sons of Adam is that the dust touched their bodies at one time, and peers are more firmly established in mutual affection. The apparent meaning is that this description applies among themselves; it was also said: among their husbands, their ages are like theirs. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he means the human women. The author of al-Ghuniyan said: they are the ḥūr (wide-eyed maidens).

Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read: "wa-hādhā mā yūʿadūna" with the third person (yā' al-ghayba), since before it is "wa-ʿindahum"; and the rest of the seven read with the second person (tāʾ al-khiṭāb) by iltifat (shift of person), and the meaning: this is what the promise was made for, for the Day of Recompense.

"Inna hādhā": that is, what was mentioned for the righteous of what preceded, "la-rizquna," lasting forever, that is, it has no end.

"This, and indeed for the transgressors is an evil place of return." Al-Zajjaj said: that is, the matter is this. Abu ʿAli said: this is for the believers. Abu al-Baqa said: a subject with omitted predicate, or a predicate with omitted subject. The transgressors here are the disbelievers. Al-Jubba'i said: the people of major sins, whether they were disbelievers or not.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning is those who transgressed against Me and denied My messengers; for them is an evil place of return, that is, a place of return and destination.

"So wretched is the resting place": that is, "hādhā" is in the place of nominative case as subject whose predicate is "jahannam" (Hell), "wa-ghassāq," or a predicate of an omitted subject, that is, the punishment is this; and "ḥamīm" is the predicate of a subject, or in the place of accusative by the mode of occupation (ishtighāl), that is: "let them taste this, so let them taste it, scalding water," that is: it is scalding water, or an omitted-predicate subject, that is: from it is scalding water and from it is dark liquid, as the poet said:

"Until, when dawn shone in darkness, and the herbs were left, twisted and mown."

That is: from it is twisted, and from it is mown. These parsings are reported as sayings. It was also said: "hādhā" is the subject, and "fa-l-yadhūqūhu" is the predicate, and this is according to al-Akhfash's permission of it, such as: "Zayd, so strike him," citing the poet's words:

"And a sayer said: Khawlan, so marry their maidens."

"Al-ghassāq," according to Ibn ʿAbbas: the zamharir (extreme cold); and also from him, and from ʿAta', Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd: what flows of the pus of the people of the Fire.

From Kaʿb: a spring in Hell into which flows the venom of every venomous creature, a snake or scorpion or others, in which one is immersed, so the skin and flesh fall off from the bone.

From al-Suddi: what flows from their tears. From Ibn ʿUmar: pus flows from them, and they are given it to drink. Ibn Abi Ishaq, Qatadah, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, Hamzah, al-Kisai, Hafs, al-Fadl, Ibn Saʿdan, and Harun from Abu ʿAmr read with a doubled sin (ghassaqq). If it is an adjective, then it is of those whose modified noun is omitted; and if it is a noun, then fa"al is rare among nouns, of which there came: al-kallaʾ, al-jabbān, al-fannād, al-ʿaqqār, al-khaṭṭār. The rest of the seven read with a single sin.

The majority read "wa-ākharu" in the singular. It was said: a subject whose predicate is omitted, its estimate being: "and for them is another punishment." It was also said: its predicate is within the sentence, because "azwājun" is a subject, and "min shaklihi" is its predicate, and the sentence is the predicate of "wa-ākharu."

It was also said: its predicate is "azwājun," and "min shaklihi" is in the place of an adjective; and it is permissible that the plural be predicated of the singular, in terms of it being degrees and ranks of punishment, or he named each part of that other by the name of the whole.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "wa-ākharu," that is, "wa-ʿadhābun ākharu" (and another punishment), or "madhūqun ākharu" (another thing tasted); and "azwājun" is an adjective of "ākharu," because it is permissible that it be kinds (ḍurūb), or an adjective of the three: "ḥamīmun wa-ghassāq" and "wa-ākharu min shaklihi." End of quotation.

This is a parsing he took from al-Farra'.

Al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Jahdari, Ibn Jubayr, ʿIsa, and Abu ʿAmr read "wa-ukharu" in the plural. It is a subject, "min shaklihi" is in the place of an adjective, and "azwājun" is its predicate, that is: and other tastes of this taste, of the like of it in severity and horror. "Azwājun" means kinds.

Mujahid read "min shaklihi" with a kasra on the shin; the majority with a fatha; both are dialects with the meaning of "like" and "kind." As for when it means "opening," it is with a kasra on the shin only. From Ibn Masʿud: "wa-ākharu min shaklihi" is the zamharir.

The apparent meaning is that His saying: "This is a troop rushing in with you" is from the speech of their leaders to one another. "Fawj" is a large group. "Muqtaḥimun maʿakum," that is, into the Fire; they are the followers. Then they invoked curses on them by saying: "No welcome for them," because when the leader sees the lowly one joined with him in punishment, it grieves him that equality in punishment occurred, and that he was not the one spared from punishment while his followers were in punishment.

"Marḥaban" means: come to ample space and not narrowness; it is in the accusative by a verb that must be omitted; and because their height is an explanation of those cursed against.

It was also said: "This is a troop" is from the speech of the angels, the guardians of the Fire; and that the curse on the troop and the reason given by His saying "They are the ones who will burn in the Fire" are from their speech.

It was also said: "This is a troop rushing in with you" is from the speech of the angels, and the curse on the troop and the report that they will burn in the Fire are from the speech of the leading ones who were followed.

They said, that is, the troop: "No welcome for you," a reply to the leaders' curse upon them. Then they mentioned that what they fell into of punishment and burning of the Fire is only by what you cast upon us and adorned for us of disbelief; so it is as if you had brought the punishment or burning forward for us.

Since "no welcome for them" is from the speech of the guardians, the construction did not come as: "They say: rather, these, no welcome for them." Rather it came as the address of the followers to the leaders, so that the confrontation would be with those whom they could not confront in the world with something ugly that would heal their chests, since they caused their disbelief, and more painful to the leaders.

"So wretched is the abode": that is, the Fire; this is the intended meaning, and the supplication is like His saying: "Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister" [al-A'raf: 38]. The followers did not suffice with returning the curse on their leaders, nor with confronting them by saying: "You brought it upon us," until they asked Allah to increase their leaders double the Fire. The meaning: whoever compelled us to evil deeds until our reward became the Fire, "so increase for him the punishment double," as came in the saying of the followers: "Our Lord, give them" [al-Ahzab: 68], that is, their masters, "double the punishment" [al-Ahzab: 68], "Our Lord, these misled us, so give them a double punishment of the Fire" [al-A'raf: 38].

[p. 407] Since the leaders were themselves misguided and misled their followers, it was fitting that they be called upon to be given double punishment, as in the saying: "Upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection." On this reading, the pronoun in His saying (qalu, "they said") refers to the followers.

﴿Whoever brought this upon us﴾ refers to the leaders. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: "﴿They say: Our Lord...﴾ up to the end is the speech of all the people of the Fire." al-Dahhak said: "﴿Whoever brought this upon us﴾ is Iblis and Qabil (Cain)." Ibn Mas'ud said: "The double punishment is snakes and scorpions."

(And they said), that is, the nobles of the disbelievers: ﴿What is wrong with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the wicked?﴾ That is, the lowly ones who have no good in them and who are not upon our religion, just as He said: ﴿And we see no one following you except those who are our lowest (arazil)﴾ [Hud: 27].

It is related that those among the disbelievers of the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) who spoke these words were Abu Jahl, Umayya ibn Khalaf, and the people of the well (al-qalib). Those they did not see were Ammar, Suhayb, Salman, and those who went their way. This was said by Mujahid and others. It is said that they would ask: "Where is Ammar? Where is Suhayb? Where is so-and-so?" They counted them among the weak Muslims, and it would be said to them: "Those are in Paradise (al-Firdaws)."

al-Nahwiyyan (the two grammarians, i.e., al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'? the reading is attributed to the two Kufan/Basran grammarians named in the source) and Hamza recited (ittakhadhnahum) with continuous pronunciation (wasl). Abu Hatim, al-Zamakhshari, and Ibn Atiyya said: it is an attributive (sifah) to rijal (men). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Like His saying: ﴿We used to count them among the wicked﴾." Ibn al-Anbari said: it is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: "and we had taken them."

Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, al-Hasan, Qatada, and the rest of the seven readers recited it with the interrogative hamza (a-ittakhadhnahum), to make them confront themselves with this, in a manner of rebuke and regret. That is: "Did we take them as objects of ridicule (sikhriyyan), when that was not the case?" Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) and his companions, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-A'raj, Nafi', Hamza, and al-Kisa'i recited (sukhriyyan) with a dammah on the sin, and its meaning is from al-sukhrah (servitude) and al-istikhdam (employment). al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Isa, Ibn Muhaysin, and the rest of the seven recited it with a kasrah on the sin, and its meaning is the well-known one of al-sukhr, which is mockery (al-huzu'). The poet said:

"There came to me a tongue by which I am not gladdened,
from a height, in which there is no lie and no mockery (sakhar)."

It is also said that with the kasrah it means from al-taskhir (subjugation).

As for "am" (or): if ittakhadhnahum is an interrogative, either with its hamza stated explicitly as in the reading of those who recited thus, or understood as interrogative with the hamza elided for indication, then "am" is apparently a connecting (muttasilah) particle, since the hamza precedes it. The meaning is: which of the two actions did we perform toward them, taking them in mockery, or disdaining and belittling them? And "our eyes were rising above them and passing over them."

It may be an interrogative in the sense of denial directed at themselves, for both mockery and deviation (of gaze). al-Hasan said: "All of that they did: they took them as objects of ridicule, and their eyes turned away from them, belittling them."

And if ittakhadhnahum is not an interrogative, then "am" is disjunctive (munqati'ah). It is also permissible for it to be disjunctive even with an interrogative preceding it, as in your saying: "Is Zayd with you, or is 'Amr with you?" You asked about Zayd, then turned away from that and asked about 'Amr. So the implied meaning is: "Rather, the eyes have turned away from them." It is also permissible that their saying ﴿Or have our eyes turned away from them?﴾ is connected to their saying ﴿What is wrong with us that we do not see men﴾, because the first interrogation indicated the absence of seeing them, and that is evidence that they were not with him. Then they allowed that they might have been with him, but their eyes did not see them.

﴿Indeed, that﴾, that is, the exchange which We have related from them, ﴿is truly (la-haqqun)﴾, that is: established and certain, which must occur among them.

The majority read ﴿mukhasamatu﴾ with a raf' (nominative) and in construct with Ahl (people). Ibn Atiyya said: it is a substitute (badal) for (la-haqqun). al-Zamakhshari said: he explains what it is, saying: ﴿mukhasamatu﴾ with tanwin, and (Ahlu) in the nominative, governed by the verbal noun with tanwin. al-Farra' does not permit this, but Sibawayh and the Basran grammarians permit it.

Ibn Abi Abla read ﴿mukhasamata ahli﴾ with a fathah on the mim and a kasrah on Ahl. al-Zamakhshari said: this is an attributive (sifah) to "that," because demonstrative nouns are described by common nouns.

In the Kitab al-Lawami' (a book of grammatical readings): "If ﴿mukhasamata ahli al-nar﴾ were read with a fathah, it would be permissible as a substitute for "that."

Ibn al-Sumayqa read ﴿mukhasama﴾ as a past verb, with (Ahlu) as its subject. He (Exalted is He) named that exchange which took place between the leaders of the disbelievers and their followers "a dispute (takhasum)," because their saying ﴿There is no welcome for them﴾ and the followers' saying ﴿Rather, you—there is no welcome for you﴾ belong to the category of disputation. So He called the whole exchange a dispute, because it was used in that sense.

(Say): O Muhammad, ﴿I am only a warner﴾, that is, a warner of the polytheists of the punishment, and that Allah—there is no god but Allah, He has no rival and no partner, and He is the One, the Subduer of everything, and that He is the Owner of the world, its high and its low, [p. 408] the Mighty who cannot be overcome, the Forgiving to those who believe in Him and follow His religion.

This is part 1 of 2 of the commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 38, verses 49–66.

﴿This is a reminder. And indeed, for the righteous is an excellent place of return,﴾ ﴿gardens of perpetual residence, whose gates are opened for them,﴾ ﴿reclining therein, calling therein for abundant fruit and drink.﴾ ﴿And with them will be women restraining their gazes, of equal age.﴾ ﴿This is what you were promised for the Day of Reckoning.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which will have no end.﴾ ﴿This is so. And indeed, for the transgressors is an evil place of return:﴾ ﴿Hell, which they will burn in, so wretched is the resting place.﴾ ﴿This, so let them taste it: scalding water and dark, cold liquid,﴾ ﴿and other punishments of similar kind, in pairs.﴾ ﴿This is a troop rushing in with you; no welcome for them. They will surely burn in the Fire.﴾ ﴿They will say, "Rather, it is you; no welcome for you! You brought this upon us, so wretched is the abode."﴾ ﴿They will say, "Our Lord, whoever brought this upon us, increase for him the punishment double in the Fire."﴾ ﴿And they will say, "What is wrong with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the wicked?﴾ ﴿Did we take them in mockery, or have our eyes turned away from them?"﴾ ﴿Indeed, that is true: the disputing of the people of the Fire.﴾ ﴿Say, "I am only a warner, and there is no deity except Allah, the One, the Subduer,﴾ ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, the Mighty, the Forgiving."﴾

(p-404) When Allah commanded him to be patient with the foolishness of his people, and mentioned a number of the prophets and their circumstances, He mentioned what the state of the believers and the disbelievers will lead to in terms of recompense, and the abode of each of the two groups. Since what He mentions is a kind of revelation, He said: "This is a reminder," as if He separated what came before it from what came after it. Do you not see that when He mentioned the people of Paradise and followed it with mention of the people of the Fire, He said: "This. And indeed, for the transgressors..."?

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "This is the mention of those prophets who have passed." It was also said: "This is a reminder," meaning: it is an honor by which you will be mentioned forever.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "jannāti" (gardens) in the accusative, and it is a substitute (badal). If ʿAdn (Eden) is a proper noun, then it is a definite substitute from an indefinite; and if it is indefinite, then it is an indefinite substitute from an indefinite.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Jannāti ʿadnin" is definite, due to His saying: "Gardens of perpetual residence which the Most Merciful has promised" [Maryam: 61]; and its accusative is as an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to "ḥusna maʾāb" (an excellent place of return), and "mufattaḥatan" (opened) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and its operator is what is in "al-muttaqīn" of the meaning of a verb. In "mufattaḥatan" there is a pronoun referring to the gardens, and "al-abwāb" (the gates) is a substitute from the pronoun, its estimate being: "opened, they are the gates," as in their saying: "Zayd was struck, the hand and the foot," and this is from substitution of part of the whole (badal al-ishtimal). End of quotation.

It is not necessary that "jannāti ʿadnin" be definite by the evidence he relied upon, namely His saying: "Gardens of perpetual residence which," [Maryam: 61]; for he believed that "allatī" is an adjective of "jannāti ʿadnin," and what he mentioned is not necessary, since it is permissible that "allatī" be a substitute from "jannāti ʿadnin." Do you not see that "alladhī" and "allatī" and their plurals are used as nouns, and so they follow the operators, and it does not necessarily follow that they are adjectives? As for its accusative as an explanatory apposition, that is not permissible; for the grammarians have two positions on this: one of them is that this only occurs in definites, so explanatory apposition follows only a definite; this is the position of the Basrans. The second is that it is permissible for it to occur in indefinites, so explanatory apposition may follow an indefinite, just as a definite may follow a definite in it; this is the position of the Kufans, and al-Farisi followed them.

As for their differing in indefiniteness and definiteness, no one has held this except this author. He permitted that in His saying: "The station of Ibrahim" [al-Baqarah: 125], parsing it as an explanatory apposition following an indefinite, namely "āyātun bayyinātun" [al-Baqarah: 99], while "maqām Ibrahim" [al-Baqarah: 125] is definite; and we have refuted him on this in its place in Al ʿImran.

As for his saying: "In 'mufattaḥatan' there is a pronoun referring to the gardens," the majority of grammarians parsed "al-abwāb" as a deputy subject (nāʾib fāʿil). Abu ʿAli came and said: If that is so, there is no pronoun returning to "jannāti ʿadnin" either in the circumstantial clause, if "mufattaḥatan" is parsed as a ḥāl, or in the adjectival clause, if it is parsed as an adjective of "jannāti ʿadnin." So he said: "In 'mufattaḥatan' there is a pronoun returning to the gardens, so that the circumstantial clause is linked to its referent, or the adjective to its modified noun, and 'al-abwāb' is a substitute." He said: whoever parses "al-abwāb" as a deputy subject, the returning pronoun to the gardens is omitted, its estimate being: "the gates of them." Abu ʿAli held that a substitute in such a case must have a pronoun, either pronounced or estimated. And when the sentence needs one estimate, it is preferable to one that needs two. As for the Kufans, the linking element for them is "al" (the definite article), because it takes the place of the pronoun, so it is as if he said: "opened for them are its gates."

As for his saying: "It is from substitution of part of the whole," if by "his saying" he means "the hand and the foot," then it is a mistake; rather, it is a substitution of part from whole (badal baʿḍ min kull). If he means "al-abwāb," then it may be correct, because the gates of the gardens are not part of the gardens.

As for his likening what he estimated from "mufattaḥatan hiya al-abwāb" to "Zayd was struck, the hand and the foot," its basis is that "al-abwāb" is a substitute from that hidden pronoun, just as "the hand and the foot" is a substitute from the apparent noun which is Zayd. Abu Ishaq said, and Ibn ʿAtiyya followed him: "Mufattaḥatan" is an adjective of "jannāti ʿadnin." Al-Hawfi said: "Mufattaḥatan" is a circumstantial clause, and its operator is an omitted verb indicated by the meaning, its estimate being: "they enter them." Zayd ibn ʿAli, ʿAbdullah ibn Rufayʿ, and Abu Haywa read: "Jannātu ʿadnin mufattaḥatun" with nominative case for both, as subject and predicate, or each of them is a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "it is the gardens of Eden, they are opened."

Al-Witakaʾ (reclining) is among the conditions of the people of felicity. "Yadʿūna fīhā" (calling therein) indicates that they have with them one whom they employ in what they request, as in His saying: "And there will circulate among them eternal youths" [al-Insan: 19].

Since the description of fruit varies in abundance, and its abundance is by the variety of its kinds, and the abundance of each kind; and since drink is one kind, which is wine, it was made singular.

"And with them are women restraining their gazes." Qatadah said: its meaning is "upon their husbands." "Atrāb" means: equals in one age; and its origin in the sons of Adam is that the dust touched their bodies at one time, and peers are more firmly established in mutual affection. The apparent meaning is that this description applies among themselves; it was also said: among their husbands, their ages are like theirs. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he means the human women. The author of al-Ghuniyan said: they are the ḥūr (wide-eyed maidens).

Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read: "wa-hādhā mā yūʿadūna" with the third person (yā' al-ghayba), since before it is "wa-ʿindahum"; and the rest of the seven read with the second person (tāʾ al-khiṭāb) by iltifat (shift of person), and the meaning: this is what the promise was made for, for the Day of Recompense.

"Inna hādhā": that is, what was mentioned for the righteous of what preceded, "la-rizquna," lasting forever, that is, it has no end.

"This, and indeed for the transgressors is an evil place of return." Al-Zajjaj said: that is, the matter is this. Abu ʿAli said: this is for the believers. Abu al-Baqa said: a subject with omitted predicate, or a predicate with omitted subject. The transgressors here are the disbelievers. Al-Jubba'i said: the people of major sins, whether they were disbelievers or not.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning is those who transgressed against Me and denied My messengers; for them is an evil place of return, that is, a place of return and destination.

"So wretched is the resting place": that is, "hādhā" is in the place of nominative case as subject whose predicate is "jahannam" (Hell), "wa-ghassāq," or a predicate of an omitted subject, that is, the punishment is this; and "ḥamīm" is the predicate of a subject, or in the place of accusative by the mode of occupation (ishtighāl), that is: "let them taste this, so let them taste it, scalding water," that is: it is scalding water, or an omitted-predicate subject, that is: from it is scalding water and from it is dark liquid, as the poet said:

"Until, when dawn shone in darkness, and the herbs were left, twisted and mown."

That is: from it is twisted, and from it is mown. These parsings are reported as sayings. It was also said: "hādhā" is the subject, and "fa-l-yadhūqūhu" is the predicate, and this is according to al-Akhfash's permission of it, such as: "Zayd, so strike him," citing the poet's words:

"And a sayer said: Khawlan, so marry their maidens."

"Al-ghassāq," according to Ibn ʿAbbas: the zamharir (extreme cold); and also from him, and from ʿAta', Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd: what flows of the pus of the people of the Fire.

From Kaʿb: a spring in Hell into which flows the venom of every venomous creature, a snake or scorpion or others, in which one is immersed, so the skin and flesh fall off from the bone.

From al-Suddi: what flows from their tears. From Ibn ʿUmar: pus flows from them, and they are given it to drink. Ibn Abi Ishaq, Qatadah, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, Hamzah, al-Kisai, Hafs, al-Fadl, Ibn Saʿdan, and Harun from Abu ʿAmr read with a doubled sin (ghassaqq). If it is an adjective, then it is of those whose modified noun is omitted; and if it is a noun, then fa"al is rare among nouns, of which there came: al-kallaʾ, al-jabbān, al-fannād, al-ʿaqqār, al-khaṭṭār. The rest of the seven read with a single sin.

The majority read "wa-ākharu" in the singular. It was said: a subject whose predicate is omitted, its estimate being: "and for them is another punishment." It was also said: its predicate is within the sentence, because "azwājun" is a subject, and "min shaklihi" is its predicate, and the sentence is the predicate of "wa-ākharu."

It was also said: its predicate is "azwājun," and "min shaklihi" is in the place of an adjective; and it is permissible that the plural be predicated of the singular, in terms of it being degrees and ranks of punishment, or he named each part of that other by the name of the whole.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "wa-ākharu," that is, "wa-ʿadhābun ākharu" (and another punishment), or "madhūqun ākharu" (another thing tasted); and "azwājun" is an adjective of "ākharu," because it is permissible that it be kinds (ḍurūb), or an adjective of the three: "ḥamīmun wa-ghassāq" and "wa-ākharu min shaklihi." End of quotation.

This is a parsing he took from al-Farra'.

Al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Jahdari, Ibn Jubayr, ʿIsa, and Abu ʿAmr read "wa-ukharu" in the plural. It is a subject, "min shaklihi" is in the place of an adjective, and "azwājun" is its predicate, that is: and other tastes of this taste, of the like of it in severity and horror. "Azwājun" means kinds.

Mujahid read "min shaklihi" with a kasra on the shin; the majority with a fatha; both are dialects with the meaning of "like" and "kind." As for when it means "opening," it is with a kasra on the shin only. From Ibn Masʿud: "wa-ākharu min shaklihi" is the zamharir.

The apparent meaning is that His saying: "This is a troop rushing in with you" is from the speech of their leaders to one another. "Fawj" is a large group. "Muqtaḥimun maʿakum," that is, into the Fire; they are the followers. Then they invoked curses on them by saying: "No welcome for them," because when the leader sees the lowly one joined with him in punishment, it grieves him that equality in punishment occurred, and that he was not the one spared from punishment while his followers were in punishment.

"Marḥaban" means: come to ample space and not narrowness; it is in the accusative by a verb that must be omitted; and because their height is an explanation of those cursed against.

It was also said: "This is a troop" is from the speech of the angels, the guardians of the Fire; and that the curse on the troop and the reason given by His saying "They are the ones who will burn in the Fire" are from their speech.

It was also said: "This is a troop rushing in with you" is from the speech of the angels, and the curse on the troop and the report that they will burn in the Fire are from the speech of the leading ones who were followed.

They said, that is, the troop: "No welcome for you," a reply to the leaders' curse upon them. Then they mentioned that what they fell into of punishment and burning of the Fire is only by what you cast upon us and adorned for us of disbelief; so it is as if you had brought the punishment or burning forward for us.

Since "no welcome for them" is from the speech of the guardians, the construction did not come as: "They say: rather, these, no welcome for them." Rather it came as the address of the followers to the leaders, so that the confrontation would be with those whom they could not confront in the world with something ugly that would heal their chests, since they caused their disbelief, and more painful to the leaders.

"So wretched is the abode": that is, the Fire; this is the intended meaning, and the supplication is like His saying: "Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister" [al-A'raf: 38]. The followers did not suffice with returning the curse on their leaders, nor with confronting them by saying: "You brought it upon us," until they asked Allah to increase their leaders double the Fire. The meaning: whoever compelled us to evil deeds until our reward became the Fire, "so increase for him the punishment double," as came in the saying of the followers: "Our Lord, give them" [al-Ahzab: 68], that is, their masters, "double the punishment" [al-Ahzab: 68], "Our Lord, these misled us, so give them a double punishment of the Fire" [al-A'raf: 38].

[p. 407] Since the leaders were themselves misguided and misled their followers, it was fitting that they be called upon to be given double punishment, as in the saying: "Upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection." On this reading, the pronoun in His saying (qalu, "they said") refers to the followers.

﴿Whoever brought this upon us﴾ refers to the leaders. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: "﴿They say: Our Lord...﴾ up to the end is the speech of all the people of the Fire." al-Dahhak said: "﴿Whoever brought this upon us﴾ is Iblis and Qabil (Cain)." Ibn Mas'ud said: "The double punishment is snakes and scorpions."

(And they said), that is, the nobles of the disbelievers: ﴿What is wrong with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the wicked?﴾ That is, the lowly ones who have no good in them and who are not upon our religion, just as He said: ﴿And we see no one following you except those who are our lowest (arazil)﴾ [Hud: 27].

It is related that those among the disbelievers of the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) who spoke these words were Abu Jahl, Umayya ibn Khalaf, and the people of the well (al-qalib). Those they did not see were Ammar, Suhayb, Salman, and those who went their way. This was said by Mujahid and others. It is said that they would ask: "Where is Ammar? Where is Suhayb? Where is so-and-so?" They counted them among the weak Muslims, and it would be said to them: "Those are in Paradise (al-Firdaws)."

al-Nahwiyyan (the two grammarians, i.e., al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'? the reading is attributed to the two Kufan/Basran grammarians named in the source) and Hamza recited (ittakhadhnahum) with continuous pronunciation (wasl). Abu Hatim, al-Zamakhshari, and Ibn Atiyya said: it is an attributive (sifah) to rijal (men). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Like His saying: ﴿We used to count them among the wicked﴾." Ibn al-Anbari said: it is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: "and we had taken them."

Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, al-Hasan, Qatada, and the rest of the seven readers recited it with the interrogative hamza (a-ittakhadhnahum), to make them confront themselves with this, in a manner of rebuke and regret. That is: "Did we take them as objects of ridicule (sikhriyyan), when that was not the case?" Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) and his companions, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-A'raj, Nafi', Hamza, and al-Kisa'i recited (sukhriyyan) with a dammah on the sin, and its meaning is from al-sukhrah (servitude) and al-istikhdam (employment). al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Isa, Ibn Muhaysin, and the rest of the seven recited it with a kasrah on the sin, and its meaning is the well-known one of al-sukhr, which is mockery (al-huzu'). The poet said:

"There came to me a tongue by which I am not gladdened,
from a height, in which there is no lie and no mockery (sakhar)."

It is also said that with the kasrah it means from al-taskhir (subjugation).

As for "am" (or): if ittakhadhnahum is an interrogative, either with its hamza stated explicitly as in the reading of those who recited thus, or understood as interrogative with the hamza elided for indication, then "am" is apparently a connecting (muttasilah) particle, since the hamza precedes it. The meaning is: which of the two actions did we perform toward them, taking them in mockery, or disdaining and belittling them? And "our eyes were rising above them and passing over them."

It may be an interrogative in the sense of denial directed at themselves, for both mockery and deviation (of gaze). al-Hasan said: "All of that they did: they took them as objects of ridicule, and their eyes turned away from them, belittling them."

And if ittakhadhnahum is not an interrogative, then "am" is disjunctive (munqati'ah). It is also permissible for it to be disjunctive even with an interrogative preceding it, as in your saying: "Is Zayd with you, or is 'Amr with you?" You asked about Zayd, then turned away from that and asked about 'Amr. So the implied meaning is: "Rather, the eyes have turned away from them." It is also permissible that their saying ﴿Or have our eyes turned away from them?﴾ is connected to their saying ﴿What is wrong with us that we do not see men﴾, because the first interrogation indicated the absence of seeing them, and that is evidence that they were not with him. Then they allowed that they might have been with him, but their eyes did not see them.

﴿Indeed, that﴾, that is, the exchange which We have related from them, ﴿is truly (la-haqqun)﴾, that is: established and certain, which must occur among them.

The majority read ﴿mukhasamatu﴾ with a raf' (nominative) and in construct with Ahl (people). Ibn Atiyya said: it is a substitute (badal) for (la-haqqun). al-Zamakhshari said: he explains what it is, saying: ﴿mukhasamatu﴾ with tanwin, and (Ahlu) in the nominative, governed by the verbal noun with tanwin. al-Farra' does not permit this, but Sibawayh and the Basran grammarians permit it.

Ibn Abi Abla read ﴿mukhasamata ahli﴾ with a fathah on the mim and a kasrah on Ahl. al-Zamakhshari said: this is an attributive (sifah) to "that," because demonstrative nouns are described by common nouns.

In the Kitab al-Lawami' (a book of grammatical readings): "If ﴿mukhasamata ahli al-nar﴾ were read with a fathah, it would be permissible as a substitute for "that."

Ibn al-Sumayqa read ﴿mukhasama﴾ as a past verb, with (Ahlu) as its subject. He (Exalted is He) named that exchange which took place between the leaders of the disbelievers and their followers "a dispute (takhasum)," because their saying ﴿There is no welcome for them﴾ and the followers' saying ﴿Rather, you—there is no welcome for you﴾ belong to the category of disputation. So He called the whole exchange a dispute, because it was used in that sense.

(Say): O Muhammad, ﴿I am only a warner﴾, that is, a warner of the polytheists of the punishment, and that Allah—there is no god but Allah, He has no rival and no partner, and He is the One, the Subduer of everything, and that He is the Owner of the world, its high and its low, [p. 408] the Mighty who cannot be overcome, the Forgiving to those who believe in Him and follow His religion.

This is part 1 of 2 of the commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 38, verses 49–66.

﴿This is a reminder. And indeed, for the righteous is an excellent place of return,﴾ ﴿gardens of perpetual residence, whose gates are opened for them,﴾ ﴿reclining therein, calling therein for abundant fruit and drink.﴾ ﴿And with them will be women restraining their gazes, of equal age.﴾ ﴿This is what you were promised for the Day of Reckoning.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which will have no end.﴾ ﴿This is so. And indeed, for the transgressors is an evil place of return:﴾ ﴿Hell, which they will burn in, so wretched is the resting place.﴾ ﴿This, so let them taste it: scalding water and dark, cold liquid,﴾ ﴿and other punishments of similar kind, in pairs.﴾ ﴿This is a troop rushing in with you; no welcome for them. They will surely burn in the Fire.﴾ ﴿They will say, "Rather, it is you; no welcome for you! You brought this upon us, so wretched is the abode."﴾ ﴿They will say, "Our Lord, whoever brought this upon us, increase for him the punishment double in the Fire."﴾ ﴿And they will say, "What is wrong with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the wicked?﴾ ﴿Did we take them in mockery, or have our eyes turned away from them?"﴾ ﴿Indeed, that is true: the disputing of the people of the Fire.﴾ ﴿Say, "I am only a warner, and there is no deity except Allah, the One, the Subduer,﴾ ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, the Mighty, the Forgiving."﴾

(p-404) When Allah commanded him to be patient with the foolishness of his people, and mentioned a number of the prophets and their circumstances, He mentioned what the state of the believers and the disbelievers will lead to in terms of recompense, and the abode of each of the two groups. Since what He mentions is a kind of revelation, He said: "This is a reminder," as if He separated what came before it from what came after it. Do you not see that when He mentioned the people of Paradise and followed it with mention of the people of the Fire, He said: "This. And indeed, for the transgressors..."?

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "This is the mention of those prophets who have passed." It was also said: "This is a reminder," meaning: it is an honor by which you will be mentioned forever.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "jannāti" (gardens) in the accusative, and it is a substitute (badal). If ʿAdn (Eden) is a proper noun, then it is a definite substitute from an indefinite; and if it is indefinite, then it is an indefinite substitute from an indefinite.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Jannāti ʿadnin" is definite, due to His saying: "Gardens of perpetual residence which the Most Merciful has promised" [Maryam: 61]; and its accusative is as an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to "ḥusna maʾāb" (an excellent place of return), and "mufattaḥatan" (opened) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and its operator is what is in "al-muttaqīn" of the meaning of a verb. In "mufattaḥatan" there is a pronoun referring to the gardens, and "al-abwāb" (the gates) is a substitute from the pronoun, its estimate being: "opened, they are the gates," as in their saying: "Zayd was struck, the hand and the foot," and this is from substitution of part of the whole (badal al-ishtimal). End of quotation.

It is not necessary that "jannāti ʿadnin" be definite by the evidence he relied upon, namely His saying: "Gardens of perpetual residence which," [Maryam: 61]; for he believed that "allatī" is an adjective of "jannāti ʿadnin," and what he mentioned is not necessary, since it is permissible that "allatī" be a substitute from "jannāti ʿadnin." Do you not see that "alladhī" and "allatī" and their plurals are used as nouns, and so they follow the operators, and it does not necessarily follow that they are adjectives? As for its accusative as an explanatory apposition, that is not permissible; for the grammarians have two positions on this: one of them is that this only occurs in definites, so explanatory apposition follows only a definite; this is the position of the Basrans. The second is that it is permissible for it to occur in indefinites, so explanatory apposition may follow an indefinite, just as a definite may follow a definite in it; this is the position of the Kufans, and al-Farisi followed them.

As for their differing in indefiniteness and definiteness, no one has held this except this author. He permitted that in His saying: "The station of Ibrahim" [al-Baqarah: 125], parsing it as an explanatory apposition following an indefinite, namely "āyātun bayyinātun" [al-Baqarah: 99], while "maqām Ibrahim" [al-Baqarah: 125] is definite; and we have refuted him on this in its place in Al ʿImran.

As for his saying: "In 'mufattaḥatan' there is a pronoun referring to the gardens," the majority of grammarians parsed "al-abwāb" as a deputy subject (nāʾib fāʿil). Abu ʿAli came and said: If that is so, there is no pronoun returning to "jannāti ʿadnin" either in the circumstantial clause, if "mufattaḥatan" is parsed as a ḥāl, or in the adjectival clause, if it is parsed as an adjective of "jannāti ʿadnin." So he said: "In 'mufattaḥatan' there is a pronoun returning to the gardens, so that the circumstantial clause is linked to its referent, or the adjective to its modified noun, and 'al-abwāb' is a substitute." He said: whoever parses "al-abwāb" as a deputy subject, the returning pronoun to the gardens is omitted, its estimate being: "the gates of them." Abu ʿAli held that a substitute in such a case must have a pronoun, either pronounced or estimated. And when the sentence needs one estimate, it is preferable to one that needs two. As for the Kufans, the linking element for them is "al" (the definite article), because it takes the place of the pronoun, so it is as if he said: "opened for them are its gates."

As for his saying: "It is from substitution of part of the whole," if by "his saying" he means "the hand and the foot," then it is a mistake; rather, it is a substitution of part from whole (badal baʿḍ min kull). If he means "al-abwāb," then it may be correct, because the gates of the gardens are not part of the gardens.

As for his likening what he estimated from "mufattaḥatan hiya al-abwāb" to "Zayd was struck, the hand and the foot," its basis is that "al-abwāb" is a substitute from that hidden pronoun, just as "the hand and the foot" is a substitute from the apparent noun which is Zayd. Abu Ishaq said, and Ibn ʿAtiyya followed him: "Mufattaḥatan" is an adjective of "jannāti ʿadnin." Al-Hawfi said: "Mufattaḥatan" is a circumstantial clause, and its operator is an omitted verb indicated by the meaning, its estimate being: "they enter them." Zayd ibn ʿAli, ʿAbdullah ibn Rufayʿ, and Abu Haywa read: "Jannātu ʿadnin mufattaḥatun" with nominative case for both, as subject and predicate, or each of them is a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "it is the gardens of Eden, they are opened."

Al-Witakaʾ (reclining) is among the conditions of the people of felicity. "Yadʿūna fīhā" (calling therein) indicates that they have with them one whom they employ in what they request, as in His saying: "And there will circulate among them eternal youths" [al-Insan: 19].

Since the description of fruit varies in abundance, and its abundance is by the variety of its kinds, and the abundance of each kind; and since drink is one kind, which is wine, it was made singular.

"And with them are women restraining their gazes." Qatadah said: its meaning is "upon their husbands." "Atrāb" means: equals in one age; and its origin in the sons of Adam is that the dust touched their bodies at one time, and peers are more firmly established in mutual affection. The apparent meaning is that this description applies among themselves; it was also said: among their husbands, their ages are like theirs. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he means the human women. The author of al-Ghuniyan said: they are the ḥūr (wide-eyed maidens).

Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read: "wa-hādhā mā yūʿadūna" with the third person (yā' al-ghayba), since before it is "wa-ʿindahum"; and the rest of the seven read with the second person (tāʾ al-khiṭāb) by iltifat (shift of person), and the meaning: this is what the promise was made for, for the Day of Recompense.

"Inna hādhā": that is, what was mentioned for the righteous of what preceded, "la-rizquna," lasting forever, that is, it has no end.

"This, and indeed for the transgressors is an evil place of return." Al-Zajjaj said: that is, the matter is this. Abu ʿAli said: this is for the believers. Abu al-Baqa said: a subject with omitted predicate, or a predicate with omitted subject. The transgressors here are the disbelievers. Al-Jubba'i said: the people of major sins, whether they were disbelievers or not.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning is those who transgressed against Me and denied My messengers; for them is an evil place of return, that is, a place of return and destination.

"So wretched is the resting place": that is, "hādhā" is in the place of nominative case as subject whose predicate is "jahannam" (Hell), "wa-ghassāq," or a predicate of an omitted subject, that is, the punishment is this; and "ḥamīm" is the predicate of a subject, or in the place of accusative by the mode of occupation (ishtighāl), that is: "let them taste this, so let them taste it, scalding water," that is: it is scalding water, or an omitted-predicate subject, that is: from it is scalding water and from it is dark liquid, as the poet said:

"Until, when dawn shone in darkness, and the herbs were left, twisted and mown."

That is: from it is twisted, and from it is mown. These parsings are reported as sayings. It was also said: "hādhā" is the subject, and "fa-l-yadhūqūhu" is the predicate, and this is according to al-Akhfash's permission of it, such as: "Zayd, so strike him," citing the poet's words:

"And a sayer said: Khawlan, so marry their maidens."
